**СТР. 13 — Reflection (продолжение)**

Part 2: Self and Peer Review — каждый студент выполняет онлайн peer review: оценивает свой вклад и вклад каждого члена команды в team report.
При оценке вкладов учитывать:

- evidence of research completed and contributed
- amount and quality of written contribution
- submission of work in a timely manner
- open two-way productive communication on the LMS team discussion forum
- timely attendance (или virtual) at team meetings, agreed by the team
- willingness to take part in team discussions, present ideas or solutions
- level of cooperation to decisions agreed by the team
- any collaborative issue important to the team’s effectiveness
  Цель: объективно оценить собственный уровень участия и каждого члена команды в период Team Report (идеи, качество работы, частота встреч и коммуникации на LMS, своевременность по стандарту team contract). Self and peer review виден только маркеру, не делится с командой (конфиденциальность).

GUIDELINES FOR SUCCESS: оценка по presentation style и professional appearance. Нужно показать, что усвоил и можешь применить теории организационного поведения к личному опыту. Визуальные средства (напр. PowerPoint slides) не использовать. Тайминг строгий — штрафы за превышение 3.5 минут. При self/peer evaluation — без личной предвзятости (позитивной/негативной), оценивать только перформанс (навык, нужный выпускникам в performance evaluations).

HOW TO SUBMIT: видео в формате .mp4 или .mov (неверный формат → может не открыться → ноль баллов). Загрузка занимает время — не оставлять на последний момент. Имя файла: Unit Code, Assessment Task, Surname, First Initial, Student number. Пример: BUS293IRRSpencerC12345678. Сохранять копию. Peer review — через tool на LMS.

**СЛАЙД 9 — Survival on the Moon Stage 1 (5 minutes)**
INDIVIDUALLY rank the 15 items listed in the exercise according to their importance to an individual's survival.

**СЛАЙД 10 — Survival on the Moon Stage 2 (15 minutes)**
IN TEAMS reach a consensus on the rank order of each of the 15 items. Survival depends on the team's ability to AGREE on the importance of these items, as well as logical explanation of their value and how to use them.

**СЛАЙД 11 — Survival on the Moon Stage 3 (5 minutes)**

- Compare your team AND individual rankings with the expert rankings.
- Compute your team and individual scores.
- Example: For the 'food item' you ranked it as 5, the team ranked it as 2, the experts ranked it as 3. Your score is the difference between 5 and 3 (2). The team score is the difference between 2 and 3 (1).
- Complete this for every item, then add up for yourself, and for the team.

**СЛАЙД 12 — Survival on the Moon — Discussion Questions (15 minutes)**
(Заголовок и подзаголовок; конкретные вопросы на слайде не вынесены текстом.)

**СЛАЙД 13 — Декоративный** (крупный знак «?», футер «BUS293 Murdoch University»). Пропускаю.

**СЛАЙД 14 — Critical Thinking Questions (раздел)**
McShane and Glinow. (2024) Chapter 1, Questions 1, 5, and 8.

**СЛАЙД 15 — Chapter 1, Question 1**
A friend suggest that organisational behaviour courses are useful only to people who will enter management careers. Discuss the accuracy of your friends statement.

**СЛАЙД 16 — Ch1 Q1 (LO 1-2)**

- OB is useful for anyone who works in an organisation
- They will need to work as an individual, in groups and teams, or in an organisation with people at all levels and from other countries.
- Everyone need to understand how people think and feel and what they do in and around organisations.
- OB explains employee behaviour, decisions, perceptions and emotional responses at multiple levels AND how organisations interact with the external environment.
- This knowledge and understanding can help everyone get things done while conducting business.

_Speaker notes (Слайд 16):_ This chapter explains that although technical skills and knowledge are important in many occupations, the skills and knowledge that employers tend to rank above anything else are the topics associated with organisational behaviour, such as problem-solving, teamwork, communicating, and adaptability/initiative. In addition to helping students acquire these valuable skills and knowledge foundations, organisational behaviour helps students to adopt better personal theories to understand, predict, and influence organisational events. By adopting better personal theories, we are able to make more accurate sense of what goes on around us and are better able to coordinate our work objectives with coworkers and other organisational stakeholders. In other words, OB knowledge helps us to get things done more effectively in organisations. The above benefits of OB lead to a key principle in this book, namely that OB is for everyone who works in and around organisations. Although managers may require OB knowledge more intensively, people in all jobs ultimately require the skills that employers seek out, and people need to develop more accurate personal theories of why events and behaviour occur in organisational settings.

**СЛАЙД 17 — Chapter 1, Question 5**
Most companies actively hire and retain employees with diverse backgrounds, particular race, ethnicity, gender, disability, and sexual orientation. Based on this ongoing effort, many claim their organisation is an inclusive workplace. Explain why the existence of a diverse workforce differs from an inclusive workplace.

**СЛАЙД 18 — Ch1 Q5 (LO 1-4)**

- There is surface level diversity (observable and overt differences) and deep level diversity (such as differences in beliefs, values and attitudes)
- Employing a diverse workforce isn't enough to have an inclusive workplace.
- An inclusive workplace values people of all identities and allows them to be fully themselves while contributing to the organisation.
- An inclusive workplace gives diverse groups voice through formal structures such as diversity councils and in everyday processes such as in teams and casual gatherings and representation

_Speaker notes (Слайд 18):_ Workforce diversity differs from an inclusive workforce. Diversity refers to the characteristics (typically surface-level, but potentially also deep-level) of employees, whereas an inclusive workforce refers to how well the organisation values diversity and allows people of all identities to be fully themselves while contributing to the organisation. This distinction is evident when people in some groups are not given the opportunity to fully participate in the organisation due to their diversity characteristics. It also occurs when people of a particular group (ethnicity, sexual orientation, etc.) are members of the organisation, but their self-concept needs to be suppressed to actively participate. In other words, diversity refers only to the demographics or more subtle characteristics of the organisation. An inclusive workplace is an ongoing process that enables people of all backgrounds to feel psychologically safe, engaged, valued, authentic, listened to, and respected. For example, an inclusive workplace monitors organisational systems to ensure that they do not unfairly differentiate or discriminate against people with some forms of diversity.

**СЛАЙД 19 — Chapter 1, Question 8**
Automatic and several other businesses (e.g., Emisoft, Gitlab) are completely remote (distributed) companies. Everyone who works for these firms performs their jobs from homes and cafes. In your opinion will distributed companies become more common in the future? Why or Why not? Would you prefer working in a remote company with no physical location, maybe just an occasional gathering of staff at a conference venue setting? Or would you prefer working with co-workers face-to-face most days at a company site?

**СЛАЙД 20 — Ch1 Q8 (LO 1-4)**

- Remote work potentially benefits both employers and employees.
- Not suitable for all roles.
- Employees – potentially better work life integration but when appropriate space is unavailable at home it can be difficult.
- Enables employees to continue working during incidents such as bad weather or pandemic.
- Research indicates general higher productivity. Likely due to less stress, travel time and travel costs.
- Lower real estate costs for employers

_Speaker notes (Слайд 20):_ The viability of completely remote organisations touches on the issues at Yahoo and other companies that reduced or completely withdrew employee opportunities for remote work. But there is also plenty of writing about the success of Automattic and a few other completely remote companies. Some job and organisational features that are important for remote work are even more critical for entirely remote organisations. Things to consider: Do remote firms require leadership skills that are difficult to develop. Do people need more social integration than occurs in remote firms or remote work. Does the average employee perform better under guidance (or close watch) of a "manager" rather than working autonomously from home. Are remote companies more viable in some knowledge work businesses than in others. Consider how employees interact with customers and other external stakeholders. Consider how the confidentiality of information used by staff might limit the viability of remote work and organisations. Do financial arrangements—from salaries to financial benefits—get too complex in completely remote companies, particularly where employees are located in several countries (or would global remote firms simply shift to contract-based workers). Can remote companies overcome or manage the potentially heightened conflict and misunderstanding that tends to occur when staff rely on leaner communication channels (text messaging, online chat, etc.). Regarding preferences for working in remote organisations, a variety of personal characteristics and conditions are likely to be considered. Personal characteristics associated with personality, values, past experiences, and so forth may include: High self-motivation; High self-organisation; High need for autonomy; Good skill with information technology; Able to fulfill their social needs outside work.

**СЛАЙД 21 — Class Exercise (раздел)**
McShane and Von Glinow. (2024) – IT ALL MAKES SENSE.
Футер: Cassandra Spencer · BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour · Topic One.

**СЛАЙД 22 — Class Exercise (Chpt1 P34)** — утверждения TRUE/FALSE (часть 1)

1. A happy worker is a productive worker. TRUE/FALSE
2. A decision maker's effectiveness increases with the number of choices or alternatives available to them. TRUE/FALSE
3. Organisations are more effective when they minimise conflict among employees. TRUE/FALSE
4. Employees have more power with many close friends than with many acquaintances. TRUE/FALSE
5. Companies are more successful when they have strong corporate cultures. TRUE/FALSE

**СЛАЙД 23 — Class Exercise (Chpt1 P34)** — утверждения TRUE/FALSE (часть 2) 6. Employees perform better without stress. TRUE/FALSE 7. The best way to change people and organisations is by pinpointing the source of the current problems. TRUE/FALSE 8. Female leaders involve employees in decisions to a greater degree than do male leaders. TRUE/FALSE 9. The best decisions are made without emotion. TRUE/FALSE 10. If employees feel they are paid unfairly, nothing other than changing their pay will reduce their feelings of injustice. TRUE/FALSE

**СЛАЙД 24 — Class Exercise: IT ALL MAKES SENSE (ответы)**

1. A happy worker is a productive worker. — True, to some extent. Research indicates job satisfaction has a moderately strong association with job [performance]. See Chapter 4.
2. A decision maker's effectiveness increases with the number of choices… — FALSE. At some point as alternatives increase, the decision maker becomes less efficient and effective in choosing among them. See Chapter 7.
3. Organisations are more effective when they minimise conflict… — FALSE. Dominant OB research indicates constructive (task-oriented) conflict is often beneficial (e.g. in decision making). See Chapter 11.
4. Employees have more power with many close friends than acquaintances. — FALSE. Social network research: people with many acquaintances tend to have more career success and related outcomes than those with mainly close friends. See Chapter 10.
5. Companies are more successful with strong corporate cultures. — FALSE. There is a weak relationship between corporate culture strength and organisational performance. See Chapter 14.
6. Employees perform better without stress. — FALSE. Some level of stress is essential for life; we need a certain level to energise us. See Chapter 4.
7. The best way to change people/orgs is by pinpointing the source of current problems. — FALSE. Emerging knowledge suggests a positive rather than problem-focused approach may be more effective in many/most circumstances. See Chapter 5.
8. Female leaders involve employees in decisions more than male leaders. — [Answer: TRUE.] Men and women are mostly similar in leadership styles; female leaders involve employees in decisions to a greater degree. Generally female leaders are more participative. See Chapter 12.
9. The best decisions are made without emotion. — FALSE. All decisions involve and require emotion; without it people can't recognise problems/opportunities or make choices. See Chapter 7.
10. If employees feel paid unfairly, nothing other than changing pay reduces injustice. — FALSE. Underpaid employees might reduce injustice by working less, taking nonmonetary resources, or quitting. See Chapter 5.

_Speaker notes (Слайд 24):_ [Расширенные пояснения к каждому пункту.] 1) TRUE, to some extent — latest research: job satisfaction has a moderately strong association with job performance (correlation ~0.30); see Chapter 4. 2) FALSE — when alternatives become very large, decision makers reduce motivation to decide and may avoid the decision; they process a finite amount of information; see Chapter 7. 3) FALSE — constructive (task-oriented) conflict often beneficial, relationship conflict has negative consequences; but constructive conflict can generate relationship conflict (hard to separate); Chapter 11. 4) FALSE — "weak ties" (acquaintances) give less redundant social capital, unique information (expert power), unique connections/opportunities (referent power), wider visibility; strong ties give faster but redundant resources; Chapter 10. 5) FALSE — "it depends"; weak relationship between culture strength and performance for three reasons: strong culture problematic when values inconsistent with environment; can blind employees to other perspectives; suppresses dissenting values important for future change; Chapter 14. 6) FALSE — some stress essential to energise us; problem is stress beyond the beneficial level; Chapter 4. 7) FALSE — dominant model identifies problem before solutions; emerging knowledge favours a positive approach; strengths-based coaching/feedback (Chapter 5); focusing on weaknesses creates defensiveness; appreciative inquiry introduced in Chapter 15. 8) TRUE — debate about whether men/women lead differently; mostly similar (end of Chapter 12), one exception: female leaders involve employees in decisions more; generally more participative. 9) FALSE — all decisions involve and require emotion; people form emotionally anchored preferences before consciously thinking; rational evaluation must be processed by emotional centre(s) to make a choice (Chapter 7; noted in Chapters 3, 4, 5); distinct from "getting emotional." 10) FALSE — people play "mind games" to avoid overreward inequity; underrewarded employees may work less, take nonmonetary resources, change the comparison other, or leave the field (quit); injustice is affected by procedures as much as distribution — reduced by allowing appeals, considering all information, treating people with respect, and giving voice; Chapter 5.

**СЛАЙД 25 — Case Study Questions (раздел)**
McShane and Von Glinow. (2024) — WYE & VALVE PLUMBING: A MARS DIAGNOSTIC EXERCISE (Page 32).
Футер: Cassandra Spencer · BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour · Topic One.

**СЛАЙД 26 — Case Study Question**
Diagnose W&V's customer service issues and discuss specific ways the retailer can improve customer service at the company. The discussion should explain whether and in what ways each MARS element can guide better customer service. All four elements of the MARS model should be considered.
_(Фреймворк: MARS model = Motivation, Ability, Role perceptions, Situational factors.)_

**СЛАЙД 27 — Case Study: M for Motivation**
Diagnosis: Lack of motivation by some (most?) of W&V staff seems a major cause of poor customer service. Staff generally do not actively volunteer information or recommendations even though customers value it. Some low motivation could stem from situational factors (difficult physical layout reduces motivation to retrieve parts). Role perceptions could be another reason (staff unaware it's important). But lack of motivation seems a factor beyond these — likely employees don't care about customer satisfaction (know it's their duty but don't engage). Possible counter-motivational influences such as status-like behaviour over DIY clients, or norms where staff aren't encouraged to improve service. No information on how staff are financially rewarded, though targeted performance rewards aren't always necessary. Overall, motivation is a strong explanation for poor service.
Recommendations: (1) Alter store norms so customer service is continually highlighted (beyond role perceptions — like a corporate-culture value; employees eventually engage in desired behaviours or seek work elsewhere). (2) More carefully recruit/hire people whose values and natural customer-service skills exceed current staff (motivation is influenced by personality/values, hard to change). (3) Incentivise employees through bonuses based on customer-service skills and feedback — treat cautiously, as financial rewards can have unintended consequences and may discourage non-rewarded activities.

**СЛАЙД 28 — Case Study: A for Ability**
Diagnosis: Many staff have industry experience and receive regular training on new products/techniques, so a large percentage can answer almost all DIY queries and most tradesperson questions (at least knowing existence/whereabouts of specialised parts). Overall, some specific staff may lack sufficient ability for specific issues (especially serving tradespeople), but ability is NOT a major factor in the service issues W&V is trying to resolve.
Recommendations: Although most staff have sufficient ability, identify specific staff uncomfortable with low-level plumbing knowledge and/or W&V's products. These people might receive better training or be moved to secondary roles such as (re)stocking shelves and cashiering.

**СЛАЙД 29 — Case Study: R for Role Perceptions**
Diagnosis: Knowledge/skills don't translate into awareness of required work behaviours — staff may have poor role perceptions about appropriate behaviour toward clients. They can answer questions but show a lack of initiative to answer respectfully. Employees assume customers know what parts/tools they need — further evidence of poor role perceptions (inaccurate perceptions of customer needs). Some staff may not realise they need to be more proactive and provide supplies that take more effort to retrieve. May require further investigation but likely means staff need customer-service training to improve role perceptions. Some staff may be ill-suited to retail work as they don't view serving customers politely as part of their role.
Recommendations: Introduce customer-service training that makes staff aware of specific role behaviours needed; include behaviour modelling and sessions where staff hear candid customer feedback. Emphasise proactive, respectful behaviour (effect of lost accounts, how competitors excelled in customer experience). The learning process should help staff realise specific behaviours (proactively approaching customers, showing empathy and friendliness, etc.) are important to their jobs and company success.

**СЛАЙД 30 — Case Study: S for Situational Factors**
Diagnosis: Staff are particularly inhospitable when asked for specialised parts only staff can retrieve; retrieving requires effort. Thousands of parts, many retrievable only by staff behind the main customer desk. May require further investigation, but suggests the layout of supplies hampers good service — challenge locating specific parts, cumbersome physical area, or many similar parts to bring and restock. The physical layout may be an impediment to effective customer service.
Recommendations: Investigate store layout for more efficient display/restocking. Alternatively, divide staff so some retrieve/restock specialised behind-counter parts, while those most knowledgeable about trade practices and with strong service presentation skills work in the front area. Behind-counter staff become more proficient at retrieving/restocking even if not plumbing experts.

**СЛАЙД 31 — For Next Week** (иконочные блоки)

- 📚 Complete the required readings
- 🎙 Watch the lecture podcast
- ✍ PREPARE ANSWERS TO THE WORKSHOP QUESTIONS!
- 💬 Let me know if you won't be able to attend as group formation for the team report will occur in next week's class

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-01-Introduction/Topic_1_Podcast_Transcript.md

Связь: [[Topic 1 — Intro]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Hi, and welcome to BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour. This unit provides an
overview of the different dynamics of individual and group behaviour in organisations
and explores, organisational theories and management processes. The first topic is an
introduction to organisational behaviour, which will define organisational behaviour and
explain its importance, introduce four perspectives of organisational effectiveness, and
discuss challenges and changes to the field of organisational behaviour.
Organisations have existed since the beginning of time and are defined as “people
working together to achieve a common goal or purpose” and they are not just for-profit
businesses. Throughout history, craftspeople and merchants have formed guilds to
achieve common purposes. Large-scale irrigation projects in Egypt and Mesopotamia,
and the building of ancient temples, required the organisation and coordination of
massive numbers of people. And organisations continue to exist because of the synergy
created through this effective division of labour – through humans being able to achieve
more as a team than as individuals.
Organisational Behaviour is the study of what people, as individuals and groups, think,
feel, and do in and around organisations. It is examined on three levels, the individual
level, the work group level, and the organisational level. The purpose is to apply this
knowledge to improve the organisations performance through the management of
human behaviour.
The effectiveness, or performance of the organisation, was traditionally gauged on how
well it achieved its stated goals or objectives. However, if a company achieved goals or
sales targets that were set too low, or weren’t relevant to the current industry, economic,
or social environment, this still wouldn’t result in success. Now, organisations are seen as
effective if they have a good fit with their external environment, are a learning
organisation, have efficient and adaptive internal subsystems, and satisfy their
stakeholders.
The open systems perspective is the foremost method of thinking about organisations
and their interactions with the external environment. It describes the organisation as a
complex organism that uses inputs from the external environment, like raw materials,
human resources, information, financial resources, and equipment, and transforms them
through all the interdependent organisational subsystems, into outputs that are then put
back into the external environment. These outputs can include products or services,
shareholder dividends, community support and services, and waste and pollution. Some
organisational outputs, such as dividends, services, and community support, are valued
by the external environment, but others, like pollution and employee layoffs, are seen as
less desirable, and throughout this process those evaluations are received as feedback by
the organisation. Organisations also receive feedback about the availability of inputs such
as skilled labour shortages, or changing population demographics, and through this
combined feedback have the opportunity to adjust their subsystems, and thus the
behaviours in the organisation, to ‘fit’ and continue to be effective in the changing
external environment. The other perspectives on organisational effectiveness can be
explained in relation to the open systems perspective.
An input that is occasionally looked over in the open systems perspective is knowledge.
The organisational learning perspective suggests the effectiveness of an organisation
depends on the organisations ability to acquire, share, use, and store valuable knowledge.
Knowledge is seen as a resource, or asset, called intellectual capital, and it exists in three
forms.
Human capital is the stock of knowledge, skills, and abilities among employees that
provide economic value to the organisation. It is valuable and rare, as employees are
essential for organisational survival and success, and talented people are difficult to find
and replicate. Human capital cannot easily be replaced by technology and is thus a
competitive advantage and a huge risk, as when people leave the organisation their
knowledge goes with them.
Structural capital is what would remain if every employee left the organisation and is
embedded in organisations systems and structures. It includes documentation of work
procedures, physical layout of the production line, and finished products that can be
reverse engineered.
Finally, relationship capital is the value of an organisations’ relationships with its
suppliers, customers, and other stakeholders. This includes the goodwill and brand image
of the organisation.
An organisations intellectual capital develops and is maintained through the four
organisational learning processes of Acquiring knowledge, Sharing knowledge, Using
knowledge, and Storing knowledge.
The High-Performance Work Practices perspective of organisational effectiveness looks
closely at the transformational subsystems of the open systems perspective and suggests
four work practices that improve effectiveness. Although each of these practices will
improve effectiveness, they have a stronger effect when bundled together. They are
employee involvement in decision making, employee autonomy, employee development,
and rewards valued by employees linked with performance and skill development. These
practices improve organisational effectiveness by improving individual employee
performance, increasing organisational adaptability to changing external environments,
and improving employee motivation and job satisfaction.
The stakeholder perspective of organisational effectiveness expands on the external
environment aspect of the open systems perspective. It identifies specific people and
groups that affect, or are affected by, the organisations objectives and actions, and
recognises that stakeholder relations are dynamic. This perspective incorporates values,
ethics, and corporate social responsibility, and in general, organisations are more
effective when they satisfy stakeholder needs and expectations.
The increasing focus on corporate social responsibility is one of the current challenges
facing organisations. The concept of corporate social responsibility is that an
organisation has a responsibility to the society in which it operates, and it should be
sustainable, not just as a going concern in continuing to profit, but also in ensuring that it
meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to
meet their own needs. Managers are therefore challenged to ensure that all their inputs,
social, environmental, and financial are used in a way that all stakeholders receive value
and that the resources required by future generations are not exploited.
Technological change is another challenge facing organisations. It has always been a
disruptive force in organisations and society, boosting productivity but displacing
employees and sometimes making entire occupational groups obsolete. Other
technologies have altered our relationships and patterns of behaviour with co-workers
and stakeholders, like the introduction of the internet, smartphones, email, social media,
and data analytics. These new technologies have both positive and negative impacts on
organisations and the people within them, facilitating ease in communication and
networking, yet tethering people to their jobs for longer hours, reducing work-life
balance, and increasing techno-stress.
Globalisation is the increasing interconnectedness to other countries and cultures
through liberalisation of trade and immigration policies and the ability to communicate
using new forms of technology. It benefits organisations through access to larger and new
markets, lower costs of production, and greater access to knowledge and innovation. It
can also have less positive impacts and has been attributed to work intensification, and
the reduction of job security and work-life balance in developed countries. It increases
the complexity of teamwork, diversity, values, organisational structure, leadership, and
other subsystems that impact behaviour in the organisation.
The nature of work is also changing due to globalisation and technology, with knowledge
work increasing. This makes knowledge management and brain drain – where employees
leave jobs and take their knowledge with them – a new area managers need to pay
attention to.
The composition of the workforce is shifting as well, with increasing cultural diversity
through globalisation which impacts leadership, motivation, and decision making. The
population is aging and this changing demographic could mean labour shortages, loss of
organisational memory, and generational differences in terms of values, skills, loyalty,
occupational mobility, and technical skills. Increasing gender equality, with more women
in the workforce, and in senior positions is also altering organisational membership
demographics, as well as breaking down the traditional idea that some jobs are gender
specific.
Employment relationships, and the psychological contract, are another challenging
aspect as flexible work arrangements become standard along with remote work. There is
also the growing casualisation of roles, which promotes flexibility for the organisation
but decreasing job security for employees, and encourages a gig economy. The emerging
gig economy, where people independently contract or freelance for multiple
organisations, also offers increased flexibility for workers, but is criticised as workers do
not receive sick leave, annual leave, or parental leave, and have very little job security.
These challenges change the way managers and organisations need to be, think, and act
in order to succeed and perform effectively. We study organisational behaviour to
understand the dynamics of why things happen in organisations, and to know how to
predict, and manage these events through adjusting the behaviours in and of the
organisation. As organisational behaviour practices are powerful predictors of an
organisations survival and success they are therefore important for both managers and
employees to know and understand.
Thank you.

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-01-Introduction/Topic_1_Workshop_Solution.md

Связь: [[Topic 1 — Intro]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

**BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour**

Topic 1 - Workshop Activities

Murdoch University

Name: Faiaz Dzhafarov  Student No: 35553299

# Activity 1: Unit Guide, Assessments and Expectations

Everything we need for the unit lives on the Learning Management System (LMS, myMurdoch Learning). That includes the Unit Guide and all learning materials: the readings, the lecture podcasts, My Unit Readings, and the assignment submission portals.

The unit is assessed in four parts. There are Online Quizzes (15%), a Team Report (30%), an Individual Reflection and Review worth 15% (a video reflection plus a self and peer review), and the Final Examination (40%).

As for expectations, we are meant to do the required readings, watch the podcasts and have a go at the set questions before each workshop. We should also attend at least 80% of sessions and keep all formal team communication on the LMS team discussion forum.

# Activity 2: Team Activity (Survival on the Moon)

This is a team exercise. Each member first ranks the 15 items on their own, the team then works out a consensus ranking, and both sets of rankings get compared against the expert (NASA) ranking and scored.

What it shows is that teams usually beat the average individual score, thanks to synergy and the division of labour. A group can pool what its members know and get further together than any one person would alone. The catch is that this only happens when people genuinely share information and reach a real consensus. If the team just defers to whoever sounds most confident, the advantage disappears.

# Activity 3: Critical Thinking Questions (Chapter 1, p.31)

## Question 1

A friend suggests that organisational behaviour courses are useful only to people who will enter management careers. Discuss the accuracy of this statement.

We do not think the statement is accurate. Organisational behaviour (OB) is useful for anyone who works in and around organisations, not just managers. Everyone works as an individual, in groups and teams, and within an organisation alongside people at every level and from different countries. So everyone needs some understanding of how people think, feel and behave at work.

OB explains employee behaviour, decisions, perceptions and emotional responses at several levels, and it explains how organisations interact with their external environment. Managers might draw on this knowledge more intensively, but the skills OB develops (problem solving, teamwork, communication and adaptability) are exactly the ones employers rank most highly for all employees. That is why OB helps everyone, not only managers, get things done more effectively at work.

## Question 5

Explain why the existence of a diverse workforce differs from an inclusive workplace.

Diversity is about the characteristics of employees. Those can be surface-level, meaning observable differences such as race, gender or age, or deep-level, meaning differences in beliefs, values and attitudes. Hiring people with diverse backgrounds, on its own, does not create an inclusive workplace.

Inclusion is a different thing. It is about how well the organisation values that diversity and lets people of all identities be fully themselves while still contributing to the organisation. An inclusive workplace is an ongoing process that gives diverse groups a genuine voice. That happens through formal structures such as diversity councils and representation, and through everyday processes such as teams and casual gatherings. The aim is for people to feel psychologically safe, valued, listened to and respected, rather than having to suppress their self-concept just to take part.

## Question 8

Will completely distributed (remote) companies become more common in the future? Which would you prefer, a fully remote company or working face-to-face at a company site?

Distributed companies will probably become more common for a lot of knowledge-work roles, though remote work clearly does not suit every job. The upside cuts both ways. For employees it offers better work-life integration and lets work carry on through disruptions like bad weather or a pandemic, and research generally shows higher productivity because there is less stress and less travel time and cost. Employers, for their part, save on real estate.

There are real limits, though. Remote work is hard when employees do not have suitable space at home, and it brings its own challenges: leadership at a distance, social integration, keeping information confidential, and the extra conflict and misunderstanding that creep in through leaner communication channels. Whether a particular person suits remote work comes down to personal characteristics such as self-motivation, self-organisation, a need for autonomy, decent IT skills, and being able to meet social needs outside work.

Personally, I would go for a hybrid arrangement. It keeps the flexibility and productivity of remote work while still giving you the face-to-face contact that helps communication, relationships and a sense of belonging at work.

# Activity 4: Class Exercise - “It All Makes Sense” (Chapter 1, p.34)

For each statement, here is the answer and the chapter where it is explained.

**1. A happy worker is a productive worker. True, to some extent.** Job satisfaction has a moderately strong association with job performance, around 0.30. (Chapter 4)

**2. A decision maker’s effectiveness increases with the number of alternatives available. False.** Past a certain point, more alternatives actually reduce both the motivation to decide and the quality of the choice. (Chapter 7)

**3. Organisations are more effective when they minimise conflict. False.** Constructive, task-oriented conflict is often a good thing, for example in decision making. (Chapter 11)

**4. Employees have more power with many close friends than many acquaintances. False.** Weak ties (acquaintances) tend to bring more unique information, connections and visibility, and that is linked to greater career success. (Chapter 10)

**5. Companies are more successful when they have strong corporate cultures. False.** The relationship between culture strength and performance is only weak, and strong cultures can blind employees and suppress useful dissent. (Chapter 14)

**6. Employees perform better without stress. False.** We actually need some stress to energise us. The problem is stress beyond the beneficial level. (Chapter 4)

**7. The best way to change people and organisations is by pinpointing the source of current problems. False.** A positive, strengths-based approach is often more effective than zeroing in on problems. (Chapter 5)

**8. Female leaders involve employees in decisions to a greater degree than male leaders. True.** Men and women lead in mostly similar ways, but female leaders are generally more participative. (Chapter 12)

**9. The best decisions are made without emotion. False.** All decisions involve and require emotion. Without it, people cannot recognise problems or make choices at all. (Chapter 7)

**10. If employees feel they are paid unfairly, nothing other than changing their pay will reduce the feeling of injustice. False.** Underpaid employees may also reduce effort, take nonmonetary resources, change their comparison, or quit. Fair procedures and giving people a voice also reduce feelings of injustice. (Chapter 5)

# Activity 5: Case Study - Wye & Valve Plumbing (MARS Diagnostic, Chapter 1, p.32)

The poor customer service at Wye & Valve (W&V) can be diagnosed using the four elements of the MARS model: Motivation, Ability, Role perceptions and Situational factors. We worked through each one in turn.

## M - Motivation (a major cause)

Diagnosis: a lack of motivation looks like a major cause here. Staff generally do not volunteer information or recommendations, even though customers value exactly that, which suggests many of them simply do not care about customer satisfaction.

Recommendations: make customer service an ongoing store norm and cultural value, and recruit people whose values and natural service orientation are stronger than the current staff. Service-linked bonuses are worth considering too, but use them cautiously, since financial rewards can have unintended effects.

## A - Ability (not a major factor)

Diagnosis: ability is not really a major factor. Most staff have industry experience and get regular product training, so they are able to answer most DIY and many trade questions.

Recommendations: identify the few staff who do lack the necessary knowledge and give them further training, or move them into secondary roles such as restocking shelves or cashiering.

## R - Role Perceptions (significant)

Diagnosis: the staff have the knowledge but show poor role perceptions. They lack initiative, are not always respectful, and assume customers already know which parts and tools they need. They do not seem to view proactive, polite service as part of the job.

Recommendations: run customer-service training using behaviour modelling and candid customer feedback, so staff come to understand that proactively approaching customers, showing empathy and being respectful are genuine parts of their role, and matter to the company’s success.

## S - Situational Factors (contributing)

Diagnosis: staff are at their most unhelpful when asked for specialised parts that only they can retrieve from behind the main desk, because fetching them takes effort. That points to the store layout being an impediment to good service.

Recommendations: look into the layout for more efficient display and restocking. Alternatively, split the staff so that some handle behind-counter retrieval and restocking while the most knowledgeable and service-skilled staff work the front area serving customers.

**Conclusion:** The customer-service problems at W&V come down mainly to Motivation and Role perceptions, with Situational (layout) factors contributing, while Ability is largely adequate.



## 📄 02-topics/Topic-02-Team-Dynamics/BUS293_Workshop_2.md

Связь: [[Topic 2 — Team Dynamics]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Workshop 2 (Team Dynamics, Chapter 8), 27 слайдов.

---

**SLIDE 1 — Title**
BUS293 / Organisational Theory and Behaviour / CHAPTER EIGHT / BUS293 Murdoch University / Team Dynamics

**SLIDE 2 — Acknowledgement of Country**
We acknowledge that Murdoch University is situated on the lands of the Whadjuk and Binjareb Noongar people. We pay our respect to their enduring and dynamic culture and the leadership of Noongar elders past and present. The boodjar (country) on which Murdoch University is located has, for thousands of years, been a place of learning. We at Murdoch University are proud to continue this long tradition.

_Speaker notes (Slide 2 / general team theory):_ Under the right conditions teams make better decisions, develop better products and services, and create a more motivated workforce. Individuals are more motivated when working in teams than when working alone because: they develop a bond with their team and are motivated to fulfil the goals of groups; they feel accountable to fellow team members, who monitor performance more closely than a traditional supervisor; they see team members become benchmarks of comparison, motivating them to work harder because of apprehension that their performance will be compared against others'. Two limitations of teams are: **process losses** — resources (including time and energy) expended towards team development and maintenance rather than the task; **social loafing** — this occurs when people exert less effort (and usually perform at a lower level) in teams than when working alone.

**SLIDE 3 — Workshop Two Outline**

- Critical thinking questions (20 minutes)
- Case study questions (20 minutes)
- 5 minute break(?)
- Team Formation (10 minutes)
- Team Meeting (40 minutes)

**SLIDE 4 — Critical Thinking Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow. (2024) Chapter 8, Questions 2, 4, 5, and 8. Page 310.

**SLIDE 5 — Chapter 8 Question 2**
Although teams have limitations, they can also be very effective. Identify three reasons why a team of six students potentially produce a better report for a major course assignment than the average quality of their reports completed individually. Detail the motivational benefits as one reason why teams are potentially better.

**SLIDE 6 — Ch8 Q2 (answer)**

- **Larger pool of expertise:** Teams will have a wider range of expertise/knowledge helping them to discover relevant information more quickly and easily than a student working alone.
- **More hands on deck:** Individuals cannot read through as much content as a team of six students. Although there are challenges of coordinating the work, ultimately a team report will be based on a larger volume of conceptual resources.
- **Potentially higher motivation to prepare the report:** Team members are potentially motivated more when working in teams than when working alone because: each student has high accountability to fellow team members; they feel accountable to fellow team members, who monitor performance more closely; they develop a bond with their team and are motivated to fulfil the goals of groups.

**SLIDE 7 — Chapter 8 Question 4**
Consider the six team roles summarized in 8.6 (page 297). Which two of these best describes your role tendency or role preference in a typical team at school or work. What factors do you think influence a person's role preferences?
ROLES:

- **Organiser** – Structures what the team is doing. Keeps track of team progress and achievements relative to goals and timelines.
- **Doer** – Accepts tasks, reliably completes work, and meets deadlines to ensure team success.
- **Challenger** – Pushes the team to explore all aspects of the situation, consider alternative assumptions, explanations and solutions. Debates, critiques and asks why.
- **Innovator** – Regularly generates new and creative ideas, strategies and approaches.
- **Team Builder** – Establishes norms, supports decisions, maintains a positive ambience. Calms members when stressed and motivates when discouraged.
- **Connector** – Boundary spanner who helps build bridges and connects the team with external stakeholders. Ensures good working relationships between the team and outsiders.

_Speaker notes (Slide 7):_ To discuss the factors influencing a person's role preferences, consider comparing each role with the five-factor personality model and with Schwartz's personal values circumplex (4 quadrants and 10 value categories), page 59.

**SLIDE 8 — Ch8 Q4 (1/2)**
**Schwartz's personal values.** Fifty-seven specific values cluster into 10 broad value categories—further clustered into four quadrants:

- Openness to change – Motivated to pursue innovative ways
- Conservation – Motivated to preserve the status quo
- Self-enhancement – Motivated by self-interest
- Self-transcendence – Motivated to promote the welfare of others and nature
  **Five-Factor Personality Model:**
- Conscientiousness: organized, dependable
- Agreeableness: trusting, helpful, considerate
- Neuroticism: anxious, insecure, depressed, temperamental
- Openness to experience: imaginative, creative, unconventional, curious
- Extraversion: outgoing, talkative, energetic, sociable, assertive
  To discuss the factors influencing a person's role preferences, consider comparing each role with Schwartz's personal values circumplex and with the Five-Factor personality model.

_Speaker notes (Slide 8):_ [Same value/personality definitions as above, plus examples:] For example, "organizer" would relate to conscientiousness in the Big Five and to power or achievement (self-enhancement) in Schwartz's values model. "Innovator" would be most relevant to people with higher openness to experience in the Big Five and openness to change in Schwartz's values model.

**SLIDE 9 — Ch8 Q4 (2/2)**
Other team roles to consider:

- **Encourager** – These team members have a strong tendency to praise and support the ideas of other team members, thereby showing warmth and solidarity to the group.
- **Gatekeeper** – These team members have a strong tendency to encourage all team members to participate in the discussion.
- **Harmonizer** – These team members have a strong tendency to mediate intragroup conflicts and reduce tension.
- **Initiator** – These team members have a strong tendency to identify goals for the meeting, including ways to work on those goals.
- **Summarizer** – These team members have a strong tendency to keep track of what was said in the meeting (i.e., act as the team's memory).

**SLIDE 10 — Chapter 8 Question 5**
You have been given the task of forming an eight-member team of software engineers to secretly develop an important new component (feature) for the company's main software, which is used widely by financial advisors and their clients. Suppose that high team cohesion is critical for this team, whose members will be working on the team for up to six months. The company's software engineers are located in several cities in North America, as well as three locations in Europe and Asia. What actions would you take to create a software team that would quickly become highly cohesive, while still maintaining the company's standards of an inclusive workplace?

_Speaker notes (Slide 10):_ This team has a few important features to consider for developing cohesion. All members have similar occupational backgrounds (software engineering) but may differ in cultural backgrounds. This is a remote team in which members are located around the planet, so in-person gatherings would be costly. This team is a special group, completing a secret project. The team is also relatively small with eight members. Finally, the group will exist for only six months. We do not know if any members previously worked together. To answer this question, work through the six main influences on team cohesion and identify ways to apply those factors to improve cohesion.

**SLIDE 11 — Ch8 Q5 (1/2)**

- **Member similarity:** The team already has some advantage for cohesion because its members work in similar fields (software). However, there are cultural differences, which may slow down the team development process. This can be improved through activities that help team members understand each other, such as getting-to-know-you or my-user-manual events. Also, the team leader can organize social bonding sessions during which team members discover mutual life activities across cultures (e.g., hiking and soccer).
- **Team size:** The team is relatively small with eight members. This is a fixed feature of the team that can't be adjusted for the purpose of improving cohesion.
- **Member interaction:** This is likely the most important factor to speed up the team's cohesion. It can occur in a few ways. First, the team needs a routine of regular communication, and some of that communication should have high social presence, such as having video calls a few times each week. The team should also develop a routine of near-synchronous text/chat communication because synchronicity tends to improve collaboration and coordination. Second, the team should set aside time for social bonding events, such as 30-minute video gatherings to discuss nonwork ideas or amusements. Third, this remote team should kick-start its team development (including developing cohesion) by having an in-person gathering for a few days. These face-to-face sessions are perhaps the most important for accelerating team cohesion.

**SLIDE 12 — Ch8 Q5 (2/2)**

- **Somewhat difficult entry:** This team is secretly developing an important new component (feature) for the company's main software. As such, team members were likely specially selected for this project. The team leader should emphasize this point and remind team members that they have this special value and purpose to the organization.
- **Team success:** This team will have a series of completion stages as well as challenges that are conquered. Each of these occasions is a "success" along the journey toward final project completion. The team leader should ensure these events are celebrated, particularly that success is attributed to the overall team rather than to specific individuals.
- **External competition and challenges:** This company almost certainly has competitors, and the secret nature of the project highlights the competitive nature of the work. The team leader can strengthen cohesion by reminding members that other companies covet their work and are likely trying to develop a similar component. Project setbacks (difficult coding or related issues) can also be viewed as cohesion-building challenges overcome through the team's collective effort.

**SLIDE 13 — Chapter 8 Question 8**
The chief marketing officer of Sawgrass Widgets wants marketing and sales staff to identify new uses for its products. Which of the four team structures for creative decision making would you recommend? Describe and justify this process to Sawgrass' chief marketing officer.

**SLIDE 14 — Ch8 Q8 (answer)**
**Brainstorming**

- **Benefits:** Brainstorming is the most popular structure for encouraging creative ideas. It encourages divergent thinking while minimizing evaluation apprehension and other team dynamics problems. Brainstorming can bring benefits beyond the number of ideas produced. Participants interact and participate directly, increasing decision acceptance and team cohesiveness. Brainstorming rules tend to keep the team focused on the task. There is evidence that effective sessions provide valuable nonverbal communication that spreads enthusiasm; team members share feelings of optimism and excitement which may encourage a more creative climate. By involving clients in brainstorming sessions, these positive emotions may produce higher customer satisfaction than if people work alone.
- **Potential limitations:** Researchers warn that brainstorming does not completely remove evaluation apprehension; employees still know that others are silently evaluating the quality of their ideas. Production blocking and related time constraints can also prevent all ideas from being presented. Research also indicates that in some situations, individuals working alone produce more potential solutions to a problem than if they work together brainstorming.

**SLIDE 15 — Case Study Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow. (2024) – Chapter 8 Case Study: 'The Shipping Industry Accounting Team'. Page 312.

**SLIDE 16 — Case Study Question 1**
What type of team was formed here? Was it necessary, in your opinion?

**SLIDE 17 — Case Study Question 1 (answer)**
The team created in this case was a remote team that consisted of members who operate across space, time, and organizational boundaries and are linked through information technologies to achieve organizational tasks. Whether it was necessary to form this team requires consideration of a few factors, some not explicit in the case. It seems reasonable for an organization to rely on experts in a specialization to put their heads together to form a strategy to improve business in their specialization. Without making too many assumptions, it is difficult to imagine how the firm could develop strategy without the collective involvement of these people. The key question isn't whether the team should have been formed — it's how the team should be structured. Perhaps a collocated team would be more effective; these people could have been brought together face-to-face for a few days to work through the main strategy issues.

**SLIDE 18 — Case Study Question 2**
Use the team effectiveness model and related information in this chapter to identify the strengths and weaknesses of this team's environment, design, and processes.

**SLIDE 19 — Case Study Question 2 (1/2)**

- **Team environment:** Several environmental concerns make it difficult for this team to operate effectively. They rely on email, which lacks the qualities (media richness) for communicating complex, ambiguous issues about corporate strategy. Given the lack of coordination, the organizational structure appears to support individual rather than team performance — reflected in statements that they could just as well work alone. Quality of leadership influences could be a factor.
- **Team tasks:** Forming a strategic plan to improve shipping accounting business is a potentially messy affair the members don't seem to engage in individually, let alone together very often. The task is novel, complex, and ambiguous — not ideal for remote teams, particularly ones far from the performing level of team development.
- **Team size/composition:** Team size seems fine; four people should be able to develop as a remote team relatively well. However, team composition is clearly a concern. While everyone has appropriate accounting expertise, there is a lack of motivation and competencies for remote team dynamics. The author and possibly others have little desire to work in a team environment, having worked alone for some time before the merger.

**SLIDE 20 — Case Study Question 2 (2/2)**
Reviewing this case using the **Five Cs model of team competencies**:

- **Cooperating** — Mixed evidence at best. Some cooperation with some members, but the author prefers to work alone. Limited willingness to be flexible.
- **Coordinating** — Limited competencies; little evidence anyone is sensitive to each other's circumstances or tries to make the team more efficient.
- **Communicating** — Team members lack skills in communicating through information technology. One member doesn't use email well. None has used conference calling much. More effective media not mentioned.
- **Comforting (psych support)** — No evidence anyone is supportive of others through the trials of teamwork; possibly some support between two people, implied rather than stated.
- **Conflict resolving** — Conflicts are very apparent, but no evidence anyone is working effectively to resolve them.
- **Team processes:** A glaring problem is that members have had almost no opportunity or resources to develop as a team. Effective remote teams typically meet face-to-face at some point (preferably early); this has not occurred here (except the author briefly met another member). The result: members don't understand each other, can't agree on anything beyond basic issues, and have very low cohesiveness.

**SLIDE 21 — Case Study Question 3**
Assuming that these four people must continue to work as a team, recommend ways to improve the team's effectiveness.

**SLIDE 22 — Case Study Question 3 (answer)**
[Callout box:] Several things can improve the effectiveness of this remote team. The wisdom of relying on a remote team for such an ambiguous and complex problem should be questioned. A multiday retreat for these four people and perhaps other senior executives might have been wiser and, in the long run, less costly.

- One recommendation is for the team members to meet face-to-face to at least begin the strategy plan and possibly participate in some team-building activity. This personal contact may improve team dynamics by moving the team development process further along and building some level of cohesiveness.
- Another recommendation is to develop the skills in these employees (and possibly others) regarding communicating through information technology as well as working in teams. They need to become better versed in a variety of communication channels so they can choose information technology that matches the complexity of this and other tasks.

**SLIDE 23 — Break?** (section divider — minimal). Пропускаю.

---

**SLIDE 1 — Title**
Organisational Theory and Behaviour: Teams
BUS293 Topic 2 Summary

**SLIDE 2 — Introduction to Teams and Groups**

- Teams have complementary skills and shared accountability.
- Groups may be informal and focus on social interaction.
- Teams are aligned with organisational objectives.

**SLIDE 3 — Advantages of Teams**

- Better decision making and innovation.
- Improved coordination and customer service.
- Higher motivation and accountability among members.

**SLIDE 4 — Disadvantages of Teams**

- Coordination process losses increase with team size.
- Social loafing reduces individual effort.
- Integrating new members requires extra time and energy.

**SLIDE 5 — Types of Teams**

- Self-directed teams manage their own work.
- Multicultural teams bring creativity and diversity.
- Virtual teams rely on communication technology.

**SLIDE 6 — Team Effectiveness Model**

- Effective teams support organisational goals.
- Benefits include member satisfaction and long-term survival.
- Supportive environments improve performance.

**SLIDE 7 — Team Design Factors**

- Task complexity and structure affect effectiveness.
- Task interdependence can be pooled, sequential, or reciprocal.
- Team size should balance skills and coordination.

**SLIDE 8 — Team Composition**

- The Five C's: Cooperating, Coordinating, Communicating, Comforting, Conflict resolving.
- Diverse teams make better decisions.
- Roles may be formal or informal.

**SLIDE 9 — Team States**

- Norms regulate behaviour.
- Cohesion motivates members to stay committed.
- Trust and efficacy improve team performance.

**SLIDE 10 — Tuckman's Stages of Team Development**

- Forming – understanding expectations.
- Storming – conflict and role negotiation.
- Norming – cohesion and agreement.
- Performing – efficient teamwork.
- Adjourning – task completion and transition.

**SLIDE 11 — Team Building**

- Experiential activities build trust.
- Brainstorming encourages free flow of ideas.
- Challenging viewpoints improve team performance.

**SLIDE 12 — Team Decision Making Challenges**

- Production blocking limits participation.
- Evaluation apprehension reduces idea sharing.
- Groupthink prioritises consensus over quality decisions.

**SLIDE 13 — Improving Team Decision Making**

- Brainwriting reduces production blocking.
- Electronic brainstorming allows anonymous contributions.
- Nominal group technique improves evaluation of ideas.

**SLIDE 14 — Conclusion**

- Teams outperform individuals when managed effectively.
- Positive norms and communication are essential.
- Effective team design improves organisational success.

---

**Key terms / frameworks in this deck:**

- **Team Effectiveness Model**; team design / states / composition.
- **Task interdependence**: pooled, sequential, reciprocal.
- **Five C's of team competencies**: Cooperating, Coordinating, Communicating, Comforting, Conflict resolving.
- **Tuckman's Stages of Team Development**: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning.
- **Team process problems**: process losses, social loafing, production blocking, evaluation apprehension, groupthink.
- **Decision-making improvement techniques**: brainwriting, electronic brainstorming, nominal group technique, brainstorming.
- **Team types**: self-directed, multicultural, virtual.
- Concepts: norms, cohesion, trust, team efficacy.

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-02-Team-Dynamics/Topic_2_Podcast_Transcript.md

Связь: [[Topic 2 — Team Dynamics]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Welcome back to BUS293, Organisational Theory and Behaviour. As mentioned in the
previous topic, working together is a fundamental aspect of the human experience and
workplace teams are increasingly perceived as necessary for success. This topic
introduces the team effectiveness model, team processes, team decision making, and
emerging team types.
Firstly, although similar, there are some differences between teams and groups. Teams
are a type of group, where the members have complementary skills and work together as
a unit to achieve a common purpose associated with organisational objectives for which
the collectively hold themselves accountable. Teams perceive themselves as a social
entity within an organisation. Informal groups are NOT formally designated as a part of
the organisation and they emerge unofficially. These groups include friendship and
interest groups, and they help people accomplish their work, satisfy their individual
needs, reduce stress, and therefore improve employee wellbeing. The main determining
factor that separate teams from just being a group, is the shared commitment of members
towards achieving organisational objectives.
Teams have both advantages and disadvantages. Under the right conditions, teams make
better decisions, better products and services, and a more motivated and engaged
workforce than individuals working alone. Teams can quickly share information and
coordinate tasks, which speeds up processes and increases breadth of knowledge,
consequently increasing quality of customer service. People are also more motivated
when working in teams, as there is a social identity to uphold, increased accountability to
team members who monitor performance more closely than a supervisor, and the
tendency to compare performance to other team members.
Despite these advantages, there are also disadvantages in the forms of process losses
encountered by teams. Coordination process losses include the time and energy taken to
develop and maintain the team. Teams need to develop understanding of their goals,
determine strategies, negotiate roles and rules of conduct, and resolve disagreements, to
ensure the team functions effectively. Process losses increase as team size increases and
are amplified when a new member joins the team, as time and energy must be used to
accommodate and integrate the new member. Motivational process loss is seen mostly in
social loafing. Social loafing, or freeloading, is the tendency of people to not work as hard
in a team as they would individually. Social loafing is reduced when the task is interesting,
when the team’s objective is important, and when team members value team
membership.
There are a few main types of teams in the workplace. Self-directed teams are small teams
who have been empowered to manage themselves and the work they do on a day-to-day
basis. They are very project-focussed, completing an entire piece of work requiring
several interdependent tasks and usually develop their own goals. They have substantial
autonomy, operate with fewer layers than traditional teams, and the position of
supervisor is no longer needed. Self-directed teams are increasing in popularity and
research indicates they have increased productivity and job satisfaction.
Multicultural teams are also increasing as organisations become increasingly global and
their members become more diverse. The heterogeneity of multicultural teams increases
their creativity and performance; however it is important to develop norms that allow
the team to reach consensus. Cultural differences in norms about power, status, and
authority, communicating, and decision making may cause tension and frustration
between team members, however these can be managed through adaptation, variation of
team structure, or managerial intervention in setting ground rules for interaction.
Virtual teams are a response to the increasing degree of separation between team
members created by new forms of organisational structure, advances in technologies, and
globalisation. They could be separated by different floors in the same building, different
base organisations, or even different countries. Members of virtual teams require strong
communication technology skills and strong self-leadership skills, as well as access to
multiple communication channels, increased task structure, and face-to-face meetings
early in the team development process.
A team is effective when it benefits the organisation through task performance, benefits
its members through satisfying members needs, and survives long enough to accomplish
its purpose. Ensuring the right conditions for team effectiveness is therefore important,
and the team effectiveness model represents the conditions that can influence team
effectiveness.
The organisational and team environments either support or inhibit the team’s ability to
function and achieve its objectives. Team members work together more effectively when
organisationally there is team-based rewards, supportive leadership, structural support,
suitable information systems, and physical space for teamwork.
The design of the team also contributes to the team’s effectiveness. Task characteristics
are the first element of team design and consist of task complexity, task structure, and
task interdependence. Complex tasks require the skills and knowledge of more than one
person, and thus teams are more suited as the work can be divided into more specialised
roles. It then follows that well structured work is easier to coordinate in teams, in contrast
to ambiguous tasks. However, teams can perform ambiguous tasks with well-structured
roles. Finally, task interdependence, the way in which members must share information,
materials, or expertise, in order to do their jobs, impacts team effectiveness, and the
higher the level of interdependence, the greater need for coordination and use of teams.
If the members do not directly interact with each other and are only indirectly affected
by the others’ actions, this is pooled, or low, interdependence. In this case, very little
attention is needed to the management of team dynamics.
If teams are designed in such a way that the outputs of one member become inputs for
another member, this is sequential, or medium, interdependence. The second member
depends on the first and cannot perform effectively if the first member is not performing
effectively. In this situation there is more potential for problems in team dynamics, which
creates a need for greater coordination and attention to team functioning.
The third interdependence, reciprocal, or high interdependence - occurs when each
member has outputs that are inputs to the other member. This increases the complexity
of team dynamics as there will be frequent and varied interactions between the members
on a daily basis. Any problems will spill over to other points of contact, and so teams need
to not only pay attention, but have skills in creating and maintaining effective team
dynamics and relationships.
The second element of team design is team size. The most effective number of team
members is debated, however it must be large enough to provide the necessary
competencies and resources to perform the work, yet small enough to allow efficient
coordination and meaningful involvement of each member. Smaller teams have less
process losses, are more engaged because they have a greater influence on the teams
norms and goals, experience more mutual trust and perceptions of support, and feel more
responsible for the team’s success and failure.
The final element of team design is team composition. The members capability to work
well in a team, or their team member competency, affect both task performance and team
maintenance. Team member competency is summarised in the five C’s: Cooperating,
Coordinating, Communicating, Comforting, and Conflict resolving. Team diversity is the
second aspect of team composition, with diverse teams making better decisions than
homogenous teams. Diverse teams also have a broader range of abilities and skills.
However, increased team diversity poses challenges as diverse teams tend to take longer
to bond and thus progress towards becoming a high-performance team. They also have
increased challenges in communication and motivation to coordinate. Team roles are the
third aspect of team composition, and are the set of behaviours a member is expected to
perform because they hold a certain position in a team and/or organisation. Roles can
either be formally assigned, or informally assumed. Finally, transactive memory is
knowing who knows what, or more simply put, allocating the right tasks and roles to the
most suited members.
Once the team is effectively designed, or formed, it must then then follow effective team
states and processes.
Norms are the informal rules and shared expectations that teams establish to regulate
the behaviours of their members. They can become deeply anchored, so the best way to
avoid norms that are detrimental to the team is to establish positive norms when the team
is first formed, for example by establishing a code of conduct which sets out basic
principles and rules governing team norms and behaviours.
Team cohesion is the degree to which members are attracted to and motived to remain a
part of the team. It strongly influences the extent to which members of a team conform to
team norms, and thus when team performance norms are positive, high cohesiveness has
positive effects for the organisation, but when team performance norms are negative,
high cohesiveness has detrimental effects on the organisation. The factors that improve
team cohesion include higher member similarity, smaller team size, increased member
interaction, difficulty of entry, team success, and external competition and challenges.
Team efficacy is the collective belief among team members of the team’s ability to
successfully complete the task, and as a general rule, the higher the team efficacy, the
higher the performance.
The final team state is team trust. Trust is both cognitive and emotional, based on
perceptions of competence and social identity. It is usually high in team formation, and
then events of poor individual performance, or other violations of trust, decrease the
level. A lower level of trust results in team members being less forgiving and less
cooperative, which undermines team and organisational effectiveness.
Team processes are both internal and external and are the interactions and activities,
generally classified as team work or task work behaviours, or team boundary spanning,
that the team engage in as they work towards their goal.
In the process of becoming an effective work unit, teams go through stages of team
development. Tuckman’s model of team development shows systematic stages that
teams go through to become a cohesive, effective team. Initially there is the forming stage,
where members discover team expectations and test he boundaries of behaviour. They
then progress to the storming stage where there is interpersonal conflict and negotiation
of roles, goals, and norms. As these roles, goals, and norms are established, the team
moves to the norming stage, where a sense of cohesion is established and there is a
consensus around objectives and behaviours. The team is then able to perform, as
members have learned to efficiently coordinate and resolve conflicts. For high-
performance teams, there is high level of cooperation, trust, commitment to group
objectives, and identification with the team. Once the team objective is complete, teams’
transition to the adjourning stage, and members shift their focus to relationships, away
from the task. Although Tuckman’s model depicts team development very well, it is not a
perfect representation of the process, and different teams will develop differently. There
may be inertia, revisiting of stages, or skipping of stages, as the team progresses through
their own individual experience.
Team development can also be accelerated through team building. Team building uses
formal activities to improve the development and functioning of a team. Experiential
activities include games that help to build cooperation, competition, and trust.
Challenging viewpoints approaches helps team members to break down unhelpful
viewpoints that are impeding team performance through using techniques like the
‘devil’s advocate’ process, or redefining roles within the team. Reaching consensus
approaches like brainstorming reduce members fear of criticism or failure and result in
enthusiasm, involvement, and a free flow of ideas. These team building techniques can be
conducted in a range of settings, from formal retreats, to regular meetings in a vein of
continual improvement, or outdoor experiences, however ongoing reflection of the teams
work experiences and a willingness to experiment is generally more effective.
By ensuring that the organisational and team environment, team design, team states, and
team processes are all optimised for team performance, teams are much more likely to
be effective.
Teams are expected to make decisions, and under certain conditions do better at this than
individuals alone. However, there are some constraints that reduce the effectiveness of
team decision making. Time constraints such as production blocking, where only one
team member can speak at a time, undermines idea generation. Evaluation apprehension,
where people are reluctant to mention ideas in case they will be judged or seen as silly,
also reduces idea generation. Pressure to conform causes team members to not speak out
if they disagree with an idea, which could lead to the team making a suboptimal decision.
Overconfidence can also reduce the quality of decision made as overconfident teams are
less vigilant when making decisions and are less likely to seek out outside information.
Finally, groupthink is when highly cohesive groups focus on consensus rather than
decision quality. It limits both idea generation and idea quality, and is usually present
when pressure to conform and overconfidence are also factors.
To improve effective decision making, teams can use the following techniques to reduce
the constraints. Brainstorming helps to increase idea generation and minimise evaluation
apprehension, however it is still impacted by production blocking and pressure to
conform.
Brainwriting, which is a version of brainstorming where team members write ideas on
cards and place them in the centre of the table, helps remove production blocking, and
arguably produces more and better quality ideas than brainstorming.
Electronic brainstorming, where brainwriting is done anonymously using technology,
again improves on the benefits of brainwriting, and minimises production blocking,
evaluation apprehension, and pressure to confirm, however it tends to be too structured
and technology bound. Finally, nominal group technique is another variation of
brainwriting conducted in three stages. Firstly, members individually and silently
document their ideas, then they collectively describe these to the group without criticism,
and then again silently and independently the members evaluate the ideas presented.
This technique again improves on the benefits of brainstorming, however production
blocking and evaluation apprehension do still occur to some extent. Despite the
limitations, using techniques for team decision making can improve the effectiveness of
the decisions made.
Team work is essential, as research has shown that teams consistently out-perform
individuals or random groups,
but as this topic has discussed, they are not easy to create or manage.
In order to ensure teams have positive norms, desired team behaviours need to be
actively shaped and reinforced.
This is relevant not just for its importance to organisational behaviour, but also to your
performance in your assignment teams.
Try using this new knowledge to form and develop an effective team, and if there is
disfunction, or a lack of performance, consider modifying one or more of the inputs or
processes, to try and improve the outputs of the team. Thank you, and all the best.
