## 📄 02-topics/Topic-02-Team-Dynamics/Topic_2_Workshop_Solution.md

Связь: [[Topic 2 — Team Dynamics]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

**BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour**

Topic 2: Workshop Activities (Team Dynamics)

Name: Faiaz Dzhafarov  Student No: 35553299

# Activity 1: Critical Thinking Questions (Chapter 8)

## Question 2

*Identify three reasons why a team of six students could potentially produce a better report than the average quality of their reports completed individually, including the motivational benefits.*

There are three main reasons I would point to. First, a team of six has a wider range of knowledge and skills than any single student, so it can locate relevant information more quickly and cover the topic more thoroughly. That larger pool of expertise is hard for one person to match.

Second, there are simply more hands on deck. One student cannot read and process as much material as six can. The work does need coordinating, sure, but the report is ultimately built on a much larger volume of conceptual resources.

The third reason is motivational. Members are often more motivated in teams than alone. Each student feels accountable to the others, fellow members monitor performance more closely than a supervisor would, and over time members develop a bond and want to fulfil the team's goals.

## Question 4

*Consider the six team roles (Exhibit 8.6). Which two best describe your role preference, and what factors influence a person's role preferences?*

In most team settings my two strongest role tendencies are the Organiser and the Doer. As an Organiser I tend to structure what the team is doing and keep track of progress against goals and deadlines. As a Doer I reliably take on tasks and complete them on time to help ensure the team succeeds.

A person's role preferences are influenced by their personality and values, along with past experience and skills. Using the Five-Factor (Big Five) model, my preference for the Organiser and Doer roles reflects high conscientiousness, meaning being organised and dependable. Using Schwartz's values model, these roles align with achievement and a degree of conservation (valuing order and reliability). By contrast, the Innovator role tends to suit people high in openness to experience and openness to change, while the Team Builder role suits people high in agreeableness. Prior experience in similar teams and a person's confidence in particular skills also shape which role they gravitate toward.

## Question 5

*How would you quickly build high cohesion in an eight-member, secret, remote software team spread across several countries, while maintaining an inclusive workplace?*

I would work through the main influences on team cohesion and apply each to this team.

The members already share a similar occupational background (software engineering), which helps cohesion, but they differ culturally. To work with that member similarity, I would run getting-to-know-you and 'my user manual' sessions plus social bonding activities that surface shared interests across cultures, which also supports inclusion. On team size, eight members is relatively small and is a fixed feature of this project, so that is already favourable for cohesion.

Member interaction is the most important lever for a remote team. I would establish a routine of frequent communication with high social presence (regular video calls), near-synchronous chat for coordination, short social video gatherings, and ideally an initial in-person meeting for a few days to kick-start development.

A few other levers matter too:

* **Somewhat difficult entry.** Members were specially selected for a confidential, important project. I would emphasise this special status and purpose so members feel they belong to an elite group.
* **Team success.** I would break the project into milestones, celebrate each completed stage, and attribute success to the whole team rather than to individuals.
* **External competition and challenges.** I would remind the team that competitors are likely working on a similar feature, and frame setbacks as challenges the team overcomes together, which strengthens cohesion.

## Question 8

*Which of the four team structures for creative decision making would you recommend to Sawgrass' chief marketing officer for identifying new uses for its products?*

I would recommend brainstorming. It is the most popular structure for encouraging creative ideas because it promotes divergent thinking while reducing evaluation apprehension and other team-dynamics problems. Beyond the number of ideas generated, members participate directly, which increases decision acceptance and cohesiveness, and the energy and enthusiasm in a good session can create a more creative climate. Involving clients can even raise customer satisfaction.

The CMO should also be aware of the limitations. Brainstorming does not fully remove evaluation apprehension, since members know others are silently judging their ideas, and production blocking and time limits can stop all ideas being heard. In some cases individuals working alone actually generate more ideas than a group. These problems can be managed by combining brainstorming with individual idea generation beforehand and enforcing the 'no criticism' rule.

# Activity 2: Case Study - The Shipping Industry Accounting Team (Chapter 8)

## Question 1 - What type of team was formed, and was it necessary?

This was a remote (virtual) team. The members operate across space, time and organisational boundaries and are linked through information technology to achieve organisational tasks. It seems reasonable to bring together experts in the same specialisation to form a strategy, and it is hard to see how the firm could develop the strategy without their collective involvement, so forming a team was justified. The real question is not whether to form the team but how to structure it. A collocated team brought together face-to-face for a few days may well have been more effective.

## Question 2 - Strengths and weaknesses of the team's environment, design and processes

The team environment is weak. The team relies on email, which lacks the media richness needed for complex, ambiguous strategy issues. The organisational structure rewards individual rather than team performance, and leadership support appears limited. The team task is a weak fit as well: forming a strategic plan is novel, complex and ambiguous, hardly ideal work for a remote team, especially one far from the 'performing' stage.

Team size and composition are more mixed. Four members is a workable size, but composition is a concern. They all have accounting expertise, yet several lack the motivation and competencies for remote teamwork, having worked alone before the merger.

Reviewing the team against the Five C's of team competencies, every area looks weak:

* **Cooperating.** Some cooperation exists, but the author prefers to work alone and shows limited flexibility.
* **Coordinating.** Little evidence members align their work or try to make the team efficient.
* **Communicating.** Members lack skill with the communication technologies (one barely uses email; little use of conference calls).
* **Comforting.** Little evidence of members supporting each other through the difficulties of teamwork.
* **Conflict resolving.** Conflict is clearly present but no one is resolving it effectively.

Team processes are the glaring problem. The members have had almost no opportunity to develop as a team, have never met face-to-face, do not understand each other, and have very low cohesiveness.

## Question 3 - Recommendations to improve effectiveness

My first recommendation is to meet face-to-face. Bring the four members together for a short retreat to begin the strategy plan and take part in team-building. Personal contact moves the team along the development process and builds cohesion.

The team also needs to develop teamwork and technology skills. I would train members in working in teams and in using a range of communication channels, so they can match the richness of the medium to the complexity of the task.

Finally, the organisation should question the structure. Given how ambiguous and complex the task is, it should reconsider relying on a purely remote team for it. A face-to-face working session for these (and perhaps other senior) people may be wiser and cheaper in the long run.

# Activity 3: Team Formation and Team Contract

Our team registered on the LMS as Group 11 and agreed a team contract in the first workshop, which we uploaded to the LMS Team Discussion Forum. The completed contract covered the points below.

**Team name and members.** Group 11: Bobur, Faiaz Dzhafarov (35553299), Owethu and Wahid. Wahid later left the unit, and his work was reallocated across the three remaining members.

**Communication.** All formal communication and document sharing goes through the LMS Team Discussion Forum, which is mandatory, with a group chat for quick day-to-day coordination. We agreed to reply within 24 hours on working days.

**Meeting schedule.** A standing meeting each week straight after the workshop, held in person where possible and online through Teams when a member could not attend. Attendance was expected at every meeting, and anyone who had to miss one would post their update to the forum beforehand.

**Roles and responsibilities.** A coordinator kept the agenda and posted the minutes, and every member owned specific report sections, set out in Activity 4. Each person was responsible for delivering their section to the agreed internal deadline.

**Expectations.** Equal contribution, work delivered to internal deadlines that sat ahead of the 26 June due date, and drafts written to the standard set by the marking rubric and the Detailed Report Guidelines.

**Conflict management.** Disagreements were raised openly in the meeting and settled by discussion and, where needed, a majority view; anything that could not be resolved would be taken to the workshop tutor. This is the problem-solving approach we later used when a genuine dispute came up over the recommendations and the shared reference list.

**Records.** All agreements, task allocations, meeting records and drafts are kept on the Team Discussion Forum, since failing to use the forum carries a 10% individual penalty.

**Acknowledgement.** All members acknowledged and accepted the contract on the forum.

Готово — Workshop 3 (Chapters 2 & 3: Personality/Values + Perception), 33 слайда. Полный дамп на английском:

---

**SLIDE 1 — Title**
BUS293 / Organisational Theory and Behaviour / CHAPTER TWO + CHAPTER THREE / BUS293 Murdoch University

- Individual Differences: Personality and Values
- Perceiving Ourselves and Others in Organisations

**SLIDE 2 — Acknowledgement of Country**
We acknowledge that Murdoch University is situated on the lands of the Whadjuk and Binjareb Noongar people. We pay our respect to their enduring and dynamic culture and the leadership of Noongar elders past and present. The boodjar (country) on which Murdoch University is located has, for thousands of years, been a place of learning. We at Murdoch University are proud to continue this long tradition.

**SLIDE 3 — Workshop Three Outline**

- Critical thinking questions (20 minutes)
- Case study questions (20 minutes)
- 5-minute break(?)
- Bonus Team Exercise (20 minutes)

**SLIDE 4 — Critical Thinking Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow (2024). Chapter 2, page 70 — Questions 2, 6, and 8. AND Chapter 3, page 109 — Questions 4, 6, and 7.

**SLIDE 5 — Chapter 2 Question 2**
All candidates applying for a management trainee position are given a personality test that measures the five dimensions in the five-factor model. Which personality traits would you consider most important for this type of job? Explain your answer.

**SLIDE 6 — Ch2 Q2 (1/2)**
Each Big Five personality dimension is associated with various forms of behavior and performance. All five dimensions predict employee performance and related behaviors to some extent, but three probably apply best to managerial roles.
**Conscientiousness** (especially industriousness and dutifulness) is important because it is the best predictor of proficient task performance in almost every job group. Conscientious employees set higher personal goals, are more motivated, and have higher performance expectations than those with low conscientiousness. They also tend to have higher levels of organizational citizenship and are less likely to engage in counterproductive work behaviors.

**SLIDE 7 — Ch2 Q2 (2/2)**
**Extroversion** is the second best predictor of proficient task performance. Extraverts frame situations as challenges and are comfortable interacting with and influencing people. Extraversion is one of the strongest predictors of both adaptive and proactive performance. All of these factors—proficient, adaptive, proactive task performance, organizational citizenship, low counterproductive behavior, comfort in social and influence situations—make it important for managerial positions.
**Emotional stability** (lower neuroticism) is a significant predictor of adaptive task performance, relating to managing change. It is also associated (moderately or inconsistently) with task proficiency, organizational citizenship, and counterproductive behaviors. Emotionally stable people cope better with ambiguous situations, which applies to managers in more strategic roles.

**SLIDE 8 — Chapter 2 Question 6**
The CEO and two other executives at an automotive parts manufacturer were recently fired after being charged with fixing prices on several key automotive parts sold to the auto industry. Executives at competing manufacturers face the same charges for also participating in this collusion. Profit margins have come under intense pressure in the industry, which could cause one or more auto parts firms (possibly this company) to go bankrupt. When the wrongdoing was discovered, most employees involved in product pricing (but not implicated in price-fixing) were surprised. The executives were highly respected in their fields of expertise, so many staff members interpreted the unusual pricing decisions as a new strategy, not an illegal activity. Apply your knowledge of personal and ethical values and behavior to explain why the unethical activity may have occurred.

**SLIDE 9 — Ch2 Q6 (1/2)**
There are two parts to the answer: (a) ethical concepts related to the wrongdoing; (b) ethical concepts related to how others reacted to the unethical decisions.
**Ethical analysis of the wrongdoing**—These companies are experiencing lower profit margins and one or more firms could go bankrupt. At least short-term, executives could be under tremendous pressure from shareholders to maintain profit margins, motivating them to do so illegally. Some could be motivated by the prospect of running a business into bankruptcy, which is disastrous for an executive's résumé and would face strife/anger from employees who lose their jobs. These "situational" conditions are actually motivational influences—they do not require or prohibit the executives from engaging in wrongdoing.

**SLIDE 10 — Ch2 Q6 (2/2)**
**Ethical analysis of product pricing employees**—Product pricing employees were surprised when executives were charged with price-fixing, highlighting their low moral sensitivity. They failed to detect the moral issue, likely because they had less expertise regarding prescriptive norms and rules. They had core knowledge due to job expertise, but believed executive directives reflected even greater knowledge rather than illegal activity. (NOTE: This misunderstanding has actually occurred in some of the most serious corporate accounting fraud incidents.) Staff may also have had fairly low mindfulness of price-fixing risks in their day-to-day work; greater sensitivity might have led some to question the executive directives.

**SLIDE 11 — Chapter 2 Question 8**
People in a particular South American country have high power distance and high collectivism. What does this mean, and what are the implications when you (a senior executive) visit employees working for your company in that country?

**SLIDE 12 — Ch2 Q8**
In **high power distance** cultures, people tend to accept the power differential in their society, which extends to the workplace. I would expect employees to address me by my surname; I would not interpret this as aloof or unfriendly. Social interchange would be formal.
People from **high collectivism** cultures define themselves by group membership and value the well-being of people within those groups. It would encourage me to celebrate the achievements of everyone as a group. Any discussion would emphasize improving or maintaining group harmony and teamwork.

**SLIDE 13 — Chapter 3 Question 4**
Several years ago, senior executives at energy company CanOil wanted to acquire an exploration company (HBOG) owned by another energy company, AmOil. Rather than face a hostile takeover and unfavourable tax implications, CanOil's two top executives met with the CEO of AmOil to discuss a friendly exchange of stock. AmOil's chief executive was previously unaware of CanOil's plans, and as the meeting began, warned that he was there merely to listen. The CanOil executives were confident AmOil wanted to sell HBOG because energy legislation at the time made HBOG a poor investment for AmOil. AmOil's CEO remained silent for most of the meeting, which CanOil executives interpreted as implied agreement to proceed to buy AmOil stock on the market. But when CanOil launched the stock purchase a month later, AmOil's CEO was both surprised and outraged. He thought he had given them the cold shoulder, remaining silent to show disinterest. The misunderstanding nearly bankrupted CanOil because AmOil reacted by protecting its stock. What perceptual problem(s) occurred that led to this misunderstanding?

**SLIDE 14 — Ch3 Q4**
This incident describes true events in Dome Petroleum's acquisition of Conoco subsidiary Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas (HBOG). [See: J. Lyon, *The Rise and Fall of the House that Jack Built* (Toronto: McMillan, 1983).] HBOG's high acquisition price (due to Conoco's resistance strategy), other debts, increasing interest rates, and falling oil prices put Dome on the brink of bankruptcy. The company was later acquired by Amoco.
This is a classic example of the **false-consensus effect**. The CanOil executives interpreted the AmOil CEO's silence as tacit agreement, probably because they wanted to believe AmOil would support the stock swap. The plan was critical to the executives' personal goals and was a high-risk strategy relying on questionable accounting procedures—conditions likely to further add to the perceptual bias that the AmOil CEO was on side.

**SLIDE 15 — Chapter 3 Question 6**
During a diversity management session, a manager suggests that stereotypes are a necessary part of working with others. "I have to make assumptions about what's in the other person's head, and stereotypes help me do that," she explains. "It's better to rely on stereotypes than to enter a working relationship with someone from another culture without any idea of what they believe in!" Discuss the merits of and problems with the manager's statement.

**SLIDE 16 — Ch3 Q6**
This raises the fundamental dilemma that **stereotyping** is both a necessary and a troublesome activity in the perceptual process.
On the one hand, the manager is correct that stereotyping helps fill in missing information, such as non-observable characteristics that become apparent only after a long time. Stereotyping also helps organise information more efficiently by placing people into predetermined categories.
Although most stereotypes have some truth, there is plenty of error and distortion that could lead to employment discrimination. It is unlikely someone perfectly fits the stereotype category, and when we stereotype we tend to assign traits that are untrue. Stereotyping makes it difficult to alter beliefs about a person regarding traits that conflict with the stereotype.

**SLIDE 17 — Chapter 3 Question 8**
Self-awareness is increasingly recognised as an important ingredient for effective leadership. Suppose you are responsible for creating a leadership development program in a government organisation. What activities or processes would you introduce to help participants constructively develop better self-awareness of their personality, values and personal biases?

**SLIDE 18 — Ch3 Q8**
This lays the foundation for leadership development as well as improving perceptions about ourselves and others. The quick answer is for leadership trainees to receive more feedback about themselves, which can occur through novel experiences that provide feedback about their behaviour and performance. One example is an **assessment centre**, where observers monitor participant behaviours during exercises and later provide confidential feedback. A related activity is **360-degree feedback**, where trainees receive systematically compiled feedback from peers, subordinates and bosses, offering clarity about strengths and areas for improvement.

**SLIDE 19 — Case Study Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow (2024) – Chapter 3 Case Study: 'Bridging the two worlds', page 110.

**SLIDE 20 — Case Study Question 1**
What symptoms in this case suggest that something has gone wrong?

**SLIDE 21 — Case Study Question 1 (answer)**
The main symptom at the end of the case is that John, a productive employee, was upset/dissatisfied with management's offer for him to take a management skills seminar. He was ready to quit and leave the company. He also formed an even stronger negative image of George and other managers. Another symptom is the ongoing negative attitudes that shop floor employees have of management.

**SLIDE 22 — Case Study Question 2**
Explain the causes of these symptoms using your knowledge of self-concept and perceptions concepts and theories. Analyze the case facts separately for each theory and refer to the symptom(s) that the theory explains from the facts.

**SLIDE 23 — Case Study Question 2 (1/2)**
**Stereotyping:** Shop floor employees rely on stereotypes of "management" to interpret management's actions without considering alternative reasoning. Look at the foundations of stereotyping—categorization, homogenization, and differentiation. Shop floor employees cluster (categorize) all managers and assign common attributes (homogenization). They distinguish the author of the case only after some personal interaction. They reveal a negative view of managers versus their own capabilities and ethics (differentiation). This stereotyping, particularly differentiation, partly explains why John is dissatisfied with the offer of management training. A similar analysis of managers' perceptions of employees could be done, though there is less information.
**Self-concept and social identity:** It can be inferred that John has a self-view firmly anchored in his shop floor role, apparent when he considers management training an insult. His self-concept shows through his social interaction with other shop floor employees and his status in that group—discussed via social identity theory. George may also be understood through his social identity with managers and self-concept as a supervisor, though we have less information.

**SLIDE 24 — Case Study Question 2 (2/2)**
**Contact hypothesis:** Although introduced as a way to improve perceptions (a solution), it can diagnose why John and George misunderstand each other. Both have very limited direct contact—they work in separate physical spheres with limited direct communication. George's communication is formal (written), conveying status differences and power. They have no interaction through common equal-status activities. With the previous analyses, the contact hypothesis explains why George and John have low empathy—they don't understand each other's intentions or anticipated feelings.
**Communication:** George's use of memos is an ineffective communication channel that amplifies the misunderstanding. Management and shop floor employees also differ in jargon (from swearing to technical jargon), reinforcing distinct social identities.

**SLIDE 25 — Case Study Question 3**
What would you recommend to the manager and company overall to improve the situation (reduce or remove the symptoms) in the future? Provide recommendations for both immediate and longer-term actions.

**SLIDE 26 — Case Study Question 3 (answer)**
One of the clearest solutions is for management and shop floor employees to engage in **structured contact** and, ultimately, some form of meaningful interaction. A professional facilitator might get John and George together and explain the reasons for George's request. Care must be taken to present this as a reward, not a sign of dissatisfaction. Other actions: asking John to attend weekly management meetings or other management social functions, in line with future promotion.
The immediate action is to correct John's misperception of the management training program. The case author might take this communication role since he seems better at communicating underlying meaning than George. If George can communicate his true intent, a face-to-face explanation would be beneficial.

**SLIDE 27 — Bonus Team Exercise (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow (2024) page 73 — Ethics Dilemma Vignettes.

**SLIDE 28 — Bonus Team Exercise**
Stage 1 (5 minutes): In each of the four cases, within your teams discuss the extent to which the company's action in each case was ethical. Teams should be prepared to justify their evaluation using ethics principles and perceived **moral intensity** of each incident.

**SLIDE 29 — Bonus Team Exercise: Case 1**
An ethical dilemma at the forefront since the pandemic sent most employees into remote work. On one hand, the company wants to monitor employee behavior (as on premises) so customer data isn't compromised and employees maintain customer service standards and efficiency. On the other hand, monitoring in a home setting invades the individual's privacy in their personal domain. A separate work area at home might reduce this somewhat, but not everyone has a large enough home/compatible area for a separate workspace. Some monitoring methods are more precise and continuous than what employees typically experience at the office. The company's suggested benefits seem contrived—that webcams will help training, team building, and social interaction—and the "opt in" condition ignores the company's power in the employment relationship.

**SLIDE 30 — Bonus Team Exercise: Case 2**
Occurred at a small industrial services business in the UK (see: A. Levy, "Teenage Office Worker Sacked for Moaning on Facebook About Her 'Totally Boring' Job," _Daily Mail_, February 26, 2009). Several similar cases involve Facebook, blogs, and social media where employees write negative comments about employers. Parallels: (a) a Starbucks employee fired for complaining about his boss's decision; (b) a government marketing employee in northern Canada fired for posting artistic photos of garbage in the snow. Some say the teenage Facebook complainer should be dismissed for lacking commitment to and appreciation of the job. The owner explained: "We were looking for a long-term relationship with Miss Swann as we do with all our staff. Her display of disrespect and dissatisfaction undermined the relationship and made it untenable." Others say the owner's actions were unethical because (a) he was snooping on the employee's private communication (though open for others to read), (b) her statements may have accurately reflected the work, (c) no evidence her performance was undermined by her statements/attitude, and (d) she did not name the company.

**SLIDE 31 — Bonus Team Exercise: Case 3**
Describes the health incentive program at Whole Foods, which led to considerable controversy. One main concern is the incentive is unfair because a person's weight (plus blood pressure and cholesterol, also considered) is to some degree beyond their control due to heredity or metabolism. A human rights expert pointed out incentives should apply only to conditions over which people have considerable control. Human rights advocates claim the program is unfair discrimination because obesity is a disability (at least in some circumstances). Another concern: it relies on BMI, a century-old measure criticized for poor measurement of obesity. CEO John Mackey acknowledged BMI's limitations but dismissed the issue, saying measures "do have the virtues of being relatively good, easy to measure and not too expensive to monitor." (See C. Tobias, "Whole Foods Controversy," _Canadian Business_, May 2, 2011; L. Sloane, "Why Whole Foods Wellness Program Hurts Employees: An Open Letter," _Psyched in San Francisco_, December 14, 2015.)

**SLIDE 32 — Bonus Team Exercise: Case 4**
Refers to actions by Hewlett Packard (HP). (See D. Pringle and S. Stecklow, "Electronics With Borders," _Wall Street Journal_, January 17, 2005, B1.) Though the sense of freedom to purchase globally may dominate, some agree companies are buffeted by currency fluctuations so much they cannot adapt quickly to price changes and shifting supplies. E.g., a large buyer of HP printer ink in Europe might ship much of it to the US if the Euro rises against the USD, causing a shortage in Europe. Others argue this supply shift is a small portion of supply in most regions, so HP's actions are unfair. In terms of **moral intensity**, few people are affected by HP's restrictions and it has low proximity (not nearby), so moral intensity is low. If you believe there is no (or minimal) moral dilemma, why was the story on the front business page of a leading newspaper?
**Update:** HP recently introduced printers that issue failure warnings when nonbranded ink cartridges are used, even though the non-HP products work. HP claims required use of HP-branded ink (costing more than luxury perfume per quart/liter) protects its intellectual property. Rejection of budget inks occurred after a firmware update, sometimes long after consumers purchased the printer and had been using generic cartridges (see Z. Kleinman, "HP Printers Start Rejecting Budget Ink Cartridges," BBC News, September 19, 2016, http://www.bbc.com/news/technology-37408173).

**SLIDE 33 — Team Meeting 2** (icon + text rows)

- 📅 Create a plan for report completion including task allocation, progress dates, and meeting times – **This must be comprehensively completed before the end of the workshop**
- 📄 Make sure you have a rough skeleton and template created for the report
- ✏ Preliminary research and drafting should begin this week

---

**Key terms / frameworks / sources in this deck:**

- **Five-Factor (Big Five) Personality Model**: Conscientiousness (best predictor of proficient task performance), Extroversion, Emotional stability (lower neuroticism); links to proficient/adaptive/proactive task performance, organizational citizenship, counterproductive work behaviors.
- **Ethical values & behavior**: moral sensitivity, moral intensity, mindfulness, prescriptive norms; ethics principles.
- **Hofstede cultural dimensions**: power distance, collectivism.
- **Perception concepts**: false-consensus effect; stereotyping (categorization, homogenization, differentiation); self-concept; social identity theory; contact hypothesis; communication/media richness.
- **Self-awareness development tools**: assessment centre, 360-degree feedback.
- Sources/cases: McShane & Von Glinow (2024) Ch.2 (p.70), Ch.3 (p.109); case study "Bridging the two worlds" (p.110); Ethics Dilemma Vignettes (p.73); real-world references — Dome Petroleum/HBOG (J. Lyon 1983), UK Facebook firing (_Daily Mail_ 2009), Whole Foods (_Canadian Business_ 2011; _Psyched in San Francisco_ 2015), HP (_WSJ_ 2005; BBC News 2016).
- Assessment milestones: Team Meeting 2 — finalize plan, build report skeleton/template, begin preliminary research/drafting.

Внешний URL в слайдах один: http://www.bbc.com/news/technology-37408173 (Slide 32). Других ссылок на видео нет.

http://www.bbc.com/news/technology-37408173 (снизу то что написано на этом сайте)
HP printers start rejecting budget ink cartridges
Published: 19 September 2016
Large numbers of HP printer owners found their printers stopped recognising unofficial printer ink cartridges on 13 September.
Dutch printer ink vendor 123inkt said it had received more than 1,000 complaints in one day. HP said that during its last firmware update, settings had been changed so HP printers would communicate with only HP-chipped cartridges. It also said some devices already had the functionality built-in.
"The purpose of this update is to protect HP's innovations and intellectual property," it said in a statement. It has angered some of its customers as HP branded cartridges are notably more expensive than unofficial brands.
'Cartridge problem'
Reported error messages include "cartridge problem", "one or more cartridges are missing or damaged" or "older generation cartridge". One contributor to HP's support forum said the firmware had been updated "without my permission" and an error message now said the ink cartridge was damaged. "I use it daily for work and now am in trouble," he wrote. "Others must have the same problem. Is there a way to stop HP from doing this to people who have bought their equipment?"
Affected Models and Compatibility
The HP OfficeJet, OfficeJet Pro and OfficeJet Pro X printers are affected. Chipped cartridges filled with alternative ink would still work, HP told the BBC. It said: "These printers will continue to work with refilled or remanufactured cartridges with an original HP security chip. Other cartridges may not function." "In many cases, this functionality was installed in the HP printer and in some cases it has been implemented as part of an update to the printer's firmware," it added.
'(Un)intended result'
123inkt said: "Printer manufacturers regularly execute firmware-updates, claiming that they improve the operation of the printer or solve security issues. The (un)intended result usually is that the operation of lower price private label cartridges is disturbed and error messages are triggered."

The 6D model of national culture
The 6-D model of national culture
Geert Hofstede, assisted by others, came up with six basic issues that society needs to come to term with in order to organize itself. These are called dimensions of culture. Each of them has been expressed on a scale that runs roughly from 0 to 100.
Hofstede's Globe
For interactive world maps and pick-your-own-countries 3-d graphs of Hofstede dimension scores, check Hofstede's Globe in the Geert Hofstede online exhibition "An engineer's Odyssey".
Dimension maps of the world: Individualism
Each dimension has been derived by comparing many, but not all, countries in the world. The findings can be summarized into six world maps of the distribution of that dimension. Of course, in reality there can be quite a bit of within-country variation; these maps should be seen as rough 'climate maps' of culture.
Dimension maps: Power Distance
Dimension maps: Masculinity
Dimension maps: Uncertainty Avoidance
The last two dimensions
The last two dimensions were found later, and in different studies, than the first four. This is why different countries appear on the world maps. These maps are taken from the 2007 book "Why we are different and similar" by Michael Minkov. In our 2010 book they are re-scaled to a 0-100 format. The scale is also reversed for Flexhumility (long-term orientation, blue on the map) versus monumentalism (short-term orientation, orange on the map).
Remember, the numbers do not really 'mean' anything. They are just there for convenience. The world-wide pattern is what matters.
Dimension maps: Long-term Orientation
Dimension maps: Indulgence
The dimensions explained
For each dimension here is a brief description and a ten-minute video in which Geert Hofstede explains that dimension.
Individualism
Individualism is the extent to which people feel independent, as opposed to being interdependent as members of larger wholes. Read more
Individualism does not mean egoism. It means that individual choices and decisions are expected. Collectivism does not mean closeness. It means that one "knows one's place" in life, which is determined socially. With a metaphor from physics, people in an individualistic society are more like atoms flying around in a gas while those in collectivist societies are more like atoms fixed in a crystal.
Power Distance
Power Distance is the extent to which the less powerful members of organizations and institutions (like the family) accept and expect that power is distributed unequally. Read more
This dimension is thought to date from the advent of agriculture, and with it, of large-scale societies. Until that time, a person would know their group members and leaders personally. This is not possible where tens of thousands and more have to coordinate their lives. Without acceptance of leadership by powerful entities, none of today's societies could run.
Masculinity
MasculinityMasculinity is the extent to which the use of force in endorsed socially. Read more
In a masculine society, men are supposed to be tough. Men are supposed to be from Mars, women from Venus. Winning is important for both genders. Quantity is important and big is beautiful. In a feminine society, the genders are emotionally closer. Competing is not so openly endorsed, and there is sympathy for the underdog.
This is NOT about individuals, but about expected emotional gender roles. Masculine societies are much more openly gendered than feminine societies.
Uncertainty Avoidance
Uncertainty avoidance deals with a society’s tolerance for uncertainty and ambiguity. Read more
Uncertainty avoidance has nothing to do with risk avoidance, nor with following rules. It has to do with anxiety and distrust in the face of the unknown, and conversely, with a wish to have fixed habits and rituals, and to know the truth.
Long-term orientation
Long-term orientation deals with change. Read more
In a long-time-oriented culture, the basic notion about the world is that it is in flux, and preparing for the future is always needed. In a short-time-oriented culture, the world is essentially as it was created, so that the past provides a moral compass, and adhering to it is morally good. As you can imagine, this dimension predicts life philosophies, religiosity, and educational achievement.
Indulgence
Indulgence is about the good things in life. Read more
In an indulgent culture it is good to be free. Doing what your impulses want you to do, is good. Friends are important and life makes sense. In a restrained culture, the feeling is that life is hard, and duty, not freedom, is the normal state of being.
Are there more dimensions?
Since dimensions are imagined, not 'out there', there can be many more. Any study will reveal its own pattern, so yes, other dimensions can be found.
Read more
If you are interested, watch new publications by for instance Michael Minkov. Here, for now, we work with the 6D model. It has great validity and practical usability. It predicts real-world phenomena at the level of the nation (or region, in some cases).

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-03-Individual-Attributes-and-Perception/Topic_3_Podcast_Transcript.md

Связь: [[Topic 3 — Individual Attributes and Perception]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Welcome back to BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour. Previously, we have looked
at the importance of effectively managing groups in the workplace, however managers also
need to understand individual differences to influence individual performance in the workplace.
Perception, self-concept, and the perceptual process all shape the way an individual interprets
the environment around them, and thus informs and compounds these individual differences.
This topic examines individual differences in behaviour, personality, values, and perception.
The MARS model identifies the four variables of individual behaviour and performance,
Motivation, Ability, Role Perceptions, and Situational Factors. Motivation is the force within
a person that affects their willingness to perform a job.
Ability is the aptitudes – the potential abilities – and the learned capabilities – which are the
skills and knowledge people already possess. Cognitive, physical, and emotional aptitudes all
contribute towards work performance, and are usually tested for during the recruitment process.
The related job skills can then be enhanced through training and professional development.
Role perceptions are how much a person understands their job duties, and they help clarify
where the person should be directing their effort.
Situational factors are conditions outside of the employees control that help or hinder behaviour
and performance.
If one or more of motivation, ability, role perception, or situational factors are low, then
behaviour and individual performance will be impacted.
There are five main types of workplace behaviour.
Firstly, Task performance refers to goal-directed behaviours under the individual’s control that
support organisational objectives. Proficient task performance is how well the work is
performed, Adaptive task performance is how well employees respond to change in the
workplace and their duties, and Proactive task performance is how well employees take the
initiative to anticipate and change to benefit the organisation.
Organisational citizenship behaviours consist of various forms of cooperation and helpfulness
to others that support the organisation’s social and psychological context, for example assisting
co-workers and sharing work resources. They might be required behaviours, or discretionary
behaviours.
Counterproductive work behaviours are voluntary behaviours that have the potential to harm
the organisation directly or indirectly. These include creating unnecessary conflict, avoiding
work obligations, and taking shortcuts that risk work quality.
Joining and staying with the organisation refers to agreeing to become an organisational
member and remaining with the organisation. These behaviours are influenced by both
individual and organisational factors, and are important to the organisation as increased
employee turnover is costly as there is not only a high cost of replacing people who leave, but
also the cost of lost knowledge in the form of intellectual capital leaving the organisation as
well.
Maintaining work attendance includes minimising absenteeism if capable of working and
avoiding scheduled work if not fit for work. Low work attendance, or high absenteeism, is
attributed to situational factors such as illness or family demands, however aspects such as
work-related stress, or job dissatisfaction are more likely to result in absenteeism.
People exhibit a range of behaviours, however within these there are discernible patterns
referred to as personality traits. Personality is the relatively enduring pattern of thoughts,
emotions and behaviours that characterise a person, along with the psychological processes
behind those characteristics.
Personality traits are broad concepts about people that allow us to label and understand
individual differences. They are impacted by both heredity and environment, and are generally
categorised into five key dimensions of personality, known as “The Big Five”.
Conscientiousness and emotional stability (low neuroticism) predict individual performance in
most job groups. Extraversion is associated with performance in sales and management jobs,
whereas agreeableness is associated with performance in jobs requiring cooperation, and
openness to experience is associated with performance in creative jobs.
The Myers Briggs Type Indicator is another method of categorising personality, and identifies
competing orientations for getting energy, perceiving information, processing information and
making decisions, and orienting to the external world. It is popular in organisations and widely
used, however is a poor predictor of job performance and is not recommended for use in
selection or promotion activities.
These models of personality are not comprehensive, and thus miss out on some positive traits,
such as honesty, interpersonal characteristics, and resilience, as well as negative traits such as
narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy.
Personality profiling helps organisations to filter potential employees with traits that are linked
to required job-specific behaviour. however, there is still concern that it can unfairly
discriminate, and there is the potential for ‘faking’, where people fill in the questionnaires with
what they believe the organisation wants to hear, rather than an accurate representation of
themselves.
Values reflect a persons’ sense of right and wrong, and what they should do, whereas
personality traits reflect what a person naturally tends to do. They can influence workplace
attitudes, behaviours, and outputs and when personal values are similar to team shared values,
and/or organisation values, there is value congruence.
Value congruence is linked to increased job satisfaction and decreased turnover. however, too
much congruity can lead to a corporate cult which undermines creativity, flexibility, and
business ethics. Some value incongruence benefits an organisation as the diversity of opinion
leads to better decision making, and creativity.
Ethical values are viewed as highly important for corporate leaders to have, and a persons
values, their sense of right and wrong, is likely to determine the level of their ethical behaviour.
There are three ethical principles that underline ethical behaviour. End-result ethics, or
utilitarianism, is the ends justify the means, and suggests the end result is what should be
considered when making that decision. Duty based ethics, or individual rights, is the
responsibility we have to others and ourselves to do good. And social contract ethics, or
distributive justice, is the responsibility we have to the common good. All three principles
should be considered when making ethical decisions.
In addition to ethical principles and values, moral intensity- the degree to which an issue
demands the application of ethical principles, moral thresholds – a person’s ability to recognise
and deal with ethical dilemmas, moral foundations – intuition-based principles that govern
judgements and actions, and situational factors such as management pressure influence ethical
conduct in the workforce.
To support ethical behaviour in the workplace, organisations can implement codes of ethical
conduct to motivate and guide employee behaviour, anonymous hotlines for employees to
report unethical behaviour, and ethics audits to identify organisational gaps. However, the most
powerful tool to ensure ethical conduct is shared values reinforcing the ethical conduct which
is supported and modelled by corporate leaders.
Cross cultural values are those that differ across different cultures around the world. Hofstede
summarises these into five categories. Individualism, which is valuing independence and
personal uniqueness; collectivism which is valuing duty to groups we belong to and group
harmony; power distance, which is the extent to which people accept unequal distribution of
power; uncertainty avoidance, which is tolerating or feeling threatened by ambiguity and
uncertainty; and achievement orientation, which is valuing competition over cooperation. An
awareness of these differences can help in understanding different behaviours such as either a
willingness, or hesitance to, speak up to management and voice a differing opinion.
However, many studies into cross cultural values and knowledge have used small samples from
subsets of the population, and generalise, which may not represent an entire culture. They also
tend to assume that countries have one culture, which is increasingly not the case. And applying
cross-cultural knowledge without keeping this in mind can lead to stereotyping, which is one
of the errors that can influence the perceptual process.
Perception is the process of receiving information about, and making sense of, the world around
us.
The process usually follows the steps of Receiving environmental stimuli through our senses,
subconsciously selecting which stimuli to focus on, organising, and interpreting that
information using categorical thinking and mental models, to determine attitudes and
behaviours.
To efficiently manage the amount of information we have to process, our brain has developed
methods to select and sort information. These methods, although increasing efficiency,
sometimes result in errors.
Confirmation bias occurs as a result of selective attention, where we tend to focus on, or select,
the information that confirms our beliefs, and ignore information that contradicts this. For
example, if we believe that a particular project is a good investment, any evidence that
reinforces this belief will stand out more, and seem more relevant than evidence to the contrary.
In the organisation and interpretation stage, the brain categorises people, objects, and situations
with other similar items such as by gender, age, race, clothing style, proximity, or interests. It
also attempts to fill in the blanks, so if there is information you don’t know, it will assume it
based on prior images or experience.
This is how stereotyping can occur subconsciously, as the brain groups people into a category
based on a small amount of information, and then assumes other characteristics based on them
belonging to that category. Stereotypes are formed to some extent through personal experience,
but are mostly developed through exposure to media. Although everyone engages in
stereotyping as a non-conscious energy saving process that simplifies our understanding of the
world, it leads to perceptual biases and flawed decision making, as every individual is unique,
and not defined by a social group to which they belong.
The attribution process is another area of perception that can lead to perceptual errors and affect
decision making. This is where a decision is made as to whether the behaviour, action, or event
was caused by external or internal factors. Self-serving bias is the tendency to take credit for
success, and blame others for failure. For example, if your favourite sports team won, it was
due to them being more skilled, more dedicated in training, and executing a better strategy.
Whereas if your favourite sports team lost, it was due to poor referee calls, or the opposing
team playing unfairly, or unforeseen injuries.
Self-fulfilling prophecy explains the situation where our perception influences our behaviour,
which then reinforces the initial perception. For example, if a manager believes that an
employee will do well, then they are likely to provide more support and challenging goals,
which then lead the employee to do well. On the other hand, if a manager believes that an
employee will perform poorly, and reprimands and monitors them closely, the employee is
likely to become resentful and perform poorly, which they would not have done if the manager
had had an initial belief that they would perform well. Because of this, it is important that
managers maintain a positive, but realistic, perception of all employees and that organisations
have a culture of support and learning.
Halo effect is similar to stereotyping, however rather than assuming characteristics of a person
based on a group to which they belong, you assume characteristics of a person based on one
prominent characteristic or event. For example, assuming someone is a bad student who doesn’t
care about their grades because they turned up unprepared, or late, to class.
False-consensus effect is where we assume that the way we think or behave is the way most
people are thinking or behaving. For example if you believe the company you work for doesn’t
care about their employees and treats them poorly, you would also assume that most of your
coworkers also feel the same way.
Primacy effect is the term for judging a book by its cover, or the lasting nature of first
impressions. A negative first impression is very difficult to change, as after categorising that
person negatively, we selectively focus on information that confirms that impression.
Finally, recency effect is when the most recent information takes precedence in our perception
and decision making. This is seen when managers undertaking an annual review of an
employees performance focus on the most recent performance as it’s most easily recalled,
rather than looking at the whole year overall.
As we are all human, we cannot bypass the perceptual process, however we should try to
minimise perceptual errors and biases to make sure our decision making is as objective as
possible. We can improve perception firstly through an awareness of perceptual biases, as
knowing they exist makes it easier to identify when you are potentially making a perception
error. Secondly, improving self-awareness involves becoming more aware of your own beliefs,
values, and attitudes, which increases understanding of patterns and biases in your own
decision making and behaviours, and tends to make people more open minded and less
judgemental. Finally, meaningful interaction is spending time with, and working closely with,
others. This increases our knowledge about individuals and as we get to know them, and their
unique attributes, better, we have increased empathy and understanding towards them, and rely
less on the mental shortcuts that result in perceptual errors.
These methods for improving perception are also needed for developing a global mindset, as it
is the ability to perceive, appreciate, and empathise with people from other cultures and to
process complex cross-cultural information. With increasing globalisation, diversity, and
transnational corporations, having a global mindset is becoming increasingly valued in
organisations. A global mindset enables people and organisations to develop better cross-
cultural relationships, digest huge volumes of cross-cultural information, form networks and
exchange resources more rapidly across borders, and to identify and respond more quickly to
emerging global opportunities.
Self-concept is internal perceptions, or how we perceive ourselves. It is the self-beliefs and
self-evaluations that guide decisions and actions, including whether or not a role or company
is a good fit with who you are and who you want to be.
Self-concept has three facets, complexity, consistency, and clarity. Complexity is the number
of distinct identities or roles people fill, for example mother, sister, daughter, friend, student,
engineer, and manager. High complexity protects self-esteem when one identity is damaged by
failure, and contributes to adaptive decision making and performance, however maintaining
and juggling these can be stressful. Low complexity people who identify mostly with their
work identity often invest more in skill development and have lower absenteeism and turnover.
Consistency is how similar these roles or identities are. Some people move between roles and
identities more easily than others, and occupational self-concept, or the ability for a person to
focus on their work-self, is important for when someone is working from home. Finally, Clarity
is the confidence in, and awareness of their important identities. High clarity is seen as essential
for leadership, and enables people to more efficiently direct their effort towards career
objectives, it also reduces the threat of interpersonal conflict and so leads to more constructive
problem solving behaviours to resolve conflict. However, it can also contribute to role
inflexibility and make it difficult to adapt to changing job duties and organisational conditions.
Low self-concept clarity leads to increased stress when making decisions and increased threat
of social forces that undermine self-confidence and self-esteem.
Wellbeing generally increases with higher levels of the aspects of self-concept.
There are four processes that shape self-concept. Self enhancement is the motivation to have a
positive self-concept, and have others perceive them favourably. It tends to lead to
overconfidence, with individuals rating themselves above average, and can contribute to a can-
do attitude, however this also increases risk-taking behaviour and taking longer to recognise
their mistakes.
Self verification is the motivation to confirm and maintain their self-concept, for example when
people accept compliments that confirm their beliefs about themselves, but reject those that
don’t. This affects the giving of and acceptance of feedback in the workplace.
Self-evaluation is mostly defined by three elements. Self-esteem represents an overall
evaluation and is how much a person likes, respects and is satisfied with themselves. Self-
efficacy is how much someone believes they can accomplish a task, and locus of control is how
much belief a person has in their ability to control personal life events. Having high self-esteem,
high self-efficacy, and an internal locus of control is generally associated with increased
wellbeing.
Finally, the social self identifies the motivation for individuality – someone’s personal identity,
and the motivation for belonging – their social identity. Everyone tries to balance these
identities, but an individual’s priorities can differ, for example a doctor may have a high priority
towards their social identity due to the status awarded by being a member of the medical
profession. People who prioritise social identities are more likely to abide by team norms and
be influenced by peer pressure.
Self-concept has quite a significant effect on individual behaviour in many ways, including
perception and decision making, motivation, team dynamics and leadership, and several other
organisational behaviour topics, and thus will be revisited in later podcasts.
Managers, and team members, need to understand individual differences in order to influence
individual performance in the workplace. These individual differences impact the motivation,
ability, and role perceptions aspects of the MARS model of individual behaviour, and should
be used to maximise the performance of an organisation, and your assignment teams. Try
reducing perceptual biases and increasing meaningful interactions with your team members to
improve communication and interactions, and consequently produce a better report overall.
Thank you.
