## 📄 02-topics/Topic-05-Job-Satisfaction/Topic_5_Podcast_Transcript.md

Связь: [[Topic 5 — Job Satisfaction]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Welcome back to BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour. Last time, we looked at the
conceptual foundations of employee motivation and the practical applications. Job satisfaction
can also be impacted by emotions, attitudes, and stress. In addition, intrinsic job satisfaction
can be improved through effective job design and flexible work arrangements. This topic
introduces various types of job design, and organisational strategies to manage stress and
improve individual satisfaction.
Job satisfaction represents a person’s evaluation of their job and work context, and
dissatisfaction with their job affects behaviour and results. There are four types of job
dissatisfaction consequences, which are similar to those experienced when there is inequity in
the workplace.
Exit – which is quitting or otherwise getting away from the dissatisfying situation.
Voice – which is attempting to change the dissatisfying situation
Loyalty – which is patiently waiting for the problem to sort itself out,
and Neglect – which is reducing work effort and performance.
Loyalty is the employee’s emotional attachment to, identification with and involvement in a
particular organisation. This contrasts with continuance commitment, which is a logical,
calculated bond with the organisation. Organisations can increase commitment through justice
and support, shared values, trust, organisational comprehension and employee involvement.
Emotions such as those that contribute to organisational loyalty, are physiological, behavioural
and psychological episodes experienced towards an object, person or event that create a state
of readiness. They are brief experiences, and influence behaviour without cognitive awareness
by predisposing us to either approach or avoid objects, people, or events based on the emotion
experienced. Emotions differ from attitudes, as while emotions are subconscious, fleeting
experiences, attitudes are judgements that are generally conscious, and stable over time.
Attitudes have traditionally been described as a purely rational process, but we now know that
emotions have an influence on behaviour that is equal to or greater than that of cognition. This
dual process is apparent when we experience an internal conflict between what logically seems
good or bad and what we emotionally feel is good or bad in a situation.
Emotional intelligence is the ability to perceive and express emotion, assimilate emotion in
thought, understand and reason with emotion, and regulate emotion in oneself and others. This
concept includes four components arranged in a hierarchy:
Self-awareness, which is perceiving and understanding your own emotions
Self-management, which is keeping disruptive emotions in check and displaying positive
emotions when required. This also includes generating and suppressing emotions.
Social awareness, which is perceiving and understanding the emotions of other people, this
includes having empathy, but also being organisationally aware and sensing office politics and
understanding social networks.
Finally, relationship management which is managing others’ emotions through consoling
someone who is sad, inspiring team members to complete a project, getting strangers to
comfortably work with you, and managing dysfunctional conflict between team members.
Emotional intelligence can be learned to some extent, particularly through personal coaching.
Jobs requiring a variety of emotions and more intense emotions, as well as in jobs where
interaction with clients is frequent and has a long duration, generally involves a large amout of
emotional labour. Emotional labour consists of the effort, planning and control needed to
express organisationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions.
Cultures also differ on the norms of displaying or concealing a person’s true emotions.
Emotional dissonance occurs when required and true emotions are incompatible with each
other. Deep acting, which is visualising reality differently to produce emotions more consistent
with the required emotions, can minimise this dissonance, as can the practice of hiring people
with a natural tendency to display desired emotions.
Stress another somewhat subconscious adaptive response to a situation that is perceived as
challenging or threatening to a person’s wellbeing. It is generally seen as negative, called
distress, however some level of stress activates and motivates people to achieve their goals,
and this is known as eustress. The causes of stress include any environmental conditions that
place a physical or emotional demand on a person, and three stressors that have received
considerable attention are harassment and incivility, work overload, and low task control.
Interventions to manage work-related stress include removing the stressor, withdrawing from
the stressor, changing stress perceptions, controlling stress consequences and receiving social
support.
One of the main organisational strategies to remove stressors is the introduction of policies to
improve work-life balance. These include flexible work time, job sharing, telecommuting,
personal leave, child care support, and job crafting.
The design of a job is a situational factor and can significantly increase or decrease the stressors
of work overload and task control.
Job design is the process of assigning tasks to a job, including the interdependency of those
tasks with other jobs.
Job specialisation is standardising work procedures and employing people in clearly defined
and specialised tasks, for example jobs on an assembly line in car manufacturing. Advantages
include increased operating efficiency, low skill and low-cost labour, minimal training
requirements, and controlled production quality. However, specialised jobs lack challenge and
lead to boredom, and there are then costs in terms of higher rates of absenteeism and turnover,
and the need to pay higher wages for people to do these “unattractive” jobs. Increasingly, the
natural extension of job specialisation is automation, with machines replacing the employees
needed to complete these highly repetitive jobs.
Job enlargement emerged in the 1950s as an attempt to reduce the boredom associated with
simplified jobs. Employees were given an increased number of tasks, and this increased task
variety was presumed to reduce the disadvantages of job simplification and therefore increase
intrinsic motivation. However, job enlargement doesn’t necessarily increase responsibility, or
autonomy, it may simply just increase the number of mundane tasks an employee performs, so
there are limits as to how much it can satisfy an employee.
Job rotation is similar to job enlargement in that it increases task variety, but does this through
periodically shifting workers between jobs involving different tasks at a similar level. It has
the advantage of enabling younger employees to learn the ropes in an organisation by rotating
them through different areas. It also increases workforce flexibility, with the workforce more
adaptable to accommodate when employees are sick, on leave, or have left the organisation. It
has a similar disadvantage to job enlargement though, as periodically changing the mundane
tasks performed does not increase their intrinsic motivation potential, only increases the
horizontal loading, or breadth of jobs, by increasing the number of tasks performed. If job
rotation includes vertical loading, where job depth is increased through adding responsibilities
previously held by supervisors, then this can contribute to employee development and reduce
some of the previous disadvantages of job rotation. Vertical loading is a key part of job
enrichment.
Job enrichment is the practice of building motivating factors into job content. It focusses on
increasing vertical loading, rather than the horizontal loading which is seen in job rotation and
job enlargement. The job characteristics model sets out five core job characteristics required
for a job to be enriched. These are skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and
feedback. The core job characteristics then need to transform into employees feeling that the
work is meaningful, they are responsible for the outcomes, and knowledge of actual results of
the work. If this occurs, it should result in high intrinsic work motivation and satisfaction, high
quality work performance, and low absenteeism and turnover. However, the job characteristics
model also takes into account individual differences of growth-need strength, knowledge and
skill, and context satisfaction, and therefore the idea that different people will respond
differently to job enrichment. Two ways to enrich jobs are clustering tasks into natural groups
and establishing client relationships.
Job design is a major influence in empowerment, particularly autonomy, task identity, task
significance and job feedback. Empowerment is also supported at the organisational level
through a learning orientation culture, sufficient information and resources, and corporate
leaders who trust employees.
Money and other financial rewards make up a fundamental aspect of the employment
relationship and are another situational factor related to job satisfaction and performance.
Financial rewards also affect our needs, our emotions and our self-concept.
Organisations reward employees for a variety of things.
Membership-based rewards are those offered for simply being an employee of the organisation
such as fixed pay, benefits, and paid leave. They may attract job applicants, and seniority-based
rewards reduce turnover, however these reward objectives also tend to discourage turnover
among those with the lowest performance.
Job status based rewards include pay increases on promotion and position-level benefits. They
try to maintain internal equity and motivate employees to compete for promotions. However,
they tend to encourage a bureaucratic hierarchy, support status differences and motivate
employees to compete and hoard resources.
Competency-based rewards such as skill-based pay are becoming increasingly popular because
they encourage skill development. However, they tend to be subjectively measured and can
result in higher costs as employees spend more time learning new skills.
Task performance based rewards include commission based pay and profit sharing. These
motivate task performance, attract performance-oriented staff, and create an ownership culture.
However, they discourage creativity and tend to address symptoms, not underlying causes of
behaviour. Employees often perceive a weak connection between individual performance and
the organisational rewards such as profit sharing.
Reward effectiveness can be improved in several ways, which can be seen in relation to
expectancy theory principles. Organisational leaders should ensure that rewards are linked to
work performance, rewards are aligned with performance within the employee’s control, team
rewards are used where jobs are interdependent, rewards are valued by employees, rewards
have no unintended consequences and rewards are adapted to suit the cultural context in which
they are used.
Financial rewards and the design of the job have traditionally been considered as the main
elements of job satisfaction, however it is now known that emotions, attitudes, and stress can
have as much, if not more impact on how someone evaluates their job. In order to maximise
job satisfaction, organisations should focus on the factors they control, such as stressors, and
individuals should aim to be aware of their emotions and improve their emotional intelligence
and perceptions of the job itself.

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-05-Job-Satisfaction/Topic_5_Workshop_Solution.md

Связь: [[Topic 5 — Job Satisfaction]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

**BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour**

Topic 5 - Workshop Activities (Emotions/Attitudes/Stress & Applied Performance Practices)

Name: Faiaz Dzhafarov  Student No: 35553299

# Activity 1: Critical Thinking Questions (Chapters 4 & 6)

## Chapter 4, Question 3 - Emotional labour for college instructors

Emotional labour gets hard when a job means dealing with people a lot, showing a range of emotions, and following strict display rules. A college instructor runs into this all the time. They have to stay calm but firm when a student asks for an extension yet again. They have to look genuinely keen in the last hour of class after already teaching for six hours. And they need to seem interested and respectful when someone asks a really basic question. That said, I think emergency call-centre operators have it worse. Their emotional events are far more extreme, they have to stay calm and console people, and they cope with the frustration of life-threatening situations. Those demands are generally more intense than anything an instructor faces.

## Chapter 4, Question 5 - Building the four components of emotional intelligence

For awareness of one's own emotions, coaching helps: trainees reflect on and describe what they felt during an observed event, then get peer feedback. This works a bit like the Johari Window, where feedback enlarges the open, self-aware area. The daily version is simple, just pause to label what you are feeling and why.

Managing your own emotions can be built through training events that force you to regulate emotion, such as handling a difficult customer, with coach or peer feedback afterwards. On a daily basis, ask coworkers how you came across emotionally once a meeting wraps up.

Awareness of others' emotions improves with practice reading emotions from facial expressions in images or clips, followed by discussion, plus genuine dialogue with people from other social groups to build empathy. Day to day, observe and describe how others seem to be feeling, and have relaxed, nondirective chats.

Finally, managing others' emotions is best developed through real-world activities or role plays where the trainee engages another party (a customer or an actor) and the coach and peers debrief on how well that person's emotions were handled.

## Chapter 6, Question 1 - Gainsharing vs profit sharing for four warehouses

I would go with a gainsharing plan in each of the four regional facilities. Gainsharing rewards a team for cutting costs and improving labour efficiency in its own work process, while profit sharing spreads a slice of corporate profits across a broad group. These warehouse employees have almost no sway over corporate profits, but they can genuinely move the needle on costs and efficiency in their own facility, and rewards land best when people actually control the outcomes being measured. Gainsharing is also team-based and targeted at the four facilities, which fits the brief: reward people inside those facilities rather than the whole organisation.

## Chapter 6, Question 4 - Five strategies for a performance-based reward system

**Link rewards to performance.** The system uses objective criteria (sales, returns, waste) and a bonus big enough to create positive emotions. The weakness is that store-level performance may weaken the individual effort-to-performance expectancy in larger stores.

**Ensure rewards are relevant.** Criteria need to sit within employees' control. Sales can be swayed by economic conditions or local demographics, so the company may need to adjust measures across stores to account for these external factors.

**Use team rewards for interdependent jobs.** A store-level reward fits here because staff are interdependent within a store but largely independent across stores. If some roles have low interdependence, the company can add individual-level criteria.

**Ensure rewards are valued.** A uniform lump-sum bonus leaves little room to tailor to individual preferences. One fix is to let employees convert part of the bonus into discounted goods or services.

**Check for unintended consequences.** The risks here are real. People may chase the measured outcomes while neglecting unmeasured ones like inventory and personal service, and some behaviours carry hidden costs, for example a reluctance to accept legitimate returns, which can harm long-term reputation. It is safer to pilot the scheme first. Gaming is unlikely given the objective data.

## Chapter 6, Question 5 - Job specialization in pizzerias

Busy pizzerias usually run fairly high specialization, with different people on dough, filling orders, unloading and cutting and boxing, the register, and delivery. That high specialization lifts efficiency: no time is lost switching tasks, skills develop faster (handy where shops lean on part-time or temporary staff), and people get matched to the task that suits them. Smaller shops tend to go the other way, with two people sharing most of the work. The contingencies behind the difference come down to shop size and volume plus technology. A conveyor oven supports two people loading and unloading, whereas a fixed oven may suit one person tracking cooking times. Some shops also rotate jobs through a shift to cut boredom and repetitive-strain injury.

## Chapter 6, Question 8 - Self-leadership to reduce supervisory costs

Self-leadership is the set of cognitive and behavioural strategies people use to motivate and direct themselves: setting their own goals, monitoring their behaviour, using positive self-talk, and rewarding themselves. It can take over some supervisory roles, which supports the city manager's aim, but it cannot cover everything. Managers are still needed for macro-level planning, dividing up work, and resolving interpersonal and interdepartmental conflict, and some employees just do not take to self-leadership easily. So the manager could reduce the number of supervisors without eliminating them, and at the very least free up supervisors' time as employees, once trained, take on more.

As a training module example, take personal goal setting. You teach the features of effective (SMARTER) goals, have participants write goals for their own job, and give feedback. A follow-up module then focuses on the daily habit, with a coach checking whether the employee set goals that day, how well they stayed focused, and how their goal-setting has improved.

# Activity 2: Case Study - ‘YakkaTech, Inc.’ (Chapter 6)

## Question 1 - Symptoms that something has gone wrong

There were several warning signs: poorer customer service, employee indifference to client problems, slow response times, and staff who lacked knowledge about each client. On top of that, staff turnover was high before the reward-system change, employee referrals were declining, and productivity dropped.

## Question 2 - Main causes

**Jobs have low motivational potential.** Run the work through the five core job characteristics and the picture is poor. Skill variety is moderate but turns monotonous. Task identity looks high per ticket yet is actually low, because the real "whole" task is the client's whole system. Task significance is low, since staff don't see their impact on clients. Autonomy is hemmed in by the ticket system. And job feedback is very low, because staff never learn whether their fix lasted. All of this predicts low meaningfulness, lower satisfaction, and lower effectiveness, which is exactly what the case shows.

**Poor alignment of money and rewards.** Raising pay and adding a vested profit-sharing plan did reduce turnover, but the design was misaligned. The rewards barely reflect individual performance in a firm this size, the bonus is delayed two years, and the system rewards individual membership even though the work is interdependent, with shared tickets and on-site teams.

**Continuance commitment ('golden handcuffs').** The vested plan makes leaving costly, which builds continuance commitment, and that tends to drag down job performance and satisfaction. Both got worse after it came in.

**EVLN.** The Exit, Voice, Loyalty, Neglect model captures the responses well: Exit (high turnover until the pay incentive), Voice (indirect complaints and survey results), little Loyalty, and Neglect (poor service, not passing on jobs).

## Question 3 - Recommended actions

**Redesign jobs through job enrichment.** Organise individuals, or better still teams, around clients so the same staff handle all of a client's IT problems. This lifts task identity and significance, sharpens client knowledge and feedback, and builds felt responsibility along with a psychological closeness to the client.

**Realign rewards.** Once jobs are redesigned around client teams, use a team-based reward tied to specific long-term client outcomes. Profit sharing could stay, but more proximate, performance-linked rewards are the better bet.

# Activity 3: Team Exercise - ‘Is Student Work Enriched?’

This exercise uses the Job Diagnostic Survey to estimate the motivating-potential score (MPS) of being a student. Each core characteristic is averaged from three survey questions, namely skill variety (SV), task identity (TI), task significance (TS), autonomy (A) and job feedback (JF), then combined as:

MPS = ((SV + TI + TS) / 3) × A × JF.

Each of us works out our own MPS from our survey answers, the team compares results, and we then benchmark them against the reference MPS scores for occupational groups (for example Managerial 156, Sales 146, US national average 128, Clerical 106). One discussion point worth raising is that student work often lands in the moderate range. Autonomy and feedback are usually the characteristics that swing the score most, up or down, and the exercise shows how the five characteristics combine to make work feel meaningful and motivating.

# Activity 4: Team Meeting - Milestone Progress

We reported progress to the workshop facilitator and recorded it on the LMS Team Discussion Forum. The meeting confirmed that the discussion section had moved from an outline to a rough draft.

Each member walked through where their challenge stood. The dot-point outlines agreed at the last meeting had been written up into draft text: Bobur on Communication and on Collaboration and Cohesion, Faiaz on Team Trust, and Owethu on Remote and flexible work, each linking the team-dynamics theory back to Westpac. We checked the drafts against the marking rubric and the Detailed Report Guidelines to make sure every challenge was analysed against theory and that the recommendations would tie back to the UN Global Compact.

We also planned the remaining research. A couple of the challenges still needed stronger Westpac-specific evidence, so we allocated who would chase which sources, and we agreed to send the lecturer a short section of the draft for feedback before finalising. Any changes to the plan, including the tighter timeline after Wahid's departure, were recorded on the Team Discussion Forum.

Готово — Workshop 6 (Chapter 13: Designing Organisational Structures), 34 слайда. Содержательных заметок докладчика нет. Полный дамп на английском:

---

**SLIDE 1 — Title**
BUS293 / Organisational Theory and Behaviour / CHAPTER THIRTEEN / BUS293 Murdoch University / Designing Organisational Structures

**SLIDE 2 — Acknowledgement of Country**
We acknowledge that Murdoch University is situated on the lands of the Whadjuk and Binjareb Noongar people. We pay our respect to their enduring and dynamic culture and the leadership of Noongar elders past and present. The boodjar (country) on which Murdoch University is located has, for thousands of years, been a place of learning. We at Murdoch University are proud to continue this long tradition.

**SLIDE 3 — Workshop Six Outline**

- Critical thinking questions (20 minutes)
- Case study questions (20 minutes)
- 5-minute break(?)
- Team activity (20 minutes)
- Team meeting (30 minutes)

**SLIDE 4 — Critical Thinking Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow (2024) Chapter 13, p491 — Questions 3, 4, 5 & 7.

**SLIDE 5 — Chapter 13 Question 3**
Administrative theorists concluded many decades ago that the most effective organisations have a narrow span of control. Yet today's top-performing manufacturing firms have a wider span of control. Why is this possible? Under what circumstances, if any, should manufacturing firms use a narrow span of control?

**SLIDE 6 — Ch13 Q3**
Flatter structures:

- less overheads (fewer middle managers, more people directly involved in the production of goods and/or services)
- greater autonomy and employee involvement (mostly due to managers having a wider span of control — more direct employees/teams means less close supervision, therefore employees/teams are given more freedom to make decisions without management review)
  A narrow span of control would be most appropriate when the workforce is: low skilled; and made up of workers with a high power distance (as the close supervision and control would be less likely to be viewed as a lack of trust).

**SLIDE 7 — Chapter 13 Question 4**
Leaders of large organisations struggle to identify the best level and types of centralisation and decentralisation. What should companies consider when determining the degree of decentralisation?

**SLIDE 8 — Ch13 Q4**
As organizations grow they tend to diversify, and as their environments become more complex it is necessary to decentralize — the burden on senior executives who must process all decisions becomes overwhelming, so dispersing decision-making authority (decentralizing) is the best response. Contingencies to consider:

- **External environment.** Decentralized structures suit complex rather than simple environments; it is best to temporarily centralize when operating in a hostile environment.
- **Organizational size.** When the organization grows larger, with more specialized jobs, more elaborate coordinating mechanisms, and greater formalization, it is better to decentralize.
- **Technology.** Where technology requires many exceptions to standard procedures (high variety) and it's difficult to standardize the transformation of inputs to outputs (low analyzability), rely on decentralized decision making.
- **Organizational strategy.** All the above contingencies are mediated by the organization's overall strategy. E.g., Johnson & Johnson's decentralized divisional structure fits its strategy of developing and delivering a diverse array of health-related products worldwide.

**SLIDE 9 — Chapter 13 Question 5**
Mechanistic and organic structures are two organisational forms. How do the three types of coordination mechanisms operate through these forms?

**SLIDE 10 — Ch13 Q5**
Three coordination mechanisms: **informal communication, formal hierarchy, standardisation.**

- **Mechanistic structures** have high formalisation and centralisation, limited lower-level decision making, and rigidly defined tasks; therefore **formal hierarchy and standardisation** are the coordination mechanisms used.
- **Organic structures** operate with a wide span of control, decentralised decision making, and little formalisation, and hence make more use of **informal communication.**

**SLIDE 11 — Chapter 13 Question 7**
From an employee perspective, what are the advantages and disadvantages of working in a matrix structure?

**SLIDE 12 — Ch13 Q7**

- **Advantages.** When properly managed, matrix structures enhance communication efficiencies, provide flexibility to balance workload with other project team members, and allow employees to interact and coordinate with others who have similar technical specialties. They require (and develop) enhanced communication and interpersonal skills, so employees may enjoy enhanced training and development opportunities. _(Note: the source slide contains a garbled clause — "lend further evidence against the argument that all of the key features of organizational structure… are found in descriptions of the several forms of departmentalization" — appears to be an editing error in the deck.)_
- **Disadvantages.** May result in increased stress, conflict, and organizational politics due to having **two bosses** with potentially divergent expectations. Some employees may struggle to adapt to the relatively fluid nature of a matrix vs. a more structured bureaucracy.

**SLIDE 13 — Case Study Questions (section)**
McShane and Von Glinow (2024) Chapter 13, Case Study: 'SLOAN & WU, INC'.

**SLIDE 14 — Case Study Question 1**
Describe the proposed changes at Sloan & Wu in terms of the four elements of organizational structure.

**SLIDE 15 — Case Study Question 1 (1/2)**

- **Span of Control** — Sloan & Wu now introduces a _narrower_ span of control at the district level but a much _wider_ one at the regional level. District managers will be responsible for an average of 10 stores (vs. 15 previously), so each manages fewer store managers, enabling closer/more effective work with each store. Merchandising and operations decision makers have been moved from regional to district offices. The new structure creates a wider regional span of control. Previously: five regions, 30 districts (avg six districts per region), plus assistant regional managers as a management layer (which may have narrowed the regional span — e.g., two assistant regional managers per region → span of 3 district managers; or one per region → six direct reports while the regional director had just one direct report). The new structure consolidates into **three regions**, removes the **assistant regional manager** layer, and expands districts from 30 to 45 — so each regional manager is now responsible for ~15 district managers.
- **Centralization/decentralization** — When the three regional retailers were acquired, Sloan & Wu centralized many activities (esp. merchandising and marketing), a key reason products were shipped to regions without demand (e.g., winter coats in Florida and Southern California). The new structure clearly **decentralizes** power — most importantly decentralizing merchandise and marketing to district and store managers ("gives more autonomy to local districts and stores to personalize merchandise and marketing for customers in that area"). The CEO calls it a "devolved" structure.

**SLIDE 16 — Case Study Question 1 (2/2)**

- **Formalization** — Increased when Sloan & Wu acquired the regional chains (standardized store designs, merchandising, marketing across all acquired stores). The new structure _reduces_ formalization to some degree because district/store managers gain autonomy (less systems control) to understand and quickly deliver what locals want ("localization"), and will have more flexible processes for working with vendors. At the same time, formalization may _increase_ through technology tracking which products are in stock at each store and documenting items, brands, garment sizes, and colors preferred by local customers — managers must abide by this increased systems feedback (a type of formalization).
- **Departmentalization** — Changes mostly in the number of units at each level: previously 30 districts across five US regions; new structure is 45 districts in three regions (East, South, West). Most other aspects of the reorganization would NOT be evident in the org chart (e.g., decentralized power, shift of merchandising/marketing/planning staff from regions and HQ to districts).

**SLIDE 17 — Case Study Question 2**
What contingencies suggest that Sloan & Wu's new organizational structure is appropriate or inappropriate?

**SLIDE 18 — Case Study Question 2 (1/3)**

- **Dynamic vs stable environment** — Customers have varied needs across regions/districts and preferences change relatively quickly (hence merchandising/marketing decentralized to district/store levels). But the environment is relatively stable in many respects (customer behavior — visiting stores, buying online, returning merchandise — is predictable over the medium term, as are supplier/vendor processes). Sloan & Wu needs a structure **between organic and mechanistic**, achieved through decentralization and somewhat less formalization at district/store levels where dynamics are felt.
- **Complex vs simple environment** — Department store chains operate in moderately complex environments (different products, diverse customers); large size and nationwide location add complexity; wide variety of products/services (clothing to white goods to restaurants) adds more. The more complex the environment, the more decentralized — which is what Sloan & Wu is doing.

**SLIDE 19 — Case Study Question 2 (2/3)**

- **Diverse vs integrated environment** — Diverse environments have greater variety of products/services, clients, regions. Sloan & Wu is diverse (diverse geography, customers with diverse needs); main diversity is likely geographic, while customer variations (age cohorts, product types) may be less distinct (clothing buyers also buy kitchen appliances). Decentralizing makes sense to accommodate area-specific variation. Less clear whether to organize into separate divisions/store brands by product or customer group. The more diversified the environment, the more a **divisional structure** aligned with that diversity is needed — but a geographic divisional structure probably isn't required here: (1) customer variation is at district/local level, not regional, and 45 divisions (one per district) would be chaotic/inefficient; (2) customers aren't "diverse" across districts in every way (vary in clothing by climate/regional style, but similar nationwide for items like kitchen appliances). So decentralization is probably sufficient without a divisional structure.

**SLIDE 20 — Case Study Question 2 (3/3)**

- **Hostile vs munificent environment** — No evidence of extreme resource scarcity/competition; lost market share due to overly standardized buying but remains competitive. Probably not an important contingency; decentralizing for other reasons also addresses any hostility.
- **Organizational size** — Relatively large, so it uses **standardization** as a coordinating mechanism (e.g., inventory management work-process systems) and elaborate formal authority (emphasis on district managers) — generally appropriate for its size, though presenting opposing challenges.
- **Technology** — Task variability and analyzability vary across employees/levels, but most employees perform tasks with fairly low variability and medium-high analyzability (predictable customer behavior and buying processes). Some task variability from changing fashion/consumer trends for some products, but trends don't dramatically alter predictability of buying/stocking/selling. With moderately low task variability and medium-high analyzability, Sloan & Wu operates best with a structure **somewhat more mechanistic than organic** — similar to the new structure.
- **Organizational strategy** — The CEO suggests a strategy shifting toward **creativity and innovation** rather than high efficiency/low cost, calling for a structure closer to **organic**. Whether the new structure is sufficiently organic is unclear, but it's moving in the recommended direction.

**SLIDE 21 — Case Study Question 3**
What problems do you think Sloan & Wu might experience with the new organizational structure? Explain why these problems might occur.

**SLIDE 22 — Case Study Question 3**
Two potential problems are stated by two retail analysts:

1. The new structure may **inflate costs** — 50% more districts than before, and merchandising/marketing now occur more at district level (likely requiring more people overall than in the regional offices). District managers have a narrower span of control ("10 vs. 115 direct reports, on average" — _в исходном слайде стоит «115», что выглядит как опечатка; по логике кейса должно быть «15»_), suggesting higher payroll costs.
2. The company's **emphasis on formal authority** as a coordinating mechanism: "It seems that centralized control is just being replaced with district manager control over the store managers and their staff" — i.e., rather than empowering district/store managers, the new structure just creates closer supervision of store managers.
   Another potential problem: decentralized decision making can create **too much variability** across the organization. Localization is valuable for some products but probably not all/most; customers visiting a store in another region may be less receptive to significant variations in store format, marketing, merchandising. Localized decision making also increases the risk of **bad and potentially unethical decisions** — beyond district-manager oversight, it isn't clear how Sloan & Wu will help managers make informed/legal decisions (e.g., district managers working directly with vendors could lead to inappropriate arrangements). Districts might also **compete with each other** for supplier merchandise; presumably HQ staff do major buying, otherwise Sloan & Wu may pay higher prices.

**SLIDE 23 — The Club Ed Exercise (section)**
McShane et al. 2019, p493 (end of Chapter 13).

**SLIDE 24 — Instructions**

- Read the scenario.
- Design an organisational chart that is most appropriate for this situation.
- You should be able to describe the type of structure drawn and explain why it is appropriate.
- There will be 4 scenarios total; you can re-use and edit, or redraw, but changes to structure will be needed for each scenario.

**SLIDE 25 — Club Ed Exercise – Scenario 1**
Determined to never suffer another cold winter, you secured venture capital funding for a new resort business called Club Ed on a small Caribbean island. The resort is under construction and is scheduled to open in less than one year. The resort will employ approximately 75 staff (most employed full-time).

- Design an organisational chart that best suits this organisation when it opens.
- Describe the type of structure drawn and explain why it is appropriate.

**SLIDE 26 — Club Ed Exercise – Scenario 2**
It is now five years later. Your resort has been wildly successful. Through profits and investment from private equity partners, Club Ed recently expanded to five resorts and plans to add 12 more within the next year. These resorts are equally spread around the Caribbean, Central America, and South Pacific.

- Design an organisational chart that would best serve this organisation.
- Describe the type of structure drawn and explain why it is appropriate.

**SLIDE 27 — Club Ed Exercise – Scenario 3**
Ten years after opening the first resort, your organization now has 30 resorts. Furthermore, your firm is about to launch a charter airline from four major cities in your home country to the destinations where its resorts are located. The airline will transport guests to your own resorts but will also serve as a charter airline for other resorts and tour operators in those regions.

- Design an organisational chart that would best serve this organisation.
- Describe the type of structure drawn and explain why it is appropriate.

**SLIDE 28 — Club Ed Exercise – Scenario 4**
Fifteen years after opening its first resort, Club Ed has 75 successful resorts throughout the Caribbean, Central America, South Pacific, and Asia. Its charter airline now has regular flights from several major cities in your country to almost a dozen destinations nearest those resorts (and serves other resorts and tour operators in those areas). This year, Club Ed acquired a rapidly growing adventure travel agency, which specializes in small-group socially responsible guided excursions to remote locations around the world. Club Ed plans to market these adventure travel excursions to travelers from other parts of the world.

- Design an organisational chart that would best serve this organisation in this situation.
- Describe the type of structure drawn and explain why it is appropriate.

**SLIDE 29 — Club Ed Exercise (discussion questions)**

- How does Club Ed's organisational structure change as it grows and diversifies? What factors drive these structural changes?
- How can Club Ed structure itself as an adaptive organisation? Does it always have to react to environmental changes or are there some ways it can be proactive?

**SLIDE 30 — Club Ed Exercise — Scenario #1 (answer)**
A **functional structure** is usually developed. A couple of teams might suggest a simple structure (assuming a very small resort), but 75 employees makes a simple structure difficult. Occasionally a team recommends a team-based structure where everyone is multiskilled — possible, but the contingencies of structure suggest a more **mechanistic than organic** form works better here.

**SLIDE 31 — Club Ed Exercise — Scenario #2 (answer)**
Most teams form a **geographic divisional structure**. A divisional structure adds a management layer (usually three people leading each region). This may be reasonable with 17 properties (~five per region), but question whether the regional layer is required at all — why can't the 17 resort owners report directly to the CEO or COO? (The exercise is derived from "Club Med," which at one time had 50 resort managers reporting directly to the CEO/COO.) If a divisional structure is justified, explain why it should be geographical — possibly these resorts differ more by clientele (some more "party" oriented, some relaxed, some catering mainly to families).

**SLIDE 32 — Club Ed Exercise — Scenario #3 (answer)**
By 30 resorts, a **divisionalized structure around geography** generally makes sense; but justify why all 30 resorts couldn't report directly to the CEO (discussion is mostly about span of control and coordinating mechanisms other than direct supervision enabling such a wide span). As in Scenario #2, justify geography over customer or function (e.g., why not a VP responsible for all food services across resorts?). The **charter airline** adds complexity: it might stand alone as a division (minimal integration needed — carries resort guests but also non-guests). Some teams recommend more closely integrating the airline with the resorts; others recommend a **matrix structure** (for the resorts, not the airline) organized by geography and function (food services, housekeeping, etc.).

**SLIDE 33 — Club Ed Exercise — Scenario #4 (answer)**
Many reorganize Club Ed into a **product-based divisional structure** with three products: resorts, airline, and adventure travel — typically with a geographic divisional structure within the resorts division and a functional structure for the other two. Consider whether the structure should support **organizational integration** (leveraging resort strengths with adventure travel and the airline), or whether the three "divisions" should be mostly independent businesses with limited interdependence (i.e., Club Ed becomes a **holding company**). Answers depend on whether the businesses need to be interdependent and, if so, how Club Ed can build synergies across divisions.

**SLIDE 34 — Team Meeting 5** (process flow / numbered steps)

1. **Check** — in on progress towards your plan for report completion – it's due in how many weeks?
2. **Ensure** — you have a decent draft
3. **Read** — marking rubric and detailed report writing guidelines for requirements
4. **Plan** — for additional research/editing/finalising
5. **Consider** — sending me questions/a draft for feedback
6. **CLARIFICATION** — the 3000 word limit is a MAXIMUM. It ONLY applies to the discussion section

---

**Key terms / frameworks / sources in this deck:**

- **Four elements of organizational structure:** span of control, centralization/decentralization, formalization, departmentalization.
- **Span of control** (narrow vs wide); flat vs tall structures; **power distance** (relevance to narrow span).
- **Contingencies of organizational design:** external environment (dynamic/stable, complex/simple, diverse/integrated, hostile/munificent), organizational size, technology (task variability, task analyzability), organizational strategy.
- **Coordination mechanisms:** informal communication, formal hierarchy, standardisation.
- **Mechanistic vs organic structures.**
- **Departmentalization forms:** functional, divisional (geographic / product / customer), matrix, team-based, simple; holding company; adaptive organisation.
- Sources: McShane & Von Glinow (2024) Ch.13 (p.491); case study "Sloan & Wu, Inc"; The Club Ed Exercise (McShane et al. 2019, p.493) — derived from "Club Med."
- Assessment milestone: Team Meeting 5 — check progress/deadline, ensure a decent draft, re-read rubric & report guidelines, plan additional research/editing/finalising, consider sending the lecturer questions/a draft; **clarification: 3000-word limit is a MAXIMUM and applies only to the discussion section.**

Один спорный момент, на который стоит обратить внимание (раз ты просил максимально внимательно): на слайде 22 в оригинале буквально написано «10 vs. 115 direct reports» — это, судя по логике кейса (15 → 10 магазинов), опечатка в самой презентации; я привёл как есть и пометил. Также на слайде 12 в исходнике есть явно «склеившийся»/повреждённый фрагмент текста про matrix-структуру — я его отметил.

## 📄 02-topics/Topic-06-Organisational-Structure/Topic_6_Lecture_Podcast_Transcript.md

Связь: [[Topic 6 — Organisational Structure]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Welcome back to BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour. This topic examines the how
the structural elements of an organisation can be selected and combined into a unique design
to improve the performance of an organisation and the individuals within it.
We previously looked at job design and how individual jobs are structured. Division of labour
is the level above that, how the work is subdivided into separate jobs assigned to different
people. Once the work is divided, putting it all together requires coordination, and this is
achieved through informal communication, formal hierarchy, and standardisation.
Informal communication is sharing information on mutual tasks and forming common mental
models to synchronise work activities. It is relied on by all organisations and is vital in non-
routine and ambiguous situations. As the number of employees in an organisation increases,
informal communication becomes chaotic, and so liaison roles and temporary cross-functional
teams are created to help structure the communication. In larger organisations, formal
hierarchies are used for coordination, assigning legitimate power to people to direct work
efforts. In the past, managers believed that formal hierarchies were the best method for
coordinating large organisations, however it makes them inflexible and in the increasingly
complex and novel situations of todays world, a formal hierarchy can quickly lead to problems.
Additionally, as the business grows, more and more layers of management are needed to
coordinate this hierarchy, and it becomes a costly bureaucratic process, and reduces employee
autonomy. Coordination through standardisation involves creating routine patterns of
behaviour or output, and depending on the nature of the organisation or task, standardising
either processes, outputs, or skills may be more effective.
How the work, that is the employees and their activities, are grouped together is
departmentalisation. It establishes the chain of command, focuses people around common
mental models and encourages coordination through informal communication among people
and subunits.
A simple structure is evident in most small, owner-operated business, where there are few
people and products or services offered, and employees perform broadly defined jobs reporting
to the owner. It depends on the owner providing direct supervision and becomes incredibly
difficult to continue with as an organisation grows.
A functional structure organises employees around specific knowledge or other resources. This
structure fosters greater specialisation and improves direct supervision, but it weakens the focus
on serving clients or developing products.
A divisional structure groups employees around geographic areas, clients or outputs. This
structure accommodates growth and focuses employee attention on products or customers
rather than on tasks. However, this structure also duplicates resources and creates silos of
knowledge.
Team-based structures are very flat, with low formalisation, and organise self-directed teams
around work processes rather than functional specialties. The matrix structure combines two
structures to leverage the benefits of both types. However, this approach requires more
coordination than functional or pure divisional structures, may dilute accountability, and
increases conflict. A network structure is an alliance of several organisations for the purpose
of creating a product or serving a client.
The basic elements of organisational structure are span of control, centralisation, and
formalisation . span of control is the number of people directly reporting to the next level in
the hierarchy, and the optimal span of control depends on the presence of coordinating
mechanisms other than formal hierarchy, whether employees perform routine tasks, and how
much interdependence there is among employees within the department.
Centralisation occurs when formal decision authority is held by a small group of people,
typically senior executives. Many companies decentralise and delegate decision making
authority as they become larger and more complex, but some sections of the company may
remain centralised while other sections decentralise.
Formalisation is the degree to which organisations standardise behaviour through rules,
procedures, formal training and related mechanisms. Companies become more formalised as
they get older and larger. Formalisation tends to reduce organisational flexibility,
organisational learning, creativity and job satisfaction.
A mechanistic structure is characterised by a narrow span of control, high centralisation and
high formalisation. Mechanistic structures have many rules and procedures, limited decision
making at lower levels, tall hierarchies and vertical communication flows. They operate better
in stable environments because they rely on efficiency and routine behaviours.
An organic structure is characterised by a wide span of control, low centralisation and low
formalisation. Organic structures are better in dynamic, rapidly changing environments
because they are more flexible and responsive to the changes. They are also more compatible
with organisational learning and high-performance work practices because they emphasise
information sharing and an empowered work force. Organic structures are reliant on employees
having well developed roles and expertise, so they are able to coordinate effectively.
There is no one size fits all for effective organisational structure, and what will be the best for
a specific organisation will depend on their external environment, size, technology, and
strategy. This is consistent with the open-systems perspective of organisational effectiveness.
If the environment is dynamic, not stable, a more organic structure will be needed so the
organisation can adapt more quickly to change. If the environment is complex, there will need
to be decentralisation, so the people and subunits with the necessary information are able to
make the most informed choices. If the environment is diverse in its products, services, clients,
or regions, then the organisation will need a divisional structure aligned with that diversity.
And if the environment is hostile, with resource scarcity and increased competition, then again,
an organic structure tends to do better as they are able to adapt.
Another contingency is size. As organisations grow, they tend to need to decentralise decisions
to those who have the information to make the best decisions, and they make greater use of
standardisation as a coordination mechanism, however informal communication is regaining
its importance in large firms through an increased emphasis on empowerment and emerging
information technologies
The contingency of technology refers to the mechanisms or processes an organisation relies on
to make its products and services. If there is low variability and high analysability, that is if
there are few exceptions to standard procedure and it is reasonable predictable, such as an
assembly line, then a mechanistic structure would be more suitable. However if there is high
variability and low analysability, such as in a research setting, then an organic structure should
be introduced.
The previous contingencies influence but do not necessarily determine structure. Instead,
corporate leaders formulate and implement strategies that shape both the characteristics of
these contingencies and the organisation’s resulting structure. For example, the strategy
determines the organisations growth targets, and thus size, or if the strategy is to compete
through innovation, then this would recommend an organic structure to increase creativity.
Over time, there has been a trend for organisations to move away from hierarchical
organisational structures to more flat, agile, team-based structures in many large organisations.
This is possibly due to the increasingly dynamic and unpredictable external environment
requiring organisations to be flexible and responsive, however every organisation needs to be
aware of their specific contingencies, and ensure their structure is fit for purpose. Thank you.

**BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour**

Topic 6 - Workshop Activities (Designing Organisational Structures)

Name: Faiaz Dzhafarov  Student No: 35553299

# Activity 1: Critical Thinking Questions (Chapter 13)

## Question 3 - Span of control in modern manufacturing

The old administrative theorists favoured a narrow span of control. They assumed direct supervision was the main way to coordinate work. Today's top manufacturers can run a much wider span, and they manage it because they coordinate through other mechanisms instead of a manager watching over each worker. Standardised work processes, self-directed teams, information systems and well-trained, multiskilled staff do a lot of the coordinating that a supervisor used to do. One manager can therefore be responsible for far more people without losing control.

A flatter structure also brings real benefits, which is part of why firms move to it. There are fewer middle managers, so overheads drop and more of the payroll goes into people who actually produce the goods. A wider span forces less close supervision. That in turn gives teams more autonomy and a real say in decisions, and that tends to suit the high-performance practices many manufacturers now use.

A narrow span still makes sense in some cases. Where the workforce is low skilled and the tasks are not yet standardised, closer supervision is needed to keep quality and safety acceptable. It also fits a workforce high in power distance, because those employees expect and accept close direction. They would not read tight supervision as a sign that management does not trust them.

## Question 4 - Determining the degree of decentralisation

As organisations grow and their environments become more complex, they usually have to decentralise. Once senior executives can no longer process every decision themselves without becoming a bottleneck, the sensible response is to push authority down to the people who hold the relevant information. The tricky part is judging how far to go, and the contingencies of organisational design give us the main things to weigh up.

The external environment matters first. Decentralisation suits complex environments, where the people closest to the situation have the information to make better calls. In a genuinely hostile environment, though, it is often better to centralise temporarily so the firm can respond quickly and decisively. Organisational size pulls the same way: larger organisations, with more specialised jobs and more elaborate coordinating mechanisms, generally need to decentralise so the top is not overloaded. Technology counts too. Where the work involves many exceptions to standard procedure (high variety) and the outputs are hard to standardise (low analysability), decentralised decision making works better.

All of the above are then filtered through strategy. Johnson & Johnson, for example, runs a decentralised divisional structure precisely because its strategy is to develop and deliver a wide spread of health products across the world. So there is no single correct level. The company has to read its environment, size, technology and strategy together and decentralise to match.

## Question 5 - Coordination mechanisms in mechanistic and organic structures

There are three coordinating mechanisms: informal communication, formal hierarchy, and standardisation. Mechanistic and organic forms lean on different ones.

A mechanistic structure has high formalisation and centralisation, a narrow span of control, and rigidly defined tasks. With decision making concentrated at the top and behaviour tied down by rules, coordination runs mainly through the formal hierarchy and standardisation. Managers direct work through their authority, and standard processes and outputs keep everyone aligned.

An organic structure works differently. It has a wide span of control, decentralised decisions and little formalisation, so there are fewer rules and less supervision to fall back on. People coordinate far more through informal communication, sharing information directly and building common mental models to synchronise their work. This is why organic forms depend on employees having well-developed roles and expertise. They have to coordinate themselves rather than wait to be told.

## Question 7 - Working in a matrix structure (employee perspective)

For employees, a well-run matrix structure has clear upsides. It improves communication across the project and the functional side of the business, and it gives some flexibility to balance workload with other members of a project team. People also get to interact and coordinate with others in their own technical speciality, which keeps their expertise sharp. Because a matrix demands strong communication and interpersonal skills, employees often pick up better training and development through working in it.

The main drawback is the two-boss problem. Reporting to both a functional manager and a project manager means dealing with two sets of expectations that may pull in different directions, and that can raise stress, conflict and organisational politics. The structure is also relatively fluid compared with a clear bureaucratic chain of command. Some employees find that ambiguity hard to adjust to, since it is not always obvious who has the final say on priorities.

# Activity 2: Case Study - 'Sloan & Wu, Inc' (Chapter 13)

## Question 1 - The proposed changes in terms of the four elements of structure

The change to **span of control** goes in two directions. At district level the span narrows: district managers now look after about 10 stores rather than 15, so they can work more closely with each store manager. At regional level the span widens sharply. The firm drops from five regions to three, removes the assistant regional manager layer, and expands from 30 to 45 districts, so each regional manager now oversees roughly 15 district managers instead of a handful.

On **centralisation / decentralisation**, when Sloan & Wu acquired the three regional chains it centralised a lot of activity, especially merchandising and marketing, which is why stock ended up in the wrong places (winter coats in Florida). The new structure clearly decentralises, handing merchandising and marketing decisions to district and store managers so they can tailor the offer to local customers. The CEO describes it as a "devolved" structure.

**Formalisation** moves both ways. It falls in some respects, because district and store managers gain autonomy and more flexible processes for dealing with vendors. But it rises in others. New technology tracks what is in stock at each store and records the brands, sizes and colours that local customers prefer, and managers must work within that system feedback, which is itself a form of formalisation.

For **departmentalisation**, the visible change is mainly in the number of units at each level: 45 districts across three regions (East, South, West) instead of 30 across five. Most of the other changes, such as the decentralised power and the shift of merchandising and marketing staff out to the districts, would not actually show up on the organisation chart.

## Question 2 - Contingencies suggesting the structure is appropriate or not

* **Dynamic vs stable.** Customer preferences vary by area and shift fairly quickly, which is why merchandising and marketing have been pushed down to the local level. But a lot of the business is stable. How customers shop, buy online and return goods is fairly predictable over the medium term, as are vendor processes. So Sloan & Wu needs a structure sitting between organic and mechanistic, and decentralising with somewhat less formalisation at the local level fits that.
* **Complex vs simple.** A national department-store chain with many products and diverse customers operates in a moderately complex environment, and the more complex the environment the more decentralisation helps. The new structure moves in that direction.
* **Diverse vs integrated.** The firm is diverse, mainly geographically. A full divisional structure aligned to that diversity is probably not warranted, since the real variation is at district level (45 geographic divisions would be unworkable) and customers are not all that different across regions for items like kitchen appliances. Decentralisation should be enough without a divisional structure.
* **Hostile vs munificent.** There is no sign of severe resource scarcity or extreme competition. The firm lost some market share through over-standardised buying but remains competitive, so hostility is not really a driving contingency here.
* **Organisational size.** It is a large firm, so it leans on standardisation (inventory systems) and formal authority through the district managers as coordinating mechanisms. That is broadly appropriate for its size.
* **Technology.** Most staff perform tasks with fairly low variability and medium-to-high analysability, because buying behaviour is reasonably predictable. That points to a structure somewhat more mechanistic than organic, close to what the new design actually is.
* **Strategy.** The CEO signals a shift toward creativity and innovation rather than pure cost efficiency, which argues for a more organic structure. Whether the new design is organic enough is debatable, but it is moving the right way.

Taken together, the new structure looks reasonably well matched to Sloan & Wu's contingencies. The main question mark is whether it is organic enough for the stated strategy.

## Question 3 - Problems the firm might experience

The first risk is **inflated costs**. There are 50% more districts than before, and merchandising and marketing now happen more at district level, which probably needs more people overall than the old regional offices did. The narrower district span (around 10 stores each) also means more managers on the payroll, so costs could climb.

A second worry is **formal authority dressed up as empowerment**. There is a real chance that centralised head-office control is simply replaced by district managers controlling store managers more closely. If that happens, store-level staff are not really empowered. They are just supervised by someone nearer to them.

The third problem is **too much variability**. Decentralised decisions can create inconsistency across the chain. Localising the offer suits some products but not all, and customers visiting a store in another region may be put off by big differences in format or merchandising. Local autonomy also raises the chance of poor or even unethical decisions. For instance, district managers dealing directly with vendors could lead to questionable arrangements, and districts might end up competing against each other for stock and paying higher prices.

# Activity 3: Team Exercise - The Club Ed Exercise

The exercise asks the team to design and justify an organisational chart for Club Ed at four stages of its growth. We need to show how the most suitable structure changes as the business grows and diversifies.

* **Scenario 1, one new resort, ~75 staff.** A functional structure works best here, grouping employees around areas such as food and beverage, housekeeping, front office, maintenance and administration. A simple owner-supervised structure is hard to sustain with 75 employees, and a fully team-based form is more organic than this fairly routine, single-site operation needs. The contingencies point to something more mechanistic than organic.
* **Scenario 2, 17 resorts across three regions.** Most teams move to a geographic divisional structure, with a regional manager over each region. It is worth questioning whether that regional layer is really needed at this size, since the resort managers could report fairly directly to the CEO or COO. If a divisional form is justified, it should be on geography mainly where the resorts genuinely differ by region or clientele (party-oriented, relaxed, family-focused).
* **Scenario 3, 30 resorts plus a charter airline.** By 30 resorts a geographic divisional structure generally makes sense, though again the span of control and the coordinating mechanisms should be examined before assuming a regional layer is essential. The airline adds complexity. It can sit as a fairly independent division, since it carries both Club Ed guests and outside customers and needs little integration with the resorts. Some teams would instead run the resorts as a matrix organised by geography and function (food services, housekeeping and so on).
* **Scenario 4, 75 resorts, the airline and an acquired adventure-travel agency.** This is best handled as a product-based divisional structure with three products (resorts, airline and adventure travel), using a geographic divisional structure inside the resorts division and a functional structure for the other two. The key judgement is whether Club Ed should integrate the three to build synergies (using resort strengths to support adventure travel and the airline), or run them as largely independent businesses, in which case it effectively becomes a holding company.

**Discussion.** Club Ed's structure shifts from simple/functional toward divisional and then product-based as it grows, driven by increasing size, a more complex and diverse environment, and a strategy of expansion and diversification. It can become adaptive rather than purely reactive by building flexibility in. That means using more organic, team-based and information-sharing arrangements, scanning its markets, and shaping its own environment through its strategy rather than only responding to changes after they hit.

# Activity 4: Team Meeting - Milestone Progress

We reported progress to the workshop facilitator and recorded it on the LMS Team Discussion Forum. With roughly two weeks left until the 26 June due date, the meeting focused on turning four separate drafts into one working report.

We confirmed the team had a solid working draft: all four discussion challenges were written (Communication and Collaboration by Bobur, Team Trust by Faiaz, Remote work by Owethu), and Owethu had started the Recommendations while Faiaz had begun the Conclusion, reference list and appendices. We re-read the marking rubric and the Detailed Report Guidelines together to confirm every requirement was covered, in particular that each recommendation aligned to at least one of the Ten Principles of the UN Global Compact and that the referencing followed the Chicago standard.

We then planned the time left for additional research, editing and finalising, and agreed to send the lecturer a specific question about the reference list. The main clarification noted in class was about length: the 3000-word limit is a **maximum** and applies only to the discussion section, not to the executive summary, recommendations, conclusion, references or appendices. All adjustments to the plan were recorded on the Team Discussion Forum.

Связь: [[Topic 7 — Organisational Culture]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

https://geerthofstede.com/culture-geert-hofstede-gert-jan-hofstede/6d-model-of-national-culture/

Вот основной текст со страницы, посвященной 6-мерной модели национальных культур Герта Хофстеде, на английском языке:
The 6D model of national culture
Geert Hofstede, assisted by others, came up with six basic issues that society needs to come to term with in order to organize itself. These are called dimensions of culture. Each of them has been expressed on a scale that runs roughly from 0 to 100.
The dimensions explained
Individualism Individualism is the extent to which people feel independent, as opposed to being interdependent as members of larger wholes. Individualism does not mean egoism; it means that individual choices and decisions are expected. Collectivism means that one "knows one's place" in life, which is determined socially.
Power Distance Power Distance is the extent to which the less powerful members of organizations and institutions (like the family) accept and expect that power is distributed unequally. Without acceptance of leadership by powerful entities, none of today's societies could run.
Masculinity Masculinity is the extent to which the use of force is endorsed socially. In a masculine society, men are supposed to be tough, and winning is important for both genders. In a feminine society, the genders are emotionally closer, and there is sympathy for the underdog.
Uncertainty Avoidance Uncertainty avoidance deals with a society's tolerance for uncertainty and ambiguity. It has to do with anxiety and distrust in the face of the unknown, and conversely, with a wish to have fixed habits and rituals, and to know the truth.
Long-term orientation Long-term orientation deals with change. In a long-time-oriented culture, the basic notion about the world is that it is in flux, and preparing for the future is always needed. In a short-time-oriented culture, the past provides a moral compass, and adhering to it is morally good.
Indulgence Indulgence is about the good things in life. In an indulgent culture it is good to be free, and doing what your impulses want you to do is good. In a restrained culture, the feeling is that life is hard, and duty, not freedom, is the normal state of being.
Are there more dimensions? Since dimensions are imagined, not 'out there', there can be many more. However, the 6D model has great validity and practical usability, predicting real-world phenomena at the level of the nation
