Связь: [[Topic 8 — Power and Influence]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

**BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour**

Topic 8: Workshop Activities (Power and Influence)

Murdoch University

Name: Faiaz Dzhafarov  Student No: 35553299

# Activity 1: Critical Thinking Questions (Chapter 10)

## Question 2 - Building power when you hold little formal authority

A lot of people assume power comes from your job title, but the chapter shows that is only part of the picture. Power is the capacity to influence others. It exists whenever someone perceives they depend on you for something they value, so even without formal authority you can hold real power if people need what you bring.

The five sources split into position power (legitimate, reward and coercive) and personal power (expert and referent). Someone in a junior or trainee role has very little position power, so the practical route is to build personal power. Expert power is the strongest lever here. If you develop knowledge or skills others value, and especially if you become the person who can manage uncertainties for the team, people respond to that expertise much as they respond to authority. Referent power is the other one to invest in. When colleagues like you, trust you and identify with you, they cooperate without being told to. The norm of reciprocity helps too, since doing genuine favours creates an informal expectation that people will help you back.

Having a source of power is not enough on its own. It only becomes real power through the four contingencies, and three of them are worth pushing on:

* **Substitutability.** Make yourself hard to replace by controlling knowledge or tasks that others cannot easily get elsewhere. Being non-substitutable is what turns expertise into leverage.
* **Centrality.** Position yourself so that a lot of people depend on you and feel the effect quickly if you are not there.
* **Visibility.** Let your competence be seen. It is the same reason professionals hang their degrees and certificates on the office wall.

The fourth contingency, discretion, is a useful warning. Front-line supervisors often look powerless because organisational rules give them little freedom to actually use the power they have. The point, then, is not just to collect sources of power. You have to operate where you have room to use them.

## Question 5 - Hard and soft influence tactics, and which are acceptable

It helps to separate power from influence. Power is only the capacity to influence. Influence is the actual behaviour that tries to change someone's attitude or behaviour, and it runs in all directions, upward to managers as much as downward to staff.

The chapter lists eight tactics. Five are hard tactics supported by position power: silent authority, assertiveness, information control, coalition formation and upward appeal. Three are soft tactics supported by personal power: persuasion, impression management (which includes ingratiation and building a personal brand), and exchange.

Soft tactics are generally seen as more acceptable than hard ones. Friendly persuasion and a bit of subtle ingratiation sit far better with people than assertiveness or going over their head with an upward appeal. Persuasion is usually the most effective for career success, particularly when the person is seen as credible, does not personally profit from the outcome, and acknowledges the other side's arguments. There is no single best tactic though. The right choice depends on three things: your own power base, whether the target is above, below or at your level, and the personal, organisational and cultural values in play. Silent authority, for example, is the most common form of influence in high power distance cultures, where simply complying with a manager's request is expected.

Two cautions are worth flagging. Extreme assertiveness can tip into workplace bullying, and excessive ingratiation reads as insincere and self-serving, so it only works in small doses and at lower levels.

## Question 6 - Organisational politics: what drives it and how to keep it in check

Organisational politics is the use of influence tactics that others see as self-serving, benefiting the individual at the expense of others and sometimes against the organisation's interests. It is not automatically a bad thing. Politics can be positive when it does not harm others and actually supports things like fair decision making, conflict resolution and maintaining relationships. The negative version is what diverts resources away from the organisation, and that is what lowers job satisfaction, commitment and morale and creates retention problems.

Politics tends to flare up under two conditions in particular: when decisions are ambiguous and involve allocating scarce resources, and when the organisation tolerates or rewards political behaviour. People with a high need for personal power are also more inclined to play this way.

Management can reduce dysfunctional politics rather than pretend it away. The main levers are clear rules for how resources are allocated, a free flow of information so people are not fighting in the dark, and using education and involvement when the organisation goes through change. Beyond that, team norms and a culture that discourages backstabbing matter, and so do leaders who model organisational citizenship instead of showing everyone that political savvy is how you get ahead. One more point: influence is read more positively when the person has high political skill, meaning they are socially astute, good at networking and come across as sincere.

## Question 8 - How social networks give people power

Power does not only come from formal roles. It also flows through social networks and the social capital they create. The two main sources of this kind of power are referent power, because people in your network identify with and trust you, and legitimate power through the norm of reciprocity, where favours owed turn into influence.

The interesting part is which connections matter most, and this is where centrality comes back in. Having weak ties across many different networks can be more valuable than a few strong ties within a similar group, because weak ties reach into places your close circle cannot and bring back information and contacts you would not otherwise get. The practical lesson follows from that: build a broad and diverse network rather than just deepening a handful of close relationships.

The flip side is that these networks are a natural part of organisations but can become a real barrier for anyone not already connected. The "boys clubs" that form in some managerial areas are the obvious example. They show why building a wide network early matters, especially for people who start outside the inner circle.

# Activity 2: Case Study - 'Resonus Corporation' (Chapter 10)

## Question 1 - Sources and contingencies of power among the executives and departments

The striking thing about Resonus is how far the real power sits from the organisation chart.

* **Doc Kalandry (research director)** holds the most power even though the chart puts him under Choy. His sources are personal: strong **expert power** as the "living genius" behind the company's successful products, and **referent power** from the quirky, enthusiastic style everyone loves, Hunt most of all. On top of that he has informal **legitimate power**, because Hunt actively supports Doc reporting straight to the CEO. All four contingencies work in his favour. He is **non-substitutable** (genius innovators cannot just be replaced), highly **central** because research drives the products and every design change ripples outward, and very **visible** through celebrated products and an over-the-top personality. He also has the **discretion** to keep launching last-minute changes.
* **Bill Hunt (CEO)** has the formal **legitimate, reward and coercive** power of a 15-year chief executive, plus **referent power** as the keeper of the founder's "family spirit." His own bias matters: he started in research and still favours that group, which is part of why Doc's informal power survives.
* **Jacqui Blanc (production director)** has formal legitimate power, but her real influence comes from credibility. By uncovering and cleaning up the earlier fraud she earned Hunt's trust, which is why he tolerates her formal style in an informal culture. Production also has **centrality** over output, since it controls what actually gets manufactured and in what order.
* **Frank Choy (director of engineering) and the ESD** are the weak point. On paper Choy oversees both ESD and research, but his position power is hollow because Doc ignores him and Hunt backs that. He is new (eight months), so he has little expert or referent power, and the role itself is structurally fragile, with the last two directors fired or gone inside 18 months. His **discretion is low** as well: he technically has authority but no freedom to use it, because saying no to Hunt or Doc risks his job. ESD is treated as highly **substitutable** and low status, getting the blame and little credit. The research engineers, not ESD, are the ones production trusts.

Power at Resonus flows to expertise, the CEO's favour and credibility, not to formal authority. That leaves Choy responsible for outcomes he cannot control.

## Question 2 - Influence tactics, and are they organisational politics?

Several tactics are visible. Doc uses **upward appeal**, taking his nano-processor idea straight to Hunt and bypassing Choy, backed by **persuasion** and his infectious enthusiasm (a form of impression management). Hunt leans on **silent authority**, both in urging everyone to "remain civil" and in asking Choy and Blanc to "show commitment," which is hard to refuse coming from the CEO. Blanc uses **assertiveness** and a conditional **exchange**, agreeing to deliver only if ESD provides accurate specs on time and the sales director stops overpromising. Choy mostly **yields and avoids**, swallowing his protest to avoid his predecessor's fate. The sales director uses a blunt political tactic, **implying Choy's incompetence** to deflect attention from his own wild delivery promises.

Whether these count as organisational politics depends on whether they are self-serving at others' or the organisation's expense. The sales director's blaming is clearly political, scapegoating Choy to protect himself. Doc's habit of pushing changes he "won't let go of," right up against production deadlines, is also political in effect: it serves his own enthusiasm while ESD and production absorb the cost in hundreds of change orders and delays. Hunt's ongoing favouritism toward research entrenches this. Blanc's conditions and insistence on guidelines are a different matter. They are not really politics, because they protect the organisation (quality, and a response to real fraud) rather than her personal interest. The case is fertile ground for politics precisely because accountability is ambiguous, time and production priority are scarce, and the culture tolerates the informal power games.

## Question 3 - Consultant's recommendation on the power dynamics

Resonus has one problem underneath the rest: a mismatch between authority and accountability. ESD is blamed for delays it cannot prevent, because the real power lies with research and the CEO. My recommendations target that.

* **Realign authority with accountability.** Either route research's work formally through engineering so Choy has genuine say over hand-offs, or stop holding ESD accountable for delays caused by late design changes. Responsibility without power is the structural fault here.
* **Introduce proper change control.** Doc's last-minute revisions are the actual cause of the delays. The firm needs a design-freeze and clear cut-off points before production begins, rather than endorsing changes three weeks out. This curbs the spec churn without killing innovation.
* **Manage Doc's power rather than remove it.** He is the innovation engine, so the aim is to channel his ideas through a feasibility and manufacturability check, and Hunt must stop reinforcing the informal bypass that lets research override engineering.
* **Raise ESD's standing and fix the politics.** Give ESD credit and visibility, route production's design-fault queries through the proper channel, set clear rules for production priority, improve information flow between the groups, and have Hunt model fairness instead of favouritism. The sales director's overpromising and scapegoating need addressing directly too.

Resonus does not need to lose its genius or its collegial culture. What has to change is Hunt letting collegiality mean that no one can say no to Doc while the engineering director is set up to fail.

# Activity 3: Team Exercise - Mapping our power and influence

Each of us identified our main source of power within the group and the influence tactics we tend to rely on, then we compared notes. We wanted to see how power actually works in a small team rather than just defining it.

Most of our power turned out to be personal rather than positional. The members others listened to were the ones with expert power on a particular part of the report, or referent power because people trusted and liked working with them. Nobody was leaning on formal authority, since there was none to lean on. On tactics, we mostly used soft ones. Persuasion and exchange ("I'll take this section if you take that one") came up far more than anything assertive, which fits the idea that soft tactics are more acceptable between peers at the same level.

One thing we only spotted afterwards was centrality. The member who held the shared documents and kept track of deadlines had quiet influence simply because everyone depended on them to keep things moving.

The exercise made it clear that even a team with no manager has a real power structure, and that it is built mostly on expertise, trust and who others depend on.

# Activity 4: Team Meeting - Finalising and submitting the Team Report

Our team (Group 11) met to review and approve the final Team Report on Westpac Banking Corporation, topic Team Dynamics, before submission. The report was essentially complete by this point, so the meeting was about confirming quality and sign-off rather than planning. We recorded the outcomes on the LMS Team Discussion Forum.

We first confirmed that all sections were written and integrated into one document: Executive Summary and Introduction (Bobur), the four Discussion challenges (Communication 3.a by Bobur, Team Trust 3.b by Faiaz, Remote work 3.c by Owethu and Collaboration & Cohesion 3.d by Bobur), plus Recommendations (Owethu), Conclusion (Faiaz), and the Reference List and Appendices (Faiaz). We also confirmed the earlier loss of a member (Wahid) had been absorbed by reallocating his work, so no section was left uncovered.

From there the meeting worked through a short checklist:

* **Read the full draft as one document** to check it reads in a single voice rather than four separate pieces, and that the Discussion section stays within the 3000-word maximum (final word count about 3305 including the non-counted sections).
* **Checked the report against the marking rubric and the Detailed Report Guidelines.** That meant making sure each of the four challenges is analysed against team-dynamics theory, that recommendations align to at least one of the Ten Principles of the UN Global Compact, and that referencing meets the Chicago standard. We flagged a final consistency pass on the in-text citations (mixing of comma and ampersand styles) and the reference list before upload.
* **Allocated the last tasks with owners and deadlines:** final edit and formatting, the citation-consistency fix, and a full proofread.
* **Confirmed the team contract, division of labour and all drafts were logged on the Team Discussion Forum,** since not using the forum carries a 10% individual penalty.

Finally we agreed who uploads the final Word file through the LMS Assignment Tool, checked the file-naming convention, and confirmed every member keeps a copy. The meeting closed by approving the report for submission by the due date.



## 📄 02-topics/Topic-09-Leadership/Topic 9 Podcast Slides.md

Связь: [[Topic 9 — Leadership]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

# BUS293 — Topic 9: Leadership

> 25 slides. Lecture/podcast deck. Every slide carries a **speaker-notes script** (the podcast narration) — included below under each slide as _Podcast notes_. Several slides have comparison tables (Path-Goal, Situational, Fiedler, Competency).
> A recurring sidebar lists the four **Leadership Perspectives**: Transformational · Managerial · Follower-centric · Competency · (Emerging).

## Slide 1 — Title

BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour — Topic 9: Leadership

_Podcast notes:_ Note: this podcast and supporting slides supplement the readings from the prescribed textbook; they cannot replace the depth of knowledge gained from actively reading and engaging with the text. This topic introduces various approaches to leadership and how these can be used to promote needed organisational behaviours and increase the performance of the organisation.

## Slide 2 — Topic 9 Learning Outcomes

- Explain perspectives on leadership
- Understand, evaluate, and apply theories of leadership
- Outline some of the current diversity issues in leadership

_Podcast notes:_ By the end of this topic you should be able to understand, evaluate, and apply theories of leadership, explain emerging perspectives on leadership, and outline some current diversity issues in leadership.

## Slide 3 — Leadership (definition)

The ability to influence, motivate, and enable others to contribute towards the effectiveness of the organisations of which they are members.

_Podcast notes:_ Leadership is one of the most researched topics in business. Leadership theories are categorised into four perspectives: transformational, managerial, follower-centric, and competency. The most popular is the transformational perspective.

## Slide 4 — Transformational Leadership

- One of the most popular perspectives and theories of leadership
- Views leaders as change agents
- Differs from charismatic leadership

_Podcast notes:_ Transformational leadership views leaders as change agents who develop, communicate, and model a shared vision for the team/organisation and encourage experimentation. They create and champion an image of the company's projected positive future state, which motivates and bonds employees. The vision is communicated by framing the message around a grand purpose, using symbols, metaphors, and stories to create a shared mental model. Transformational leaders model the vision by "walking the talk," which increases employee trust, and encourage experimentation by questioning current practices and supporting a learning orientation. Commitment is built through communicating/modelling the vision and through employee involvement in shaping it. Some models say charismatic leadership is essential, but research suggests charisma differs from transformational leadership — charisma is a personal trait providing referent power, does not necessarily attempt to change the organisation, and is associated with narcissism.

## Slide 5 — Transformational Leadership (benefits & limitations)

- **Benefits:** higher employee satisfaction; higher performance; increased organisational citizenship; increased creativity.
- **Limitations:** some models have circular logic; does not recognise or account for situational differences, especially across cultures.

_Podcast notes:_ The theory is limited by defining transformational leaders by their success rather than their behaviour, leading to circular logic with no predictive value. It is also a universal theory that doesn't account for situational/cultural differences.

## Slide 6 — Managerial Leadership

- States that effective leaders help employees improve to support current objectives and practices
- Depends on transformational leadership to set the right direction
- Is comprised of many leadership theories

|             | Managerial leadership             | Transformational leadership                         |
| ----------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Assumptions | Objectives are stable and aligned | Current direction is misaligned and needs to change |
| Focus       | Continuous development            | (setting direction)                                 |
| Orientation | More micro-focused and concrete   | More macro-focused and abstract                     |

_Podcast notes:_ Managerial leadership states effective leaders help employees improve performance and wellbeing to support current objectives/practices. It depends on transformational leadership to set direction; the perspectives differ in assumptions of organisational stability and level of focus. Generally, the higher the managerial position, the more transformational behaviours are required, but all managers use varying degrees of both.

## Slide 7 — Leadership Style Orientation

- Categorises leadership style into either task-oriented or people-oriented
- Neither orientation is more effective; each has advantages and disadvantages
- Recent research shows effective leaders rely on both styles, but in different ways

**Task-oriented leaders:** assign work and clarify responsibilities; set goals and deadlines; evaluate and provide feedback on work quality; establish well-defined best work procedures; plan future work activities.

**People-oriented leaders:** show interest in others as people; listen to employees; make the workplace more pleasant; compliment employees for their work; are considerate of employee needs.

_Podcast notes:_ Task-oriented behaviours define and structure work roles (assigning tasks, clarifying duties/procedures, ensuring rules are followed, pushing to reach performance capacity); people-oriented behaviours focus on developing relationships (mutual trust and respect, genuine concern for needs, looking out for welfare). Neither is more effective; effective leaders use both in different ways.

## Slide 8 — Servant Leadership Theory

An extension of the people-oriented style; the view that leaders:

- serve their followers and help employees fulfil their needs
- are coaches, stewards, and facilitators of employee development
- have a natural desire or 'calling' to serve others
- do not view leadership as a position of power
- have decisions/actions bounded by ethical principles and practices
  Servant leadership relies heavily on the principles of authentic leadership. Recent research found an association between higher organisational performance and CEOs demonstrating servant leadership behaviours.

_Podcast notes:_ Servant leadership is the view that leaders serve followers rather than vice-versa — helping employees fulfil needs, acting as coaches/stewards/facilitators, with a 'calling' to serve, not viewing leadership as power, bounded by ethical principles. Relies heavily on authentic leadership; research links it to higher organisational performance when CEOs demonstrate it.

## Slide 9 — Path-Goal Leadership Theory

- A contingency theory, based on **Expectancy Theory**, proposing that effective leadership depends on choosing the most appropriate leadership behaviour for the employee and situation
- The leader's job is to provide followers with the information, support, and/or other resources needed to achieve their goals
- E.g. where employees have high skills/experience, an external locus of control, a non-routine task structure, and low team cohesion → a combination of **participative** and **supportive** leader behaviours is suggested

**Contingency table — suggested leader behaviour:**

|                          | Directive      | Supportive   | Participative  | Achievement-oriented |
| ------------------------ | -------------- | ------------ | -------------- | -------------------- |
| **Skill and experience** | Low            | Low          | High           | High                 |
| **Locus of control**     | External       | External     | Internal       | Internal             |
| **Task structure**       | Non-routine    | Routine      | Non-routine    | ?                    |
| **Team dynamics**        | Negative norms | Low cohesion | Positive norms | ?                    |

(Skill/experience and locus of control = employee contingencies; task structure and team dynamics = environmental contingencies.)

_Podcast notes:_ Path-Goal proposes effective leadership depends on choosing the most appropriate behaviour for the employee and situation, to influence employee expectations about desired results and positive outcomes — by providing information, support, and resources. Contingencies: employee skills/experience and locus of control; task structure and team dynamics.

## Slide 10 — Path-Goal Leadership Theory (benefits & limitations)

- **Benefits:** higher employee motivation and satisfaction; leader acceptance; comparably significant research support.
- **Limitations:** some contingencies have limited research support; some contingencies and leadership styles have not been researched at all; as the theory expands it may become too complicated for practical use.
- Leader Behaviours: (directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented).

_Podcast notes:_ Despite comparatively significant research support, a few contingencies have limited support, some have not been investigated at all, and as the theory expands it may become too complex for practical use.

## Slide 11 — Situational Leadership Theory

A contingency theory: effective leaders vary their style with the **ability** and **motivation/commitment** of followers.

**Contingency table — suggested leader behaviour:**

|                         | Telling | Selling | Participating | Delegating |
| ----------------------- | ------- | ------- | ------------- | ---------- |
| **Follower Ability**    | Low     | Low     | High          | High       |
| **Follower Commitment** | Low     | High    | Low           | High       |

- **Benefits:** popular with practitioners; easy to use.
- **Limitations:** only empirical support for the **telling** style (when employees lack motivation and ability — also documented in path-goal theory); the rest of the theory is not supported by research.

_Podcast notes:_ Situational leadership specifies four styles — telling, selling, participating, delegating — varying with follower ability and commitment. Despite popularity, only the 'telling' style (low motivation + ability) has empirical support; the rest is unsupported.

## Slide 12 — Fiedler's Contingency Theory

- A contingency theory: leader effectiveness depends on matching leadership style (people-oriented or task-oriented) to the level of **situational control**
- Examines the situation via three factors of situational control

**Contingency table — suggested leader behaviour:**

| Leader–member relations | Good                                                                                                                     |      |        |      | Poor   |      |        |      |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---- | ------ | ---- | ------ | ---- | ------ | ---- |
| **Task structure**      | High                                                                                                                     |      | Low    |      | High   |      | Low    |      |
| **Position power**      | Strong                                                                                                                   | Weak | Strong | Weak | Strong | Weak | Strong | Weak |
| **Suggested style**     | Task-oriented → … → People-oriented → … → Task-oriented (style varies across the eight situational-control combinations) |      |        |      |        |      |        |      |

- **Benefits:** recognises the importance of leader power; recognises that changing leadership style may be difficult due to the leader's personality and values.
- **Limitations:** lacks research support due to the limited focus on two leadership styles, and flaws in the questionnaire used to measure leadership style.

_Podcast notes:_ Fiedler's model matches style (people- or task-oriented) to the situation via three situational-control factors (leader–member relations, task structure, position power). It recognises the importance of leader power and that style is hard to change (tied to personality/values), but lacks research support due to the two-style focus and flaws in the measurement questionnaire.

## Slide 13 — Leader-Member Exchange (LMX) Theory

- Focuses on the **relationship** between leaders and members, rather than the leader's style
- Views relationships as a series of exchanges, differentiated by quality
- **Low LMX** = economic exchanges (e.g. leaders providing organisational resources in return for task performance)
- **High LMX** = social exchange of resources (e.g. liking, trust, commitment)
- **Benefits:** high LMX leads to increased employee commitment and OCBs, enhanced job performance, and employee retention.
- **Limitations:** potential to alienate some employees; does not consider effects of team dynamics and social identity; does not provide specific advice on how leaders can develop high-quality relationships.

_Podcast notes:_ LMX focuses on leader–member relationships as exchanges that may develop trust and mutual commitment, differentiated by quality (low = economic; high = social). High-quality LMX improves commitment, OCBs, performance, and retention. Limitations: may alienate some employees, ignores team dynamics/social identity, and gives no specific guidance on building high-quality relationships.

## Slide 14 — Leadership Substitutes Theory

- Identifies variables (contingencies/substitutes) that limit a leader's influence or make a particular leadership style unnecessary
- Substitutes include employee ability, intrinsically satisfying tasks, unambiguous tasks, and cohesive work groups
- **Benefits:** explains the effectiveness of self-management and autonomous work groups.
- **Limitations:** empirical evidence is mixed; research suggests substitutes help, but do not completely replace, real leadership.

_Podcast notes:_ Identifies contingencies that limit a leader's ability to influence subordinates or make a style unnecessary (e.g. training and experience can replace task-oriented leadership). Substitutes help but do not completely replace real leadership.

## Slide 15 — Follower-Centric Perspective

- Recognises that leaders don't operate in a vacuum
- Proposes that leaders emerge because of the attributional and cognitive processes of their followers
- Tends to be seen in flat-structure organisations where leaders and followers are treated equally and employees have a 'voice' that greatly impacts decision-making
- **Romance of Leadership Theory:** followers want to believe leaders make a difference, so they engage in **fundamental attribution error** and other perceptual distortions to support this belief; supported by the Western belief that life events are generated more by people than by uncontrollable natural forces.
- **Implicit Leadership Theory:** followers have preconceived beliefs about effective leaders (**leadership prototypes**) used to evaluate effectiveness; followers are more likely to think a leader is effective when they fit the prototype.

_Podcast notes:_ Leaders emerge through followers' attributional/cognitive processes. The romance-of-leadership effect (leaders seen as sole cause of success) stems from wanting to believe leaders matter — fundamental attribution error and perceptual distortions to minimise cognitive processing (topic three), supported by the Western person-centric belief. Implicit leadership theory: people use leadership prototypes to evaluate leaders. "Leadership exists in the mind of the followers."

## Slide 16 — Competency Perspective (table)

- Identifies the characteristics of effective leaders
- An improvement on the 'great man theory' (popular before WWII)
- Early research: few 'traits' predicted effective leadership; recent research: several competencies are key influences on leadership potential and can predict effective leaders

| Competency                           | Description                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Personality                          | Higher extraversion (outgoing, talkative, sociable, assertive) and conscientiousness (careful, dependable, self-disciplined)                        |
| Self-concept                         | Self-beliefs and positive self-evaluation of their leadership skills and ability to achieve objectives                                              |
| Drive                                | Inner motivation to pursue goals                                                                                                                    |
| Integrity                            | Truthfulness and tendency to translate words into deeds                                                                                             |
| Leadership Motivation                | Need for socialised power to accomplish team or organisational goals                                                                                |
| Business Knowledge                   | Tacit and explicit knowledge about the company's environment enabling more intuitive decisions                                                      |
| Cognitive and Practical Intelligence | Above-average cognitive ability to process information and solve real-world problems by adapting to, shaping, or selecting appropriate environments |
| Emotional Intelligence               | Ability to monitor own/others' emotions, discriminate among them, and use the information to guide thoughts and actions                             |

_Podcast notes:_ The competency perspective identifies characteristics of effective leaders — an improvement on the pre-WWII 'great man theory'. Early research found few predictive traits; recent research suggests several competencies (skills, knowledge, values) influence leadership potential and predict effectiveness.

## Slide 17 — Charismatic Leadership Theory

- Using **referent power** gained through personal traits or relational quality to influence followers
- Charisma is both inherent and learned; charismatic leaders tend to be extraverted, self-confident, achievement-oriented
- **Benefits:** charismatic behaviours (confidence, dominance, high self-esteem) appear in many mental models of effective leaders, so via implicit leadership theory followers rate them positively; potential for high performance/achievement.
- **Limitations:** produces dependent followers; may lead to focus on self-interest rather than common good; charismatic traits also associated with **narcissism** (greater need for personal power, lack of empathy, overconfidence, unethical behaviour, inability to accept criticism).

_Podcast notes:_ Charismatic leadership (one of the older theories) can be inborn or learned, achieved through referent power, with potential to raise performance. Implicit leadership theory explains some effectiveness (many hold a 'heroic masculinity' mental model). But it produces dependent rather than empowered followers, and charismatic traits are associated with narcissism and its negative traits.

## Slide 18 — Competency Perspective (benefits & limitations)

- **Benefits:** simple to use, very popular in the past.
- **Limitations:** competencies refer to leadership **potential**, not performance; assumes leadership is within the person, but leadership is also about relations with followers; implies a universal rather than contingency approach; alternative combinations of competencies might work just as well.

_Podcast notes:_ Competencies refer to potential, not performance; the perspective assumes leadership is within the person (though it's also about relations with followers), implies a universal approach, and alternative competency combinations might work equally well.

## Slide 19 — Ethical Leadership

- Vital for organisational conduct and effectiveness
- Determined by individual characteristics and demonstrated through leaders' behaviours
- At its heart: a strong sense of social obligation, awareness of one's impact on others, and concern for followers
- Characterised by **four virtues: prudence, courage, temperance, and justice**
- **Benefits:** highly ethical leaders rated positively; followers have increased satisfaction and OCBs, lower turnover and counterproductive work behaviours; ethical leadership can change norms, increase willingness to speak up about ethical issues, and reduce interpersonal conflicts.

_Podcast notes:_ Ethical leadership sets the ethical climate, conduct, and effectiveness of an organisation; requires social obligation, awareness of impact on others, and concern for followers; characterised by the four virtues. Rated positively by followers; increases satisfaction and OCBs, lowers turnover and counterproductive behaviours; changes norms, increases speaking up about ethical issues, and reduces interpersonal conflict.

## Slide 20 — Authentic Leadership Theory

- The extent to which leaders are aware of, feel comfortable with, and act consistently with their self-concept
- As people learn more about themselves, they gain greater understanding of their inner purpose and behave consistently with their self-concept and value system
- **Benefits:** creates positive effect that heightens teamwork, team productivity, and performance; followers develop strong affective commitment to leaders who are open, candid, and practice what they preach, increasing OCBs.

_Podcast notes:_ Authentic leadership = how well leaders are aware of, comfortable with, and act consistently with their self-concept; greater self-knowledge → understanding of inner purpose and consistent behaviour with self-concept/values.

## Slide 21 — Shared Leadership

- The view that leadership is broadly distributed rather than assigned to one person
- Present in self-managed work teams
- Employees are leaders when they champion change in the company or team
- Encourages self-leadership activities
- Shared leadership calls for: formal leaders willing to delegate power; a collaborative culture (employees support each other); employee ability to influence through persuasion.

_Podcast notes:_ Shared leadership views leadership as a role rather than a formal position, so employees informally act as leaders as occasions arise (e.g. championing change). Requires formal leaders willing to delegate power, a collaborative supportive culture, and employee ability to influence through persuasion.

## Slide 22 — Virtual Leadership

- Necessary due to: globalisation increasing multinational corporations; working across the globe; increasing virtual teamwork; adoption of flexible working arrangements
- Leaders in virtual settings need to: foster team trust and cohesion; provide support; provide access to resources

_Podcast notes:_ Working in virtual settings adds challenges not present face-to-face. Virtual leaders must communicate regularly and provide support and access to resources to build trust and cohesion, preventing feelings of dislocation and disengagement from working in isolation.

## Slide 23 — Diversity and Leadership: Culture

- Societal cultural values and practices: shape leaders' values and norms; influence decisions and actions; shape follower prototype of effective leaders
- Some leadership styles are universal, others differ across cultures: **'charismatic visionary' seems universal**; participative leadership works better in some cultures than others
- For effective global leadership: lead with a culturally compatible or universally endorsed style; match or exceed culture-specific expectations of leaders

_Podcast notes:_ Societal cultural values shape leaders' values/norms, decisions/actions, and follower prototypes. Some styles are universal ('charismatic visionary'), others vary (participative). For effective global leadership, use a culturally compatible and/or universally endorsed style and match or exceed culture-specific expectations.

## Slide 24 — Diversity and Leadership: Gender

- Male and female leaders have similar task- and people-oriented leadership, despite stereotypes that women are more people-oriented
- Must be sensitive to follower expectations — the mental model of **'heroic masculinity'** is still widely prevalent, although female executives score higher on effectiveness and satisfaction in their leadership approach
- Participative and transformational leadership are used more often by female leaders
- Evaluating female leaders: still receive negative evaluations due to prototypes and gender stereotypes, but evidence they are good at emerging-leadership styles

_Podcast notes:_ Male and female leaders have similar task/people orientation; due to implicit leadership theory they must be sensitive to follower expectations. Female leaders use the participative style more often, still receive negative evaluations due to prototypes/stereotypes, but research shows they are good at emerging-leadership styles.

## Slide 25 — Topic 9 Summary

- Leadership is the ability to influence, motivate and enable others to contribute towards the effectiveness and success of the organisations of which they are members.
- Leadership perspectives include:
  - **transformational** — looks at leadership on a macro-scale, visioning for the future
  - **managerial** — focuses on day-to-day requirements of a leader
  - **follower-centric** — recognises that leaders do not operate in a vacuum and that followers' beliefs and expectations impact whether a leader is seen as effective
  - **competency** — acknowledges that there are some key predictors (competencies) of effective leaders
- Leadership theories try to predict what determines effective leadership, based on situation, people, or other factors. Each has benefits and limitations.
- Both culture and gender affect leadership effectiveness, however this is mostly based in leader prototypes, not actual ability to lead or perform leadership behaviours.

_Podcast notes:_ Summary of the four perspectives and their relationships; culture and gender (plus other contingency factors) affect perceived effectiveness. Important to reflect on the context of leaders — situation, team contingencies, work contingencies, relationship with followers — when judging effectiveness.

---

## Key terms / frameworks

- **Definition of leadership**; **four perspectives:** transformational, managerial, follower-centric, competency (+ emerging).
- **Transformational leadership** (change agents, vision; vs charismatic).
- **Managerial leadership**; **leadership style orientation** (task- vs people-oriented).
- **Servant leadership**; **authentic leadership**; **ethical leadership** (four virtues: prudence, courage, temperance, justice).
- **Contingency theories:** Path-Goal (based on Expectancy Theory; directive/supportive/participative/achievement-oriented), Situational (telling/selling/participating/delegating), Fiedler (leader–member relations, task structure, position power), Leadership Substitutes.
- **LMX Theory** (low = economic exchange, high = social exchange).
- **Follower-centric:** Romance of Leadership (fundamental attribution error), Implicit Leadership Theory (leadership prototypes).
- **Competency perspective** (8 competencies); **great man theory**; **charismatic leadership** (referent power, narcissism risk).
- **Emerging:** shared leadership, virtual leadership.
- **Diversity:** culture (charismatic visionary = universal; participative varies) and gender (heroic masculinity prototype; emerging-leadership styles).

# BUS293 Organisational Theory and Behaviour
Topic 9: Leadership

![ORGANISATIONAL BEHAVIOUR 6E](Picture2.jpg)

### Notes:
**Note: This podcast and supporting slides supplement the readings from the prescribed textbook. They can not replace the depth of knowledge gained from actively reading and engaging with the text.

Welcome back to BUS293, Organisational Theory and Behaviour. This topic introduces various approaches to leadership and how these can be used to promote needed organisational behaviours as well as increase the performance of the organisation.

<!-- Slide number: 2 -->
# Topic 9 Learning Outcomes
Explain perspectives on leadership
Understand, evaluate, and apply theories of leadership
Outline some of the current diversity issues in leadership

### Notes:
By the end of this topic, you should be able to understand, evaluate, and apply theories of leadership, explain emerging perspectives on leadership, and outline some of the current diversity issues in leadership

<!-- Slide number: 3 -->
Leadership:
The ability to influence, motivate, and enable others to contribute towards the effectiveness of the organisations of which they are members

![Businesswoman looking out of window](Picture4.jpg)

### Notes:
Leadership is one of the most researched topics in the field of business, as is defined as the ability to influence, motivate and enable others to contribute towards the effectiveness and success of the organisations of which they are members. Leadership theories are categorised into four perspectives. The perspectives are transformational, managerial, follower-centric, and competency. The most popular of these is the transformational leadership perspective.

<!-- Slide number: 4 -->
One of the most popular perspectives and theories of leadership
Views leaders as change agents
Differs from charismatic leadership

Transformational Leadership
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

### Notes:
Transformational leadership views leaders as change agents. They develop, communicate and model a shared vision for the team or organisation, and encourage experimentation. In developing the vision, they create and champion an image of the companies projected, positive, future state, which motivates and bonds employees. The vision is communicated by framing the message around a grand purpose, using symbols, metaphors, and stories to create a shared mental model of the future. Transformational leaders model the vision through walking the talk, symbolising and demonstrating the vision through their behaviour, which increases employee trust in the leader. They then encourage experimentation in new ways of operating by questioning current practices and supporting a learning orientation. Building commitment to the vision is increase through the communication and modelling of the vision, and through employee involvement in shaping the vision.

Some leadership models say charismatic leadership is essential for transformational leadership, however research suggests that charisma differs from transformational leadership as charisma is a personal trait that provides referent power, it does not necessarily attempt to change the organisation, and it is associated with narcissism.

<!-- Slide number: 5 -->
Benefits:
Higher employee satisfaction
Higher performance
Increased organisational citizenship
Increased creativity

Limitations:
Some models have circular logic
Does not recognise or account for situational differences, especially differences across cultures
Transformational Leadership
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

### Notes:
Transformational leadership contributes to higher employee satisfaction and performance, increased organisational citizenship, and creativity. However, the theory is limited by its definition of transformational leaders by their success, rather than their behaviour, leading to models with circular logic and no predictive value. It is also a universal theory, that does not recognise or account for situational differences, especially differences across cultures.

<!-- Slide number: 6 -->
Managerial Leadership
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

States that effective leaders help employees improve to support current objectives and practices
Depends on transformational leadership to set the right direction
Is comprised of many leadership theories
Managerial 
leadership
Assumes objectives are stable and aligned
Focuses on continuous development
More micro-focused and concrete
Transformational leadership
Assumes the organisation’s current direction is misaligned and needs to change
More macro-focused and abstract

### Notes:
The second perspective, Managerial Leadership, states that effective leaders help employees improve their performance and wellbeing to support current objectives and practices. It depends on transformational leadership to set the right direction, however the perspectives differ in their assumptions of organisational stability, or lack thereof, and the level of focus. At a basic level, generally the higher the managerial position, the more transformational leadership behaviours are required, however all managers will need to use varying degrees of transformational and managerial leadership.

<!-- Slide number: 7 -->
Leadership Style Orientation
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Categorises leadership style into either task-oriented, or people-oriented
Neither of these orientations is more effective than the other, each with advantages and disadvantages
Recent research shows that effective leaders rely on both styles, but in different ways.

Task-oriented leaders:
Assign work and clarify responsibilities
Set goals and deadlines
Evaluate and provide feedback on work quality
Establish well-defined best work procedures
Plan future work activities
People-oriented leaders:
Show interest in others as people
Listen to employees
Make the workplace more pleasant
Compliment employees for their work
Are considerate of employee needs

### Notes:
Managerial leadership theories include leadership style orientation, which clusters leadership behaviours into task, and people, oriented. Task-oriented leadership includes behaviours that define and structure work roles such as assigning employees to specific tasks, clarifying their work duties and procedures, ensuring they follow company rules and pushing them to reach their performance capacity, whereas people-oriented leadership includes behaviours that focus on developing relationships with employees such as showing mutual trust and respect for subordinates, demonstrating a genuine concern for their needs and having a desire to look out for their welfare. Neither of these orientations is more effective than the other, each with advantages and disadvantages, and recent research shows that effective leaders rely on both styles, but in different ways.

<!-- Slide number: 8 -->
Servant Leadership Theory
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Is an extension of the people-oriented leadership style, and takes the view that leaders:
serve their followers and help employees fulfil their needs
are coaches, stewards, and facilitators of employee development
have a natural desire or ‘calling’ to serve others
do not view leadership as a position of power
decisions and actions are bounded by ethical principles and practices.
Servant leadership relies heavily on the principles of authentic leadership
Recent research has found an association between higher organisational performance and CEO’s demonstrating servant leadership behaviours.

### Notes:
Servant leadership is an extension of the people-oriented leadership style, and is the view that leaders serve followers, rather than vice-versa; leaders help employees fulfil their needs and are coaches, stewards, and facilitators of employee development. Servant leaders have a natural desire or ‘calling’ to serve others, they do not view leadership as a position of power, and their decisions and actions are bounded by ethical principles and practices. Servant leadership relies heavily on the principles of authentic leadership, and recent research has found an association between higher organisational performance, and CEO’s demonstrating servant leadership behaviours.

<!-- Slide number: 9 -->
Path-Goal Leadership Theory
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Is a contingency theory, based on Expectancy Theory, that proposes that effective leadership depends on choosing the most appropriate leadership behaviour for the employee and the situation
Proposes it is the leader’s job to provide followers with the information, support, and/or other resources needed to achieve their goals
E.g. in a situation where employees have high skills and experience, an external locus of control, a non-routine task structure, and low team cohesion, a combination of participative and supportive leader behaviours would be suggested.

|  | Directive | Supportive | Participative | Achievement-oriented |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skill and experience | Low | Low | High | High |
| Locus of control | External | External | Internal | Internal |
| Task structure | Non-routine | Routine | Non-routine | ? |
| Team dynamics | Negative norms | Low cohesion | Positive norms | ? |

Suggested leader behaviour
Employee contingencies
Environmental contingencies

### Notes:
Path-Goal Leadership Theory proposes that effective leadership depends on choosing the most appropriate leadership behaviour, depending on the employee and the situation, to influence employee expectations about desired results and their positive outcomes. They can influence these expectations by providing followers with the information, support, and/or other resources needed to achieve their goals. The contingencies considered are employee skills and experience, and locus of control, and task structure and team dynamics. For example, in a situation where employees have high skills and experience, an external locus of control, a non-routine task structure, and low team cohesion, a combination of participative and supportive leader behaviours would be suggested.

### Notes:
Despite the comparatively significant research support, Path-Goal theory has some limitations in that a few contingencies have limited research support, some contingencies and leadership styles have not been investigated at all, and as the theory expands, it may become too complex for practical use.

Situational Leadership Theory
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Is a contingency theory based on the premise that effective leaders vary their style with the ability and motivation (or commitment) of followers

|  | Telling | Selling | Participating | Delegating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Follower Ability | Low | Low | High | High |

Suggested leader behaviour

Benefits:

Easy to use

Only empirical support for the telling style to be used when employees lack motivation and ability, which is also documented in path-goal theory.
The rest of the theory is not supported by research.

### Notes:
Situational leadership theory is another contingency theory based on the premise that effective leaders vary their style with the ability and motivation (or commitment) of followers. It specifies four leadership styles: telling, selling, participating, and delegating. However in spite of its popularity with practitioners, there is only empirical support for the ‘telling’ style to be used when employees lack motivation and ability, which is also documented in path-goal theory. The rest of the theory is not supported by research.

### Notes:
Fielders contingency Model is based on the same premise of Leader effectiveness depending on matching leadership style (people-oriented or task-oriented) to the situation and looks at the situation in terms of three factors relating to situational control. This theory recognises the importance of leader power in determining the most effective leadership style, and also that changing the style of leadership may be difficult due to a particular style being inconsistent with the leader’s personality and values. However, it lacks research support due to the limited focus on two leadership styles, and flaws in the questionnaire used to measure leadership style.

<!-- Slide number: 13 -->
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Leader-Member Exchange (LMX) Theory focuses on the relationship that exists between leaders and members, rather than the style the leader is using
Looks at relationships as a series of exchanges, differentiated based on their quality
Low LMX relationships are based on economic exchanges, e.g. leaders providing organisational resources in return for task performance
High LMX relationships are based on social exchange of resources, e.g. liking, trust, and commitment.

Benefits:
Research shows high LMX relationships lead to increased employee commitment and organisational citizenship behaviours, enhanced job performance, and employee retention

Limitations:
Potential to alienate some employees
Does not considering the effects of team dynamics and social identity
Does not provide specific advice on how leaders can develop high-quality relationships

LMX Theory

### Notes:
Leader–member exchange theory focuses on the relationship that exists between leaders and members, rather than the style the leader is using. This theory looks at relationships as a series of exchanges, that may lead to developing trust and mutual commitment. LMX relationships are differentiated based on their quality with low LMX relationships based on economic exchanges like leaders providing organisational resources in return for task performance, and high LMX relationships based on social exchange of resources such as liking, trust, and commitment. High-quality LMX leads to improved organisational outcomes such as increased employee commitment and organisational citizenship behaviours, enhanced job performance, and employee retention. Limitations of this theory include its potential to alienate some employees, not considering the effects of team dynamics and social identity, and not providing specific advice on how leaders can develop high-quality relationships.

Benefits:
Explains the effectiveness of self-management and autonomous work groups

Limitations:
Empirical evidence is mixed on the effectiveness of leadership substitutes
Research suggests substitutes help, but do not completely replace, real leadership

Leadership Substitutes Theory

### Notes:
Leadership substitutes theory identifies contingencies that either limit the leader’s ability to influence subordinates or make a particular leadership style unnecessary. Contingencies include training and experience which can replace task-oriented leadership. The research suggests that substitutes help, but do not completely replace real leadership.

<!-- Slide number: 15 -->
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial

Competency

Recognises that leaders don’t operate in a vacuum
Proposes that leaders emerge because of the attributional and cognitive processes of their followers
Tends to be seen in organisations that have a flat structure, where leaders and followers are treated equally, where employees have a ‘voice’ and can greatly impact organizational decision-making.

Romance of Leadership Theory:
Followers want to believe that leaders make a difference, so they engage in fundamental attribution error and other perceptual distortions to support this belief
Is supported by the Western belief that life events are generated more by people than by uncontrollable natural forces

Follower-Centric Perspective

### Notes:
The Follower-centric perspective recognises that leaders don’t operate in a vacuum, and it proposes that leaders emerge because of the attributional and cognitive processes of their followers. Organizations that use follower-centric styles tend to have a flat structure, where leaders and followers are treated equally. Employees have a ‘voice’ and can greatly impact organizational decision-making.

The romance of leadership effect, where leaders are seen to have a sole impact on organisational success is based in people wanting to believe that leaders make a difference, so they engage in fundamental attribution error and other perceptual distortions to support this belief in the leader’s impact. This simplification of life events is done to minimise cognitive processing (discussed in topic three) and is supported by the Western belief that life events are generated more by people than by uncontrollable natural forces.

The implicit leadership theory poses that people have preconceived beliefs about the features and behaviours of effective leaders, known as leadership prototypes, which they use to evaluate the leader’s effectiveness. People are more likely to think a leader is effective when they fit their established idea of what a leader SHOULD be. Leadership exists in the mind of the followers.

<!-- Slide number: 16 -->
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Identifies the characteristics of effective leaders
Is an improvement of the ‘great man theory’ which was popular before World War II.
Early research found that very few ‘traits’ predicted effective leadership, however recent research suggests that several competencies are key influences on leadership potential and can be predictors of effective leaders
Competency Perspective

| Competency | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Personality | Higher levels of extraversion (outgoing, talkative, sociable, and assertive) and conscientiousness (careful, dependable, and self-disciplined) |
| Self-concept | Self-beliefs and positive self-evaluation of their own leadership skills and ability to achieve objectives |
| Drive | Inner motivation to pursue goals |
| Integrity | Truthfulness and tendency to translate words into deeds |
| Leadership Motivation | Need for socialised power to accomplish team or organisational goals |
| Business Knowledge | Tacit and explicit knowledge about the company’s environment enabling them to make more intuitive decisions |
| Cognitive and Practical Intelligence | Above average cognitive ability to process information and solve real-world problems by adapting to, shaping, or selecting, appropriate environments |
| Emotional Intelligence | Ability to monitor their own and others emotions, discriminate among them, and use the information to guide their thoughts and actions |

### Notes:
The competency perspective identifies the characteristics of effective leaders. This perspective is an improvement of the ‘great man theory’ which was popular before World War II. The early research found that very few ‘traits’ predicted effective leadership, however recent research suggests that several competencies, for example skills, knowledge, and values, are key influences on leadership potential and can be predictors of effective leaders

<!-- Slide number: 17 -->
# Leadership Perspectives
Transformational
Managerial
Follower-centric
Competency
Emerging

Is using referent power gained through personal traits or relational quality to influence followers
Charisma is both inherent and learned, with charismatic leaders likely to be extraverted, self-confident, and achievement oriented.

Benefits:
Charismatic behaviours of confidence, dominance, and high self-esteem are present in a lot of beliefs (mental models) about what makes an effective leader, and so, due to the implicit leadership theory, followers are likely to rate them positively
Potential for high levels of performance and achievement

Limitations:
Produces dependent followers
May lead to focus on self-interest rather than common good
Charismatic traits also associated with narcissism which includes negative traits of greater need for personal power, lack of empathy, overconfidence, unethical behaviour, and inability to accept criticism

Charismatic Leadership Theory

### Notes:
Charismatic leadership is one of the older theories of leadership, and can be something one is born with, or it can be learned. It is achieved through using referent power gained through personal traits or relational quality to influence followers and has the potential to increase performance and achievement. The implicit leadership theory explains some of the effectiveness of charismatic leaders, as a lot of people have a mental model of ‘heroic masculinity’. However, charismatic leaders produce dependent followers, rather than empowering them, and charismatic traits are also associated with narcissism, which itself has a long list of negative traits.

Leadership perspectives include:
transformational perspective - looks at leadership on a macro-scale, visioning for the future
managerial perspective - focusses on day-to-day requirements of a leader
follower-centric perspective - recognises that leaders do not operate in a vacuum and that followers' beliefs and expectations impact whether a leader is seen as effective
competency perspective - acknowledges that there are some key predictors (competencies) of effective leaders
Leadership theories try to predict what determines effective leadership, based on situation, people, or other factors. Each have their benefits and limitations.
Both culture and gender affect leadership effectiveness, however this is mostly based in leader prototypes, not actual ability to lead or perform leadership behaviours

# Topic 9 Summary

### Notes:
There are many perspectives on leadership, and related theories. The Transformational perspective looks at leadership on a macro-scale, visioning for the future, whereas managerial perspective focusses on day-to-day requirements of a leader and contains a myriad of theories which try to predict which behaviours and styles will be effective in a given situation. The follower-centric perspective recognises that leaders don’t operate in a vacuum, and that followers' beliefs and expectations impact whether a leader is seen as effective, and finally the competency perspective acknowledges that there are some key predictors of effective leaders. Culture and gender, in addition to other contingency factors identified in theories, impact the way a leader's effectiveness is perceived, and it is important to reflect on the context of leaders - their situation, team contingencies, work contingencies, their relationship with followers, when looking at what might make them more, or less, effective.

Thank you.
