## 📄 03-assessment/BUS293_Referencing_Standards.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Assesment]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

Готово — короткий документ с правилами оформления ссылок (1 страница). Таблиц и изображений нет. Полный текст на английском, дословно:

---

**BUS293 Referencing Standards**

All assessment for BUS293 must be referenced in full using **Chicago Style Referencing**.

A full detailed guide of the style accepted for BUS293 assessment work is outlined on the Murdoch Library web site at:
http://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago

Chicago referencing is based on the convention that in the text a student needs to cite:
(Author[s] family name[s], year) and page number for all direct quotes.

Please note that a professional and consistent presentation of the format used will avoid penalties during marking. One area where students often lose marks is by presenting the page number in some in-text referencing and not in others. The in-text references do not need the page numbers unless it is a direct quote in which case the page number must always be presented and the quote placed in inverted commas. However equally acceptable is for the page numbers to be presented in all cases. A consistent approach is required.

In the Reference List students can lose marks when using brackets around the years in some references and not in others. Chicago referencing does not use brackets around the years.

A sample of the required presentation of the 'List of References' is available in the Murdoch Library web site. Take note of the required indentation of second and subsequent lines of each reference (formatted using a hanging indent).

**Group Research Report:**

Minimum requirement is 20 credible references.

The requirement is that all ideas, statements and facts are acknowledged by referencing the source.

One reference at the end of a paragraph will not be an acceptable degree of referencing.

A consistent presentation of all in-text and the reference list should be checked during the editing process.

---

**Key points:**

- Referencing style: **Chicago Style** (Murdoch Library guide: http://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago).
- In-text format: (Author family name[s], year); page number required for **direct quotes** (and quote in inverted commas). Page numbers optional otherwise — but be **consistent** (either page numbers only for quotes, or page numbers in all cases).
- Reference List: **no brackets** around years; use a **hanging indent** for second and subsequent lines.
- **Group Research Report:** minimum **20 credible references**; every idea, statement and fact must be referenced; one reference at the end of a paragraph is not acceptable; check consistency during editing.

Единственная ссылка (URL) в документе: http://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago. Ссылок на видео нет.



## 📄 03-assessment/BUS293_Team_Contract_2020.md

Готово — это бланк/шаблон командного контракта (форма для заполнения). Полный текст на английском, дословно (подчёркивания/линии для заполнения обозначаю как «**\_**»):

---

# BUS293 Team Contract

Team Number: ********\_\_******** Team Name: **************\_**************

It is a normal business practice to put into writing all agreements that are binding on the parties involved. It is suggested that you now take the time to establish the acceptable team norms and behaviours that you will enforce. It is further suggested that you decide on a conflict and dispute resolution procedure, so this is established before conflicts arise. Below is a 'team contract' that will bind all team members to what the team decides, until the team is dissolved when the final assessment is concluded.

**TEAM CONTRACT**

It is agreed that the members of this team will:

- Upload a copy of the completed and signed contract to the LMS team discussion forum.
- Accept that ****************\_**************** is the team leader and all agree to follow their directions in completing the required tasks.
- Give written warnings via the LMS team discussion forum to team members who do not meet the agreed obligations and responsibilities.
- Give a written warning to any team member who does not attend the workshop, or other scheduled team meeting, without prior notice to the team for a reason acceptable to the team.
- Give a written warning to any team member who does not submit required work to the group by the deadlines set by the team.
- Consult with the lecturer if any team member has received two written warnings.
- Remove any member from the team who receives three written warnings.
- The agreed team dispute mechanism is as follows: [пустые линии для заполнения — несколько строк]

It is freely agreed to by the parties who have **SIGNED** below, that all team members listed as signatories, are bound by their signatures to carry out all duties and obligations and in return, they bind all others to give the same assurance.

I (name)……………………………(signature)……………………… [×4 строки для подписей]

…have read and signed this understanding that the ultimate sanction of dismissal from the team will require me to do all the assignments in the outline on my own to the same standard as a full team would.

Dated: ************\_\_\_\_************

---

**Key points (что фиксирует контракт):**

- Поля: номер и название команды; имя team leader; место для прописанного dispute mechanism; до 4 подписей участников; дата.
- Обязательства команды: загрузить подписанный контракт в LMS team discussion forum; письменные предупреждения через форум за невыполнение обязательств, пропуск воркшопа/встречи без уважительной причины и заранее, несдачу работы к дедлайну команды.
- Эскалация: **2 письменных предупреждения** → консультация с лектором; **3 предупреждения** → исключение из команды.
- Санкция за исключение: исключённый участник должен выполнить **все задания из outline самостоятельно** на том же уровне, что и полная команда.

Ссылок на видео/URL в документе нет; таблиц и изображений нет.

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

1.0  PURPOSE.

Success in winning the approval and support of others for your thinking is not
just a product of the ideas themselves.  Of equal importance will be the way you
present your ideas.

Business reports sell your thinking to both managers and academics, so it is in your best interests to

digest  the  contents  of  this  outline  and  embrace  them.    While  the  writing  requirements  may  seem

stringent, it is recommended that you bear in mind that these guidelines will serve you well throughout

life, not just here at Murdoch. Adopt them as your own and you will have taken an important step in

improving not only the "packaging" of your ideas, but the value of the ideas themselves.

Additional  standards,  such  as  the  Chicago  referencing  system,  are  also  included  to  address

fundamental  academic  requirements.    While  referencing  may  seem  a  burden  to  some,  it  should  be

remembered that any business report will require the writer to state the sources of the information in

the  main  body  of  the  report  (or  in  appendices  where  appropriate).    So,  it  should  be  understood  that

we're  not  actually  asking  any  more  of you  than  would  be  the  case  in  the business  world.   Note  that

your report does not require a 'purpose' section. The following content outline will provide current

business students with some precise specifications for their report.

2


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

2.0  OUTLINE OF A REPORT FOR BUS293.
The contents of each specific element of a report are provided here in Section 2.0 to assist student in

preparing and structuring their major assessment.

2.1  Cover Page

This should include all standard requirements for a paper, which include;

1.  Unit code and title.

2.  Report title (Topic should be in large font).

3.  Student name and number.

4.  Workshop day and time.

5.  Name of the workshop facilitator (tutor).

It is important to remember that this is a cover page.  So give some thought to its presentation.  If you

cannot  find  a  snappy  graphic  that  is  appropriate,  at  least  ensure  that  some  thought  is  given  to  the

format of these elements.  Clearly the second element is most important and should be formatted with

the largest font, centre aligned.  Other elements are free to be presented in a fashion of your choosing,

but at least make an effort to have a cover that looks professional.

2.2  Report Contents Page

2.2.1  Characteristics

  This should be titled "Contents".

  It  should  have  a  comprehensive  index  showing  the  structure  of  the  report  and  its  various

elements.

  Typically, there are two to four levels of titles in the index to reflect the structure (note there are

three in this document's table of contents).

  It should be the last thing you add to the document before printing.

It will be critical for writers to know the basics of how to build an index using Microsoft (MS) Word,

a function that will enable you to build an index in the blink of an eye.  See Appendix 3.1 for a guide.

2.3  Executive Summary (ES) (Commercial format) – keep to 1 page only

In the commercial world, the ES is the most important page in the entire report.  Put yourself in the

shoes of a Business Analyst or Management consultant for a moment; you have to sell your thinking

in  this  one  page because  many  managers  do  not  have  the  time  to  read  the  entire  report.    It  is  high

impact stuff with every word chosen to ensure the "Big Picture" is summed up in one page.  Typically,

3


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

the contents of an executive summary are written last after the whole structure, content and scope of

the report is defined.  However, it does not hurt to have a draft written early as this may help define

goals  for  the  rest  of  the  report  while  it  is  being  constructed.    Furthermore,  as  new  core  ideas  of

significance  emerge,  you  can  amend  the  draft  to  reflect  these  revelations  that  naturally  occur  in  the

construction  stages.    Ultimately,  its  final  form  should  be  decided  on  after  you  are  satisfied  that  all

elements  in  the  discussion  sections  and  end  report  sections  are  finished.    The  following  elements

outline the typical contents of an ES.

Note:  Justified alignment looks best - i.e., even margins on both sides as shown here; however left

alignment will be accepted. What matters is that you are consistent throughout the report.

2.3.1  The Three Main Elements of the Executive Summary.

1.  The  topic  and  its  significance:    This  introduces  the  issue  in  question  and  its  importance  to

management.  Usually topics are linked with the key issues.

2.  The findings (conclusions):  This provides the reader with your high level evaluation on the issue

in question.  In essence, your informed opinion  - always stay  third person (No "I", "my", etc).

Here, you make it clear what the key findings of your analysis are.

3.  The recommendations and their benefits:  This provides the reader with solutions to the issue in

question along with some benefits.

The  entire  executive  summary  should  be no more  than  one  page.    To  cover  the  above  areas  in  one

page  will  be  challenging  for  most  writers  because  writing  a  good  ES  will  provide  a  reader  with  a

concise, high level understanding of all the core issues.  You do not need subsections here.

2.3.2  Benefits of an Executive Summary (ES)

As already stated, managers are very busy.  If you  cannot get the main messages across in a page,

chances are you will lose their attention.  The ES should be able to act as a stand alone, powerful

page that sells the report.  However, there are also other benefits, such as improving reader memory

retention  by providing  a  reader  with  a  broad  understanding of  an  issue  that  creates  a  framework

around which the detailed information can be more readily interpreted.

2.4

Introduction

This section ideally should not go over  one page in length.  There must be four subsections in this

page that cover specific requirements.  Their names and content descriptions are listed below:

1.  Topic:    Here,  you  introduce  the  topic  and  elaborate  on  its  significance  briefly.    Do  not  provide

findings; simply define the key purpose (which is to arrive at the findings).

4


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

2.  Limitations:    Here,  you  discuss  the  scope  and  constraints  of  the  report  by  elaborating  on  any

weaknesses or omissions.  This is often due to topic complexity  and problems relating to limited

info provided in the case  (A common problem when examining cases  is that people often distort

information for their own ends).

3.  Sources  of  Data:    State  briefly  what  sources  of  data  have  been  obtained.    Are  they  secondary

only, such as books, journals, papers, magazines and websites, or have you obtained primary data

such as direct interviews (note: primary data is NOT to be collected for this assignment).

4.  Report Organisation:  Here, simply elaborate on the structure of the main body of the report so

the reader knows what to expect and comment on whether you will provide any recommendations

and conclusions.  Do not mention the Intro or ES here.

2.5  Main Body of the Report

This  section  requires  the  writer  to  present  all  the  research  uncovered.    The  characteristics  of  the

discussion section are;

2.5.1  Characteristics

  Third person, factual, objective and impersonal.  You simply present the evidence uncovered

by research and draw attention to information of greatest significance.

  Split  into  numerous,  logical  sections  and  sub/sections  to  help  structure  the  dialogue.  The

sections  of  the  question  and  the  research  may  help  structure  the  discussion  (main  body)  of  the

report.

  The sections and subsections should have titles that reflect the content (as this guide demonstrates)

and  organise  information  logically.  The  key  issues/researched  findings  not  only  inform  your

research  effort  but  also  help  structure  the  report  discussion  itself.    The  precise  format  may

vary from topic to topic as the circumstances vary, but in BUS293 you will nearly always find it

best to have titles in major discussion sections that reflect the key issues in the topic.

  You  do  not  draw  attention  to  the  reader  or  yourself  (keep  your  writing  to  third  person

perspective).  Just present the facts found in your research (using citations/references/sources).

  Define the core theories and concepts of organisational behaviour and how they contribute to the

organisations  current  performance,  sustainability  and  alignment  to  at  least  one  of  the  Ten

Principles  of  the  United  Nations  Global  Impact  (note  ‘Guideline  for  Success’  in  BUS293  Unit

Guide, for expected coverage of sustainability).

  The  main  discussion  section  is  heavily  referenced.    You  are  presenting  the  information

uncovered in your research, so this section must be heavily referenced.

5


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

The last point here regarding referencing seems to catch out  many people.  This is not a section to

talk about your opinion; it is a section to present the data found to help make logical conclusions or

support the teams opinion/decisions using credible sources.  Additionally, some discussion of possible

solutions  that  you  may  have  found  ensures  that  when  the  reader  gets  to  the  recommendations  and

conclusions,  your  key  findings  and  solutions  are  more  likely  to  be  seen  as  credible.    A  key  point

though, is to ensure this section is thoroughly researched and has sources cited per the  Chicago

method.

2.5.2  Tips on when to reference

Aside from the referencing standards comprehensively defined in the unit outline, there are some basic

rules that can help you understand when the source needs to be cited.  These include;

  If it is not your idea - cite your source (per the Chicago format).

Note: For a comprehensive list of Chicago referencing examples, see Murdoch Library referencing

guides

  If  it  is  not  clear  by  the  wording of  the  dialogue  that  you  are  still  presenting  facts  from  a  source

cited previously - cite it again.

  Do not leave it till the end of the paragraph to cite a source. It must be cited as soon as the idea is

used (generally this is done at the end of a sentence).

  When using the same reference several times in a row, if it is not apparent to the reader by the tone

and  flow  of  the  discussion  that  you  are  still  talking  about  that  source.,  then  to  reduce  citation

frequency, you can use the authors name in the actual discussion (eg:  Vernon Smith (2002) notes

how ...) early in the first sentence where the ideas are used.

  If you are quoting word for word, put the quote in "inverted commas" and cite a page number if it

is available.  Pagination number will suffice for online databases.

2.6  Recommendations Section

Ideally you should have discussed some potential remedies and solutions in the discussion section and

thoroughly referenced these.  So when you get to this section you must outline the recommendations

you have arrived at as a result of your research.  This can be done in numbered bullet point form, but

you should at the very least briefly  discuss the benefit/s of the recommendations, or a paragraph for

each recommendation, each with a sub-heading.

If you have done your research, you may have many recommendations; the team needs to choose the

most relevant five recommendations. These should be detailed and include the benefits and not simply

state  the  recommendation;  this  will  allow  the  recommendation  to  be  explicitly  linked  to  business

needs,  a  critical  component  of  business  report  writing.  Your  recommendations  must  be  useful  and

6


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

practical for managers. Generally you do not need to reference here, as potential solutions should have

already been discussed in the discussion/appendices sections (However, you should note references if

this is not the case). Remember to stay 3rd person.

2.7  Conclusion – one page only
Here  you  provide  your  core  high  level  findings  in  no  more  than  a  page  (Stay  3rd  person).    These

should  draw  together  the  facts  found  in  research  and  your  recommendations  to  demonstrate  a  well

thought out plan of attack.  This should be a powerful section, which should end on a high note or a

note of urgency to generate reader support.  Touching on the benefits of the proposed course of action,

or  the  consequences  of  not  acting  in  accordance  with  recommendations  is  usually  a  good  way  to

accomplish this.  Generally, this section is not heavily referenced as this was done in the discussion

section.  However, if you introduce new information, you must reference it here as well (note: if

something  is  mentioned  in  the  conclusion,  it  should  be  backed  up  with  your  research  and  findings,

hence  any  new  information  in  the  conclusion  is  likely  to  warrant  scrutiny  by  the  reader/marker).

Additionally, if there are critical qualifications to your argument, raise them here to frame your ideas

appropriately.

2.8  Reference List

This  should  contain  an  alphabetical  list  of  all  sources  used  in  the  report.    It  must  comply  with  the

Chicago referencing standards. (see Murdoch Library). https://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago

2.9  Appendices - optional

▪  Look  at  the  example  appendix  at  the  end  of  the  document  titled,  Building  a  Table  of  Contents.

You will note it is in a section called "Appendices" with each appendix under its own subheading

(With name and number).  You should also remember that  citing the sources of data here is a

must if it is not an analysis or research you have conducted yourself.

▪  Do not simply copy and paste large amounts of discussion into an appendix.  Appendices should

use tables, graphs, figures and interesting formatting to help aid reader comprehension.

Remember to use appendices to keep under the size limit set (up to  3000 words) as this word count

includes all text within the discussion section.

7


BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

---

**Murdoch University — BUS293 Detailed Report Guidelines**
(Adapted from the work of Alexander Dawson - BUS145 Detailed Report Guidelines)

**Objectives of These Guidelines**

1. To demonstrate the importance of how ideas are presented.
2. Provide unit participants with a concise outline of the key requirements and elements of the report assessment.
3. Guidance for participants to provide a document that models some of the standards outlined herein.

**Note on size limits:** 3000 words includes all text contained in the discussion section only. It does not include content from the executive summary, introduction, recommendations and the conclusion.

**Copyright/authorship note (p.2):** The BUS145 Detailed Report Guidelines was originally written by Alexander Dawson in 2012. It has been adapted and revised for BUS293 by Carole Brady in 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023. © Published by Murdoch University, Perth, Western Australia, January 2023. This publication is copyright.

---

**Report Contents (table of contents structure)**

- 1.0 PURPOSE (p.2)
- 2.0 OUTLINE OF A REPORT FOR BUS293 (p.3)
  - 2.1 Cover Page (p.3)
  - 2.2 Report Contents Page (p.3) → 2.2.1 Characteristics
  - 2.3 Executive Summary (ES) (Commercial format) – keep to 1 page only (p.3) → 2.3.1 The Three Main Elements of the Executive Summary; 2.3.2 Benefits of an Executive Summary (ES)
  - 2.4 Introduction (p.4)
  - 2.5 Main Body of the Report (p.5) → 2.5.1 Characteristics; 2.5.2 Tips on when to reference
  - 2.6 Recommendations Section (p.6)
  - 2.7 Conclusion – one page only (p.7)
  - 2.8 Reference List (p.7)
  - 2.9 Appendices – optional (p.7)
- 3.0 APPENDICES (p.8)
  - 3.1 Appendix 1: Building a Table of Contents with Microsoft (MS) Word (Updated 2012 – later versions of Word may differ) (p.8)
- END OF DOCUMENT (p.9)

**"HOW to do this Table of Contents" (note under the TOC):** Note the alphanumeric format of the various sections, subsections and sub-subsections. This provides the reader with a sense of the hierarchy and organisation of the report. Contrasting font sizes, styles and the numbering system help distinguish the organisation. MS Word's **index and tables builder** (used to make this index) represents these formats in cut-down form with a few clicks (see Appendix 1). If you underline, that is how it will look here. The index builder also adds indentations to elaborate the structure.

---

**1.0 PURPOSE**
_"Success in winning the approval and support of others for your thinking is not just a product of the ideas themselves. Of equal importance will be the way you present your ideas."_

Business reports sell your thinking to both managers and academics, so it is in your best interests to digest and embrace this outline. The guidelines will serve you well throughout life, not just at Murdoch. Adopting them improves both the "packaging" of your ideas and the value of the ideas themselves. Additional standards, such as the **Chicago referencing system**, address fundamental academic requirements; any business report requires the writer to state sources in the main body (or appendices). **Note that your report does not require a 'purpose' section.**

---

**2.0 OUTLINE OF A REPORT FOR BUS293**
The contents of each specific element of a report are provided in Section 2.0 to assist students in preparing and structuring their major assessment.

**2.1 Cover Page** — should include all standard requirements:

1. Unit code and title.
2. Report title (Topic should be in large font).
3. Student name and number.
4. Workshop day and time.
5. Name of the workshop facilitator (tutor).
   Give thought to presentation. The second element (report title) is most important — largest font, centre aligned. Other elements can be presented as you choose, but the cover should look professional.

**2.2 Report Contents Page — 2.2.1 Characteristics**

- Should be titled "Contents".
- Comprehensive index showing the structure of the report and its various elements.
- Typically two to four levels of titles in the index (this document's TOC has three).
- Should be the last thing you add before printing.
  Writers must know how to build an index using MS Word (see Appendix 3.1).

**2.3 Executive Summary (ES) (Commercial format) – keep to 1 page only**
In the commercial world, the ES is the most important page. You must sell your thinking in one page because many managers don't have time to read the whole report. High-impact, every word chosen to sum up the "Big Picture" in one page. Typically written **last**, after the whole structure, content and scope are defined — though a draft written early can help define goals and be amended as core ideas emerge; finalise after the discussion and end sections are finished.
_Note:_ Justified alignment looks best (even margins both sides), but left alignment is accepted — be consistent throughout.

**2.3.1 The Three Main Elements of the Executive Summary**

1. **The topic and its significance:** introduces the issue and its importance to management; usually linked with the key issues.
2. **The findings (conclusions):** your high-level evaluation/informed opinion — always stay **third person** (No "I", "my", etc.); make clear what the key findings of your analysis are.
3. **The recommendations and their benefits:** solutions to the issue plus some benefits.
   The entire ES should be no more than **one page**. You do not need subsections here.

**2.3.2 Benefits of an Executive Summary (ES)**
Managers are busy — if you can't get the main messages across in a page you'll lose their attention. The ES acts as a stand-alone, powerful page that sells the report. It also improves reader memory retention by giving a broad understanding that creates a framework for interpreting the detail.

**2.4 Introduction** — ideally no more than **one page**, with **four subsections**:

1. **Topic:** introduce the topic and briefly elaborate on its significance. Do not provide findings; simply define the key purpose (which is to arrive at the findings).
2. **Limitations:** discuss scope and constraints — weaknesses or omissions, often due to topic complexity and limited info in the case (people often distort information for their own ends).
3. **Sources of Data:** state briefly what sources were obtained — secondary only (books, journals, papers, magazines, websites) or primary (e.g. direct interviews). _Note: primary data is NOT to be collected for this assignment._
4. **Report Organisation:** elaborate on the structure of the main body so the reader knows what to expect; comment on whether you'll provide recommendations and conclusions. **Do not** mention the Intro or ES here.

**2.5 Main Body of the Report — 2.5.1 Characteristics**

- **Third person, factual, objective and impersonal.** Present the evidence uncovered and draw attention to the most significant information.
- **Split into numerous, logical sections and sub/sections.** The sections of the question and the research may help structure the discussion.
- Sections/subsections should have titles that reflect content and organise information logically. In BUS293, you'll nearly always find it best to have titles in major discussion sections that reflect the key issues in the topic.
- **Do not** draw attention to the reader or yourself (third person). Just present facts with citations/references/sources.
- Define the core theories and concepts of organisational behaviour and how they contribute to the organisation's current performance, sustainability and **alignment to at least one of the Ten Principles of the United Nations Global Impact** (see 'Guideline for Success' in the BUS293 Unit Guide for expected coverage of sustainability).
- **The main discussion section is heavily referenced** — you're presenting researched information, so it must be heavily referenced.
  (Additional note p.6:) This is not a section for your opinion; present the data found to make logical conclusions or support the team's decisions using credible sources. Discussing possible solutions here makes your later recommendations/conclusions more credible. Ensure the section is thoroughly researched and cited per the **Chicago method**.

**2.5.2 Tips on when to reference**

- If it is not your idea — cite your source (Chicago format). _Note: for a comprehensive list of Chicago examples, see the Murdoch Library referencing guides._
- If it's not clear from the wording that you're still presenting facts from a previously cited source — cite it again.
- Do not leave it till the end of the paragraph to cite. Cite as soon as the idea is used (generally at the end of a sentence).
- When using the same reference several times in a row, if it's not apparent you're still on that source, reduce citation frequency by using the author's name in the discussion (e.g. "Vernon Smith (2002) notes how …") early in the first sentence.
- If quoting word for word, put the quote in "inverted commas" and cite a page number if available. Pagination/number will suffice for online databases.

**2.6 Recommendations Section**
Ideally you've already discussed potential remedies/solutions (referenced) in the discussion section; here, outline the recommendations arrived at from your research. Can be numbered bullet-point form, but at minimum briefly discuss the benefit(s), or a paragraph per recommendation each with a sub-heading. You may have many recommendations; **the team needs to choose the most relevant five recommendations.** These should be detailed and include benefits (not just state the recommendation), so each is explicitly **linked to business needs** — a critical component of business report writing. Recommendations must be useful and practical for managers. Generally you do not need to reference here (solutions already discussed/referenced earlier; note references if not). Remember to stay **3rd person**.

**2.7 Conclusion – one page only**
Provide your core high-level findings in no more than a page (3rd person). Draw together the researched facts and your recommendations to demonstrate a well-thought-out plan of attack. Should be a powerful section ending on a high note or a note of urgency to generate reader support — touch on benefits of the proposed course of action or consequences of not acting. Generally **not heavily referenced** (done in the discussion), but **if you introduce new information you must reference it here** (new info in the conclusion warrants scrutiny). Raise any critical qualifications to your argument here to frame your ideas appropriately.

**2.8 Reference List**
An alphabetical list of all sources used in the report. Must comply with Chicago referencing standards (see Murdoch Library): https://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago

**2.9 Appendices – optional**

- See the example appendix at the end (titled "Building a Table of Contents") — in a section called "Appendices", each appendix under its own subheading (with name and number). Citing sources of data here is a **must** if it's not your own analysis/research.
- **Do not** simply copy and paste large amounts of discussion into an appendix. Appendices should use tables, graphs, figures and interesting formatting to aid comprehension.
- Remember to use appendices to keep under the **3000-word** size limit (the word count includes all text within the discussion section).

---

**3.0 APPENDICES**
**3.1 Appendix 1: Building a Table of Contents with Microsoft (MS) Word** (Updated 2012 – later versions of Word may differ)
Word has an automatic index builder; this and the formatting of this document should guide you.

- Before using it, be familiar with the **Style** function in the **Home Tab** (to select "heading 1", "heading 2", etc. — the TOC hierarchy). Select the text for the heading/subheading first, then apply the style formatting.
- To preview the hierarchy of your style headings, use the **Document Map / Navigation Pane** function in the **View tab** (check/uncheck to hide/show). Useful for tracking sections in a large document.
- MS Word's index builder is accessed from the **References Tab** (click "Table of Contents"). Typically the **last** thing you add, on its own page. Insert the cursor on the page where you want the index before accessing this feature.
  _Note:_ If you don't like the default heading format, change it using the **Format Painter** (the button with the paintbrush, found via the Home tab).

**Side box — "Customizing a Heading Style With the Format Painter Tool":** The Format Painter copies the format of any selected text onto text you select after clicking it — useful for keeping formatting consistent. Steps:

1. After creating a heading and changing its font size/format, select the heading text and click the Format Painter button (a paintbrush appears next to the cursor).
2. Move the cursor to the left of the heading you wish to format similarly.
3. As you move from the heading to the left margin, the cursor changes to an arrow — left-click. The same style is applied to that line. If it doesn't work, repeat and at step three select the text you wish to format instead. Trouble usually comes from not selecting text correctly — drag the paintbrush/cursor over the text holding the left mouse button, and keep practising.

**END OF DOCUMENT**

---

**Key requirements at a glance:**

- **Report structure (in order):** Cover Page → Contents → Executive Summary (1 page) → Introduction (1 page, 4 subsections) → Main Body/Discussion → Recommendations → Conclusion (1 page) → Reference List → Appendices (optional).
- **Word limit:** 3000 words — **discussion section only** (excludes ES, intro, recommendations, conclusion).
- **Voice:** third person throughout (no "I"/"my").
- **Executive Summary 3 elements:** topic & significance; findings; recommendations & benefits.
- **Introduction 4 subsections:** Topic; Limitations; Sources of Data (secondary only — no primary research); Report Organisation.
- **Recommendations:** choose the **5 most relevant**, detailed, with benefits, linked to business needs.
- **Referencing:** Chicago style; cite as soon as an idea is used (not at paragraph end); quotes in inverted commas with page numbers; minimum (per Unit Guide) **20 credible references**; main body heavily referenced.
- **Content requirement specific to BUS293:** define core OB theories/concepts and link to the organisation's performance, sustainability, and **alignment to at least one of the Ten Principles of the UN Global Compact** ("Global Impact" as written in the doc).
- **Appendices:** use tables/graphs/figures (not pasted discussion); cite sources; use to stay under the word limit.

URL в документе: https://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago (Murdoch Library Chicago guide). Ссылок на видео нет.

# BUS293: Individual Reflection & Review · Part 1 Video Script
**Faiaz Dzhafarov (35553299) · Group 11 · Westpac Banking Corporation · Team Dynamics**
**Target: 3.5 min. HD = within 5 sec (aim 3:28–3:33 on a stopwatch). ~480 words at a realistic camera pace (~135 wpm).**

> Two parts: A = your contribution + key findings (~1.5 min); B = reflection using Ch.8 concepts (~2 min).
> Read it conversational, face the camera, slow down on the numbers. File: BUS293IRRDzhafarovF35553299.mp4

---

## PART A: My contribution & key findings  (~1.5 min, ~185 words)

Hi, I'm Faiaz. For our team report, my group looked at team dynamics at a company called Westpac. Westpac is one of Australia's big four banks.

My part was team trust. I also made the reference list and the appendices, and I wrote the conclusion after everyone finished.

I learned that trust is not one thing. It is built on three things. First, you see the person as honest. Second, you feel they really care about you. Third, you see they are good at their job. If one is missing, trust drops. Trust also grows slowly, so one broken promise can set you back.

What surprised me most was how trust sits under psychological safety. That means feeling safe to speak up. In a bank with strict rules, if people do not feel safe, they stay quiet about problems. Westpac learned this the hard way. In 2020 it paid a record fine of one point three billion dollars, for more than twenty-three million breaches of money-laundering law. One reason was that problems did not reach the managers. So my ideas were about safe ways to speak up, and fair, steady leadership.

---

## PART B: Reflection on our teamwork (Ch.8 Team Dynamics)  (~2 min, ~295 words)

Now let me look back at how our team really worked. Chapter eight gave me the words for it.

The first big thing was a change in team size. We started with four people. Then one person left the unit, so we were three. We had to share his work and organise again. But the chapter says something helpful: smaller teams often work together and trust each other better. That is what happened with us.

Roles were important too. Nobody was the official leader. But one teammate, Owethu, quietly became what the chapter calls the Organiser. She set up our shared document, the schedule and the forum posts, and she chased our deadlines. The chapter says people often take roles by themselves, and nobody gives them out. That is exactly what we saw.

In Tuckman's stages, losing a member pushed us back. We went from norming into a short storming, then back to norming when the roles were clear. From the Five C's, our Coordinating was strong, thanks to Owethu. But our Comforting and our face-to-face Communicating were weaker, because our team was in different time zones and we worked at different times.

This is where my own topic became real: swift trust, which means fast trust. We had no time to build trust the slow way. So we trusted clear roles and shared deadlines instead. Seeing my report topic happen in my own team was the best part for me.

To be honest, our weak point was team reflexivity. This is Schippers' idea that a team should stop and check how it works. We almost never did. So we lost time and got confused about who did what. My lesson is simple: in a remote team, clear roles do the job that sitting in the same room normally does.

---

## ✎ Notes for you (Faiaz) before recording
- **Timing (graded hard):** aim **3:28–3:33** on a stopwatch — HD is within 5 sec of 3.5 min. Time a full read-through first; if you run over 3:35, cut one sentence from Part B.
- **Facts confirmed (28 Jun):** Owethu is "she"; the swift-trust and reflexivity points are kept as honest reflection (they earn the Reflection marks). Say them in your own words.
- **Ch.8 anchors are deliberate** (composition change, Organiser role, Tuckman, Five C's, swift trust, reflexivity) — say the named terms clearly; that's what the Reflection criterion (20 of 50 marks) rewards.
- **On camera:** face the camera, smile, smart-casual minimum, clean background, clear audio, **no slides** — just you. (Marker rewards "rehearsed, conversational, suitable for senior managers.")

- **Names:** only Owethu is named, positively. Reflection is about dynamics, not blame.

- **b. high openness to experience personality** ✅
- c. high security personal value
- d. low neuroticism personality
- e. high conformity personal value

### Q18. Which of the following is identified as an ethical principle? ✅

- **a. utilitarianism** ✅
- b. power distance
- c. conservation
- d. self-enhancement
- e. conscientiousness

### Q19. Feedback to employees is most effective when it is frequent, credible, and general. ✅

- a. true
- **b. false** ✅

### Q20. Self-concept can be described by three characteristics: ✅

- a. self, enhancement, and evaluation.
- **b. complexity, consistency, and clarity.** ✅
- c. evaluation, verification, and complexity.
- d. self, consistency, and clarity.
- e. stability, clarity, and ambiguity.

### Q1. The emerging body of research does not support the theory of self-leadership. ✅

### Q2. Team-based structures are usually found… ✅

- a. Surface acting

- e. General adaptation syndrome

### Q6. Two technological contingencies that influence the best type of organizational structure are… ✅

- b. apply rewards once a year

- b. Job burnout

- d. Workaholism
- **e. Stress** ✅

### Q14. Organic structures are best suited for hostile environments. ❌

- **a. true** ← верный ответ

## 📄 03-assessment/Quiz_4_Chapters_10_&_14.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Assesment]] · [[BUS293]] · _Quiz 4 разбор (курс BUS293)_

# Quiz 4 — Chapters 10 & 14

**Предмет:** BUS293 — Organisational Theory and Behaviour (TMD 2026)
**Главы:** Chapter 10 (Power and Influence) · Chapter 14 (Organisational Culture)

> Сдан **28 июня 2026** (квитанция подтверждена). Официальная оценка Moodle ещё не выставлена — ниже **ключ с разбором** (ответы + почему). Если официальный результат где-то разойдётся, поправим.

---

### Q1. Forming a coalition…
- a. is part of a typical manager's job description.
- b. takes advantage of situations where who you know is more important than what you know.
- c. causes the decision to become more complex and ambiguous.
- **d. increases the legitimacy of its desired outcome.** ✅
- e. more effectively communicates weaknesses with opposing positions.

**Почему:** коалиция влияет тремя путями — объединяет ресурсы многих, **легитимизирует вопрос** (широкая поддержка → выглядит достойным внимания) и задействует social identity. Рост легитимности — ключевой механизм.

### Q2. Power in motion that applies sources and contingencies of power to alter another's beliefs, feelings, and behavior is called…
- a. legitimate power.
- b. politics.
- **c. influence.** ✅
- d. tactics.
- e. impression management.

**Почему:** power = только *способность* влиять; **influence** = само поведение, попытка изменить установки/поведение. «Power in motion» — это influence.

### Q3. ________ is the freedom to exercise judgment in an organization.
- a. Visibility · b. Absorption · c. Centrality · **d. Discretion** ✅ · e. Nonsubstitutability

**Почему:** одна из 4 contingencies власти. **Discretion** = свобода применять власть; её нехватка объясняет слабость front-line supervisors.

### Q4. One function of a ________ is being a spawning ground for emerging values that keep the firm aligned with stakeholders.
- a. merger · b. dominant culture · **c. subculture** ✅ · d. espoused value · e. weak culture

**Почему:** **субкультуры** — питомник новых (emerging) ценностей, держат фирму в согласии с меняющейся средой и стейкхолдерами.

### Q5. A deculturation strategy should be applied when…
- a. employees willingly embrace the acquirer's values.
- b. both firms operate successfully in different industries.
- **c. employees in the acquired firm want to hold on to their firm's culture even though it is dysfunctional.** ✅
- d. both firms have weak cultures.
- e. the companies remain distinct with minimal exchange.

**Почему:** **deculturation** (навязывание культуры покупателя) уместна, только когда культура поглощаемой фирмы дисфункциональна, а её люди этого не осознают. (Срабатывает редко.) [a=assimilation, b/e=separation, d=integration.]

### Q6. People might gain power by convincing others that they have something of value.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** власть = воспринимаемая *зависимость*. Убедив других, что у тебя есть нечто ценное, ты создаёшь зависимость → власть (особенно expert power).

### Q7. ________ values are generally socially desirable, so they present a positive public image.
- a. Enacted · b. Shared · c. Aspirational · **d. Espoused** ✅ · e. Organizational

**Почему:** **espoused** (декларируемые) ценности — то, что фирма заявляет публично; социально желательны, для имиджа. (Enacted — реально проявляемые в действиях.)

### Q8. Which statement about organizational culture norms is true?
- a. A deeper element some see as the essence of culture. *(это assumptions)*
- b. Ideal prototypes of behaviour, the correct way to think and act. *(assumptions)*
- **c. Cultural values translated into more specific behavioral guidelines.** ✅
- d. Revealed through corporate value statements. *(espoused values)*
- e. Deeply ingrained perceptions or ideal prototypes. *(assumptions)*

**Почему:** **нормы** = ценности, переведённые в конкретные поведенческие ориентиры.

### Q9. One example of a ritual is how frequently managers meet with their teams.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** ритуалы — менее формальные, запрограммированные рутины (как приветствуют, как часто встречаются и т.п.). Частота встреч с командой — ритуал.

### Q10. ________ is the strongest outcome of influence (people identify with the request and stay motivated even without extrinsic motivation).
- a. Compliance · **b. Commitment** ✅ · c. Organizational politics · d. Role modeling · e. Resistance

**Почему:** исходы влияния по силе: resistance < compliance < **commitment**. Commitment = идентификация + внутренняя мотивация.

### Q11. Which is a "soft" influence tactic?
- **a. Persuasion** ✅ · b. Upward appeal · c. Coalition formation · d. Silent authority

**Почему:** soft-тактики (на personal power) = persuasion, impression management, exchange. Остальные три — hard (на position power).

### Q12. Social networks exist everywhere because people…
- **a. have a drive to bond.** ✅ · b. are insecure. · c. are all extroverted. · d. have a need to defend their territory. · e. need to be visible.

**Почему:** у людей врождённый **drive to bond** → социальные сети образуются повсюду.

### Q13. Supervisors have three types of power: legitimate, expert, and referent.
- a. true · **b. false** ✅

**Почему:** position power = legitimate, reward, coercive. Перечень неверный; вдобавок супервайзеры часто слабы из-за нехватки discretion.

### Q14. Expertise → persuasion; a strong legitimate power base → usually more successful applying…
- a. upward appeal · b. coalition formation · **c. silent authority** ✅ · d. assertiveness · e. information control

**Почему:** **silent authority** опирается на legitimate power (подчинение без явной ссылки на власть) — типична при сильной легитимной базе.

### Q15. ________ occurs when employees at the acquired company willingly embrace the acquirer's cultural values.
- a. Deculturation · **b. Assimilation** ✅ · c. Separation · d. Integration · e. Negotiation

**Почему:** **assimilation** = поглощаемая фирма добровольно принимает культуру покупателя (её культура слабая, у покупателя — сильная/успешная).

### Q16. Which is NOT a function of a strong culture?
- a. Control system. · b. Helps people make sense of things. · c. Social glue. · d. Makes expectations clearer.
- **e. It makes the institutionalization of artifacts unnecessary.** ✅

**Почему:** функции сильной культуры — контроль, social glue, sense-making (и снижение неопределённости ожиданий). Артефакты как раз *передают* культуру, культура их не отменяет.

### Q17. Employees are more likely to comply with a supervisor's legitimate power when…
- **a. employees have high power distance.** ✅
- b. orders fall outside normal role requirements.
- c. the company encourages disobeying orders that interfere with work.
- d. the manager has little charisma.
- e. the manager has a very good reward system. *(это reward power, не legitimate)*

**Почему:** легитимная власть сильнее при **высокой power distance** (ценят конформизм/традиции, ждут указаний), при доверии и когда запрос в рамках роли.

### Q18. During which stage of socialization do people first learn about the organization and job?
- a. role management · b. encounter · **c. preemployment** ✅ · d. probation · e. orientation

**Почему:** 3 стадии — **pre-employment** (узнают об организации/работе, формируют ожидания) → encounter → role management.

### Q19. A strong organizational culture helps employees make sense of what goes on and why things happen.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** одна из трёх функций культуры — **sense-making**.

### Q20. Organizations with an adaptive corporate culture…
- a. are unlikely to survive long term.
- **b. have employees who see things from an open systems perspective.** ✅
- c. tend to be less ethical than nonadaptive ones.
- d. have no artifacts to keep their culture in place.
- e. tend to become cults.

**Почему:** **адаптивная** культура = сотрудники открыты к изменениям, мыслят с позиции **open systems** (внешняя среда, стейкхолдеры), поддерживают постоянное обновление. (Культоподобность — противоположность адаптивности.)

---

| --- | ----- | --- | ----- | --- | ----- | --- | ----- |
| 1   | d     | 6   | true  | 11  | a     | 16  | e     |
| 2   | c     | 7   | d     | 12  | a     | 17  | a     |
| 3   | d     | 8   | c     | 13  | false | 18  | c     |
| 4   | c     | 9   | true  | 14  | c     | 19  | true  |
| 5   | c     | 10  | b     | 15  | b     | 20  | b     |

## 📄 03-assessment/Quiz_5_Chapters_7_&_12.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Assesment]] · [[BUS293]] · _Quiz 5 разбор (курс BUS293)_

# Quiz 5 — Chapters 7 & 12

**Предмет:** BUS293 — Organisational Theory and Behaviour (TMD 2026)
**Главы:** Chapter 7 (Decision Making & Creativity → Topic 10) · Chapter 12 (Leadership → Topic 9)

> Сдан **13 июля 2026** (закрытие квиза). Официальная оценка Moodle ещё не выставлена — ниже **ключ с разбором** (ответы + почему). Если официальный результат где-то разойдётся, поправим.
> ⚠️ «Chapters 7 & 12» — номера глав **учебника**, не тем курса: Ch 7 = Decision Making (Topic 10), Ch 12 = Leadership (Topic 9). См. карту глав в [[BUS293_Course_Memory]].

---

### Q1. Escalation of commitment can be minimized by ensuring that…
- a. there are ready-made alternatives to resolve the problem.
- **b. those who make the decision are different from those who evaluate it.** ✅
- c. the team leader has strong opinions about the preferred options for a problem.
- d. organizational goals are relatively ambiguous.
- e. negative information is screened out to protect the self-esteem of the decision makers.

**Почему:** способы снизить escalation of commitment — **отделить тех, кто выбирает, от тех, кто оценивает**, задать заранее уровень отказа от проекта, искать чёткую обратную связь и вовлекать нескольких людей в оценку.

### Q2. When team cohesion is low, leaders should use a ________ style.
- a. implicit · **b. supportive** ✅ · c. directive · d. transformational · e. participative

**Почему:** по Path-Goal contingency table при **low cohesion** рекомендуется **supportive** поведение лидера. (Negative norms → directive; positive norms → participative.)

### Q3. Mental models make it easier for decision makers to frame a problem or opportunity.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** mental models (структуры знаний) помогают осмыслять ситуацию и **framing**. Обратная сторона — они же «слепят» от уникальных проблем/возможностей, но само утверждение верно.

### Q4. …the next stage in the creative process after such inspiration is…
- a. preparation · b. incubation · **c. verification** ✅ · d. illumination · e. morphological analysis

**Почему:** вдохновение/озарение = **illumination**; следующий этап — **verification** (проверить и доработать идею). Модель: preparation → incubation → illumination → verification.

### Q5. Females, compared to males, are evaluated negatively as leaders when they…
- a. empower employees. · b. use a participative style. · **c. use a directive style.** ✅ · d. use coaching. · e. behave according to their followers' expectations.

**Почему:** из-за прототипов и гендерных стереотипов (implicit leadership) женщин оценивают негативнее при **директивном** стиле — он расходится с ожидаемым от них.

### Q6. ________ helps us to develop and choose alternatives by visualizing the future in different ways… ⚠️
- a. Intuition · **b. Creativity** ✅ *(см. примечание)* · c. Verification · d. Confirmation bias · e. Satisficing

**Почему:** по определению это **scenario planning** (систематически представлять альтернативные варианты будущего и оценивать полезность/риск каждого выбора). Термина «scenario planning» в вариантах НЕТ — из предложенного ближе всего **Creativity** (развить/выбрать альтернативы). Вопрос спорный: если Moodle засчитает иначе, здесь просто нет корректного варианта.

### Q7. Final step in the rational choice decision-making process?
- a. developing a list of solutions · b. implementing the selected alternative · c. choosing the best alternative · **d. evaluating decision outcomes** ✅ · e. recognizing the opportunities

**Почему:** 6 шагов rational choice завершаются **evaluating decision outcomes** (оценка результатов).

### Q8. Programmed decision routines that speed up response to pattern matches are called…
- **a. action scripts.** ✅ · b. illuminations. · c. rational formulae. · d. solution-focused problems. · e. implicit favorites.

**Почему:** интуиция опирается на **action scripts** — программные рутины из mental models прошлого опыта; работают лучше для routine-решений.

### Q9. Which path-goal style is the same as task-oriented leadership?
- **a. directive** ✅ · b. supportive · c. participative · d. achievement-oriented · e. collaborative

**Почему:** **directive** = task-oriented (структурирует роли, ставит процедуры); supportive = people-oriented.

### Q10. More than communicating the vision, transformational leaders also need to model it.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** трансформационные лидеры **моделируют** vision («walk the talk») → рост доверия сотрудников. Одно из ключевых поведений.

### Q11. ________ = the view that people use pure logic and all available information about all alternatives to choose the alternative with the highest value. ⚠️
- a. Subjective expected utility maximization · **b. The rational choice decision-making process** ✅ *(см. примечание)* · c. Bounded rationality · d. Decision making · e. Intuition

**Почему:** «the view that people use pure logic and ALL information about ALL alternatives» = **rational choice** парадигма/процесс. Ловушка — **a (subjective expected utility maximization)**: это узкое правило «выбрать highest value». Если b засчитают неверным — второй кандидат a.

### Q12. Task-oriented leader behavior includes…
- **a. defining work procedures** ✅ · b. developing mutual trust and respect… · c. listening to employees' suggestions · d. doing personal favors… · e. establishing a personal relationship…

**Почему:** **defining work procedures** — task-oriented; b–e относятся к people-oriented.

### Q13. In what way does managerial leadership depend on transformational leadership?
- **a. Transformational leadership sets the right direction of the organization.** ✅
- b. …defines the day to day activities… · c. …is a form of managerial leadership. · d. …relies on managerial leadership to define the strategic vision. · e. …needs managerial leaders to communicate…

**Почему:** managerial leadership улучшает исполнение под текущие цели, но **зависит от трансформационного в задании правильного направления** (vision).

### Q14. Divergent thinking refers to calculating the conventionally accepted "right answer" to a logical problem.
- a. true · **b. false** ✅

**Почему:** это описание **convergent** thinking. **Divergent** = реформулировать проблему, искать нестандартные углы.

### Q15. Choosing an alternative that is good enough rather than the best is called…
- **a. satisficing.** ✅ · b. anchoring. · c. representing. · d. modeling. · e. intuiting.

**Почему:** **satisficing** — выбрать «достаточно хорошее» (из-за ограниченной способности/мотивации обрабатывать информацию).

### Q16. ________ leadership includes defining and structuring work roles, clarifying duties/procedures, planning work activities.
- a. Charismatic · b. Participative · **c. Task-oriented** ✅ · d. Transformational · e. People-oriented

**Почему:** это дословно поведение **task-oriented** лидера.

### Q17. ________ represents the heart of transformational leadership.
- a. Personal attributes · b. Charisma · c. Operational efficiency · **d. Strategic vision** ✅ · e. Emotional intelligence

**Почему:** сердце трансформационного лидерства — **strategic vision**. Charisma намеренно отделяют (это отдельная черта, ≠ трансформационное лидерство).

### Q18. According to the implicit leadership perspective, we believe a leader is effective if they look and act consistently with our prototype.
- **a. true** ✅ · b. false

**Почему:** **implicit leadership theory** — followers используют leadership prototypes; совпал с прототипом → воспринимается эффективным.

### Q19. Shared leadership is more likely where the formal leader…
- a. creates a competitive culture. · b. instills a fear of failure. · c. discourages employees initiative. · **d. delegates power to employees.** ✅ · e. relies on their formal authority.

**Почему:** **shared leadership** требует формального лидера, готового **делегировать власть**, коллаборативной культуры и способности сотрудников влиять убеждением.

### Q20. Incubation in the creative process assists…
- a. escalation of commitment · b. prospect theory effect · c. convergent thinking · **d. divergent thinking** ✅ · e. decision choice

**Почему:** **incubation** (отложить проблему, периодически возвращаясь) поддерживает **divergent thinking** — рождение нестандартных идей.

---

| 2   | b     | 7   | d     | 12  | a     | 17  | d     |
| 3   | true  | 8   | a     | 13  | a     | 18  | true  |

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

1.0  PURPOSE.

Success in winning the approval and support of others for your thinking is not
just a product of the ideas themselves.  Of equal importance will be the way you
present your ideas.

Business reports sell your thinking to both managers and academics, so it is in your best interests to

digest  the  contents  of  this  outline  and  embrace  them.    While  the  writing  requirements  may  seem

stringent, it is recommended that you bear in mind that these guidelines will serve you well throughout

life, not just here at Murdoch. Adopt them as your own and you will have taken an important step in

improving not only the "packaging" of your ideas, but the value of the ideas themselves.

Additional  standards,  such  as  the  Chicago  referencing  system,  are  also  included  to  address

fundamental  academic  requirements.    While  referencing  may  seem  a  burden  to  some,  it  should  be

remembered that any business report will require the writer to state the sources of the information in

the  main  body  of  the  report  (or  in  appendices  where  appropriate).    So,  it  should  be  understood  that

we're  not  actually  asking  any  more  of you  than  would  be  the  case  in  the business  world.   Note  that

your report does not require a 'purpose' section. The following content outline will provide current

business students with some precise specifications for their report.

2

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

2.0  OUTLINE OF A REPORT FOR BUS293.
The contents of each specific element of a report are provided here in Section 2.0 to assist student in

preparing and structuring their major assessment.

2.1  Cover Page

This should include all standard requirements for a paper, which include;

1.  Unit code and title.

2.  Report title (Topic should be in large font).

3.  Student name and number.

4.  Workshop day and time.

5.  Name of the workshop facilitator (tutor).

It is important to remember that this is a cover page.  So give some thought to its presentation.  If you

cannot  find  a  snappy  graphic  that  is  appropriate,  at  least  ensure  that  some  thought  is  given  to  the

format of these elements.  Clearly the second element is most important and should be formatted with

the largest font, centre aligned.  Other elements are free to be presented in a fashion of your choosing,

but at least make an effort to have a cover that looks professional.

2.2  Report Contents Page

2.2.1  Characteristics

  This should be titled "Contents".

  It  should  have  a  comprehensive  index  showing  the  structure  of  the  report  and  its  various

elements.

  Typically, there are two to four levels of titles in the index to reflect the structure (note there are

three in this document's table of contents).

  It should be the last thing you add to the document before printing.

It will be critical for writers to know the basics of how to build an index using Microsoft (MS) Word,

a function that will enable you to build an index in the blink of an eye.  See Appendix 3.1 for a guide.

2.3  Executive Summary (ES) (Commercial format) – keep to 1 page only

In the commercial world, the ES is the most important page in the entire report.  Put yourself in the

shoes of a Business Analyst or Management consultant for a moment; you have to sell your thinking

in  this  one  page because  many  managers  do  not  have  the  time  to  read  the  entire  report.    It  is  high

impact stuff with every word chosen to ensure the "Big Picture" is summed up in one page.  Typically,

3

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

the contents of an executive summary are written last after the whole structure, content and scope of

the report is defined.  However, it does not hurt to have a draft written early as this may help define

goals  for  the  rest  of  the  report  while  it  is  being  constructed.    Furthermore,  as  new  core  ideas  of

significance  emerge,  you  can  amend  the  draft  to  reflect  these  revelations  that  naturally  occur  in  the

construction  stages.    Ultimately,  its  final  form  should  be  decided  on  after  you  are  satisfied  that  all

elements  in  the  discussion  sections  and  end  report  sections  are  finished.    The  following  elements

outline the typical contents of an ES.

Note:  Justified alignment looks best - i.e., even margins on both sides as shown here; however left

alignment will be accepted. What matters is that you are consistent throughout the report.

2.3.1  The Three Main Elements of the Executive Summary.

1.  The  topic  and  its  significance:    This  introduces  the  issue  in  question  and  its  importance  to

management.  Usually topics are linked with the key issues.

2.  The findings (conclusions):  This provides the reader with your high level evaluation on the issue

in question.  In essence, your informed opinion  - always stay  third person (No "I", "my", etc).

Here, you make it clear what the key findings of your analysis are.

3.  The recommendations and their benefits:  This provides the reader with solutions to the issue in

question along with some benefits.

The  entire  executive  summary  should  be no more  than  one  page.    To  cover  the  above  areas  in  one

page  will  be  challenging  for  most  writers  because  writing  a  good  ES  will  provide  a  reader  with  a

concise, high level understanding of all the core issues.  You do not need subsections here.

2.3.2  Benefits of an Executive Summary (ES)

As already stated, managers are very busy.  If you  cannot get the main messages across in a page,

chances are you will lose their attention.  The ES should be able to act as a stand alone, powerful

page that sells the report.  However, there are also other benefits, such as improving reader memory

retention  by providing  a  reader  with  a  broad  understanding of  an  issue  that  creates  a  framework

around which the detailed information can be more readily interpreted.

2.4

Introduction

This section ideally should not go over  one page in length.  There must be four subsections in this

page that cover specific requirements.  Their names and content descriptions are listed below:

1.  Topic:    Here,  you  introduce  the  topic  and  elaborate  on  its  significance  briefly.    Do  not  provide

findings; simply define the key purpose (which is to arrive at the findings).

4

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

2.  Limitations:    Here,  you  discuss  the  scope  and  constraints  of  the  report  by  elaborating  on  any

weaknesses or omissions.  This is often due to topic complexity  and problems relating to limited

info provided in the case  (A common problem when examining cases  is that people often distort

information for their own ends).

3.  Sources  of  Data:    State  briefly  what  sources  of  data  have  been  obtained.    Are  they  secondary

only, such as books, journals, papers, magazines and websites, or have you obtained primary data

such as direct interviews (note: primary data is NOT to be collected for this assignment).

4.  Report Organisation:  Here, simply elaborate on the structure of the main body of the report so

the reader knows what to expect and comment on whether you will provide any recommendations

and conclusions.  Do not mention the Intro or ES here.

2.5  Main Body of the Report

This  section  requires  the  writer  to  present  all  the  research  uncovered.    The  characteristics  of  the

discussion section are;

2.5.1  Characteristics

  Third person, factual, objective and impersonal.  You simply present the evidence uncovered

by research and draw attention to information of greatest significance.

  Split  into  numerous,  logical  sections  and  sub/sections  to  help  structure  the  dialogue.  The

sections  of  the  question  and  the  research  may  help  structure  the  discussion  (main  body)  of  the

report.

  The sections and subsections should have titles that reflect the content (as this guide demonstrates)

and  organise  information  logically.  The  key  issues/researched  findings  not  only  inform  your

research  effort  but  also  help  structure  the  report  discussion  itself.    The  precise  format  may

vary from topic to topic as the circumstances vary, but in BUS293 you will nearly always find it

best to have titles in major discussion sections that reflect the key issues in the topic.

  You  do  not  draw  attention  to  the  reader  or  yourself  (keep  your  writing  to  third  person

perspective).  Just present the facts found in your research (using citations/references/sources).

  Define the core theories and concepts of organisational behaviour and how they contribute to the

organisations  current  performance,  sustainability  and  alignment  to  at  least  one  of  the  Ten

Principles  of  the  United  Nations  Global  Impact  (note  ‘Guideline  for  Success’  in  BUS293  Unit

Guide, for expected coverage of sustainability).

  The  main  discussion  section  is  heavily  referenced.    You  are  presenting  the  information

uncovered in your research, so this section must be heavily referenced.

5

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

The last point here regarding referencing seems to catch out  many people.  This is not a section to

talk about your opinion; it is a section to present the data found to help make logical conclusions or

support the teams opinion/decisions using credible sources.  Additionally, some discussion of possible

solutions  that  you  may  have  found  ensures  that  when  the  reader  gets  to  the  recommendations  and

conclusions,  your  key  findings  and  solutions  are  more  likely  to  be  seen  as  credible.    A  key  point

though, is to ensure this section is thoroughly researched and has sources cited per the  Chicago

method.

2.5.2  Tips on when to reference

Aside from the referencing standards comprehensively defined in the unit outline, there are some basic

rules that can help you understand when the source needs to be cited.  These include;

  If it is not your idea - cite your source (per the Chicago format).

Note: For a comprehensive list of Chicago referencing examples, see Murdoch Library referencing

guides

  If  it  is  not  clear  by  the  wording of  the  dialogue  that  you  are  still  presenting  facts  from  a  source

cited previously - cite it again.

  Do not leave it till the end of the paragraph to cite a source. It must be cited as soon as the idea is

used (generally this is done at the end of a sentence).

  When using the same reference several times in a row, if it is not apparent to the reader by the tone

and  flow  of  the  discussion  that  you  are  still  talking  about  that  source.,  then  to  reduce  citation

frequency, you can use the authors name in the actual discussion (eg:  Vernon Smith (2002) notes

how ...) early in the first sentence where the ideas are used.

  If you are quoting word for word, put the quote in "inverted commas" and cite a page number if it

is available.  Pagination number will suffice for online databases.

2.6  Recommendations Section

Ideally you should have discussed some potential remedies and solutions in the discussion section and

thoroughly referenced these.  So when you get to this section you must outline the recommendations

you have arrived at as a result of your research.  This can be done in numbered bullet point form, but

you should at the very least briefly  discuss the benefit/s of the recommendations, or a paragraph for

each recommendation, each with a sub-heading.

If you have done your research, you may have many recommendations; the team needs to choose the

most relevant five recommendations. These should be detailed and include the benefits and not simply

state  the  recommendation;  this  will  allow  the  recommendation  to  be  explicitly  linked  to  business

needs,  a  critical  component  of  business  report  writing.  Your  recommendations  must  be  useful  and

6

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)

practical for managers. Generally you do not need to reference here, as potential solutions should have

already been discussed in the discussion/appendices sections (However, you should note references if

this is not the case). Remember to stay 3rd person.

2.7  Conclusion – one page only
Here  you  provide  your  core  high  level  findings  in  no  more  than  a  page  (Stay  3rd  person).    These

should  draw  together  the  facts  found  in  research  and  your  recommendations  to  demonstrate  a  well

thought out plan of attack.  This should be a powerful section, which should end on a high note or a

note of urgency to generate reader support.  Touching on the benefits of the proposed course of action,

or  the  consequences  of  not  acting  in  accordance  with  recommendations  is  usually  a  good  way  to

accomplish this.  Generally, this section is not heavily referenced as this was done in the discussion

section.  However, if you introduce new information, you must reference it here as well (note: if

something  is  mentioned  in  the  conclusion,  it  should  be  backed  up  with  your  research  and  findings,

hence  any  new  information  in  the  conclusion  is  likely  to  warrant  scrutiny  by  the  reader/marker).

Additionally, if there are critical qualifications to your argument, raise them here to frame your ideas

appropriately.

2.8  Reference List

This  should  contain  an  alphabetical  list  of  all  sources  used  in  the  report.    It  must  comply  with  the

Chicago referencing standards. (see Murdoch Library). https://libguides.murdoch.edu.au/Chicago

2.9  Appendices - optional

▪  Look  at  the  example  appendix  at  the  end  of  the  document  titled,  Building  a  Table  of  Contents.

You will note it is in a section called "Appendices" with each appendix under its own subheading

(With name and number).  You should also remember that  citing the sources of data here is a

must if it is not an analysis or research you have conducted yourself.

▪  Do not simply copy and paste large amounts of discussion into an appendix.  Appendices should

use tables, graphs, figures and interesting formatting to help aid reader comprehension.

Remember to use appendices to keep under the size limit set (up to  3000 words) as this word count

includes all text within the discussion section.

7

BUS123 Report Guidelines (Adapted from BUS145 Guidelines)
