1.   Executive Summary

As one of Australia’s major lenders and an ASX200 stock, Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) is an expansive, multi-business entity that operates through dynamic teams. In modern, complex organizations, teams must perform effectively across communication, trust, cooperation, and overall team efficacy. Moreover, as an economy that continually moves towards further digitization and a hybridized working landscape, effective inter-organizational communication becomes indispensable for overall success and long-term sustainability. This report analyses four primary team dynamics issues that impact Westpac Banking Corporation: communication between teams, team trust, and remote working.

Also, collaboration and team cohesiveness across departments. Communication issues are significant barriers in organizations with many departments operating with conflicting interests. Disparities between departments within Technology, Risk, Compliance, Operations, and Customer Service, for instance, create barriers to clear communication. Such barriers lead to misconceptions, delays in decision-making, and interruptions in overall information dissemination.

The report further considers the role of trust in promoting teamwork. Trust enables workers to share knowledge, work constructively, and participate in collaborative processes. Especially within hybrid and remote teams, trust is a vital commodity, as it serves as a substitute for direct employee contact and helps build informal relationships. The paper reveals how trust contributes to psychological safety, employee engagement, and organizational resilience.

Lastly, the paper addresses the effects of remote and hybrid work arrangements on employee well-being, communication quality, and team integration. In addition to the benefit of work-life balance, employees face a new challenge related to their connection to the organization and to other employees. Last of all, the paper evaluates teamwork and team integration across WBC's various divisions. In that regard, the implementation of communication technology, Integrated Systems, and the cross-functional teams set up to foster effective team collaboration failed because the organization is too complex.

The research, grounded in organizational behaviour principles and academic literature, highlights the strong relationships among communication, trust, hybrid/remote work, and team integration. To improve work-life balance and organizational efficiency, it is necessary to strengthen psychological safety processes, reinforce cross-divisional communication, and provide employees with more opportunities to build a sense of togetherness and trust in the organization. Also, a system that allows employees to provide the necessary feedback in a non-anonymous manner, coupled with regular surveys on employee satisfaction and organizational processes, needs to be put in place to ensure organizational sustainability.

2.   Introduction

2.a  | Report Topic

Team dynamics refers to the observable and inferable behaviors and relational exchanges among team members that facilitate communication and interaction in the workplace (Collier, LaRocca, & Stoeber, 2012; Jones and Bartlett Publishers, 2010). It helps team members communicate, share knowledge and skills, feel valued as employees, and build trust that fosters cooperation (Jones and Bartlett Publishers, 2010). Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) is an Australian bank, a constituent of the ASX200, and one of the largest and most complex organizations in Australia; therefore, it relies on collaboration across departments, including Technology, Risk Management, Compliance, Operations, and Customer Service. The ability to communicate, trust, and cooperate has long been crucial to achieving overall organizational goals, growth, and sustainability. (Jones and Bartlett Publishers, 2010). In this report, 4 key challenges related to WBC team dynamics will be investigated to ensure the organization's sustainable operations.

2.b  | Limitations

This research is primarily based on secondary sources, including peer-reviewed journal articles, academic textbooks, official corporate reports, and publicly available data. Internal organisational data and employee viewpoints were inaccessible. The analysis focuses on organizational behaviour ideas rather than specific financial or operational performance metrics.

2.c | Sources of Data

The report is based on peer-reviewed academic research, industry publications, official Westpac reports, and sustainability-related materials. Academic sources provide theoretical frameworks for communication, trust, team cohesiveness, and virtual teams, whereas Westpac papers provide organisational context. Additional resources, such as United Nations Global Compact documents, help to further the subject of sustainability and responsible corporate practices.

2.d | Report Organisation

The report is organized into four sections: communication, trust, remote work, and collaboration/team cohesiveness. Recommendations and conclusions are then presented to solve the identified issues and improve organizational performance.

3.   Identified Challenges

3.a  | Communication problems between teams

Communication problems are a significant issue for WBC, the largest financial company trading on the ASX200; in particular, due to the close interaction among departments such as Technology, Risk, Compliance, Operations, and Customer Service, as well as the close relationships within the company. Communication transmits information necessary for trust, cohesion, coordination, and decision-making, and it creates operational risk and reduces organizational performance when communication breaks down (Mathieu et al., 2008).

One of the main issues is effective communication, as each department has a different focus; for example, technology teams focus more on innovative or digital transformation objectives, whereas risk and compliance teams are more likely to focus on governance requirements. This divergence in understanding the main expectations is likely to lead to conflicts or communication issues. According to team mental model theory, performance will increase when everyone involved in a project shares a common understanding of the goals, roles, and processes (Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006).

Communication issues further impact trust and cohesion. Trust establishes what information needs to be shared, and efforts to work with others in collaborative activities, and is actually harmed by the breakdown in communication resulting from inconsistent and delayed information transfers, potentially damaging the positive interdepartmental relationships within the organization (Edmondson 1999). In a large organization like WBC, the different departments may inhibit cross-departmental contact and restrict opportunities to build cohesion through years of shared experience and achievement.

Communication becomes even more problematic in hybrid and telecommuting workplaces. Virtual work, for example, may reduce informal communication and knowledge transfer, making collaboration more complex (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015). Even though WBC uses digital communication technologies, virtual communication cannot completely substitute for face-to-face communication.

Communication problems directly affect organizational performance. Information-sharing time lags may have slowed decision-making, reduced service delivery quality, and wasted resources. In a competitive banking industry, such an impact may cause poor customer satisfaction, organizational image, and reputation. Good communication practices are highly correlated with team effectiveness and employee commitment (Salas, Sims, and Burke, 2005).

Finally, communication challenges affect sustainability. Trust, adherence to regulation, and ethical decision-making among stakeholders are crucial to WBC's sustainability. Poor communication may contribute to increased stress and pressure on employees, greater operating risks, and regulatory violations. Such a conclusion also aligns with Principle 10 of the United Nations Global Compact, which encourages businesses to be transparent and accountable. In addition, we should also see communication as a matter of performance as well as of sustainability.

Potential recommendations

Improve cross-functional teamwork by setting shared goals and holding regular interdepartmental meetings (Mathieu et al. 2008).

Improve hybrid team communication by implementing explicit communication protocols and virtual collaboration tools (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015).

Expand team-building activities to boost cohesion, engagement, and performance (Beal et al. 2003).

3.b  | Team trust

Communication problems and team trust are closely connected, but trust deserves attention on its own. It shapes how teams at Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) cooperate, share information, and perform.

Trust usually rests on three things: a person's integrity, their benevolence, and their ability (Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman 1995; Robbins and Judge 2023). Employees are more willing to rely on a colleague or manager they see as honest, as genuinely concerned for their well-being, and as competent at their work. A weakness in any one of these can undermine it. WBC staff might doubt whether another department will provide accurate information or feel that a manager cares more about targets than about the people who meet them. Trust is also slow to build and easy to lose, so one communication failure or a single episode of perceived unfairness can damage a relationship that then takes a long time to repair (Greenberg and Baron 2008).

Hybrid and remote work make this harder. Distributed employees have fewer informal, in-person moments that normally foster trust, so it is more difficult to sustain than in a co-located team. Trust also matters more for team performance in virtual settings than in face-to-face ones (Breuer, Hüffmeier, and Hertel 2016; Cascio and Shurygailo 2003). To get work done before close relationships have formed, dispersed teams often rely on "swift trust," a provisional trust based on shared roles, professional norms, and common goals rather than personal familiarity (Meyerson, Weick, and Kramer 1996; Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). For WBC, the practical implication is that clear roles, dependable processes, and consistent leadership can do much of the work that face-to-face contact would otherwise do.

Trust also underpins psychological safety, the belief that an employee can raise a concern, admit a mistake, or challenge a decision without fear of punishment (Edmondson 1999). When trust is low, staff at a heavily regulated bank may stay quiet about errors or operational risks, narrowing problem-solving and widening compliance exposure. Leadership is decisive here. Leaders who act consistently, communicate openly, and treat people fairly create the conditions for honest discussion and genuine teamwork (Yukl and Gardner 2020). Building trust, therefore, supports WBC's operational performance, risk management, and resilience.

These dynamics play out day to day and over time. When employees trust one another, information moves faster, and decisions are made without constant second-guessing; when trust is low, people double-check, withhold information, or route it through slower formal channels, and coordination between compliance, risk, and customer service slows (Robbins and Judge 2023). The costs are concrete: slower service, a weaker customer experience, and higher operating expenses. Sustained low trust causes longer-term damage, with more stress, lower satisfaction, and higher turnover in remote, high-pressure conditions, and a workforce less willing to raise the risks the bank most needs to hear about (Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004).

It connects directly to the United Nations Global Compact and to Principle 10, which calls on businesses to work against corruption in all its forms (United Nations Global Compact 2024). The link runs through psychological safety. Anti-corruption depends on employees being willing to report misconduct, errors, and operational risk, and they do that only when they trust that speaking up will not cost them. Westpac's own history shows what is at stake. In 2020, the bank agreed to a record A$1.3 billion penalty for more than 23 million breaches of anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing law (AUSTRAC 2020), failures of monitoring and escalation that have since shaped its focus on conduct and risk culture (Westpac Banking Corporation 2024). Where trust is weak, staff stay silent, problems go unreported, and unethical behaviour has more room to take hold. Strengthening trust makes transparency and ethical conduct far more likely and keeps WBC closer to Principle 10.

Several measures could help WBC strengthen trust and stay aligned with this principle. Leadership development focused on consistency, fairness, and open communication would have managers model the behaviors that build trust (Yukl and Gardner 2020). Clear, protected speak-up channels give employees a safe way to raise concerns, reinforcing psychological safety and anti-corruption together. Firm role clarity and reliable processes help build swift trust across hybrid teams (Cascio and Shurygailo 2003; Meyerson, Weick, and Kramer 1996), while regular cross-team and in-person contact rebuilds the informal interactions through which trust usually grows.

3.c | Remote work challenges at WBC

According to McShane and Von Glinow (2024), Remote teams are teams in the organization whose members work across time, space, and organizational boundaries and are connected through Information and communication technologies. These platforms provide teams with the environments needed to connect and achieve organizational objectives. An article written by Peacock-Smith, Du, and Graham (2025) explores the case of (Karlene Chandler v Westpac Banking Corporation 2025, 3115) where WBC had adopted a 2-day per week in-office rule where employees are expected to be present at a corporate-level office regardless of travel distance from their homes to these offices. In this case, Karlene Chandler could not make the commute to the corporate office due to a 2-hour travel time and family commitments. This case highlights the prominent issue of distance in WBC's remote work policy, making it difficult for employees like Karlene to maintain good rapport at work while balancing work and life. An article by Muddit (2022) explores the negative impact of workplace bullying in virtual environments. Virtual bullying can take various forms but is not explicit, as an individual can only infer it from subtle hints. If WBC were to have an environment where bullying occurs, even within remote teams, this could lead to low individual morale, hinder the victim, cause internal conflict, decrease productivity across teams, and weaken organizational goals (Mehmood and Mushtaq 2020). Remote teams at WBC without a concrete foundation face the challenge of building team cohesion and fostering a positive culture and work environment. A lack of cohesion creates a barrier to helping employees engage, build interpersonal relationships, and maintain them with colleagues as they would in normal day-to-day office settings (Asafu-Adjaye 2025). Work-family conflict was an issue at WBC regarding its hybrid policy. WFC is a growing concern for employees, as it affects their occupational stress and can lead to negative feelings at home. This time-based conflict negatively affected WBC's reputation and reliability because its policy was neither inclusive nor adaptable to employees' lifestyles (Junça Silva and Lopes 2025). The company prioritizes what it feels is good on paper but does not consider the realities of the situation. As noted above, the company's performance has not been negatively affected; rather, over the years, obstacles have led to legal disputes, changing work dynamics, and the need for reinforcement strategies. WBC's issues with navigating remote teams and successfully integrating hybrid work models can be seen as misaligned with Principle 4 of the UN Global Compact. The principle states "the elimination of all forms of forced and compulsory labor." (United Nations Global Compact 2024). WBC has to be open to feedback and flexible with work arrangements to maintain high team cohesion and employee satisfaction.

Potential Recommendations:

1.     Team building exercises (McShane and Von Glinow 2024)

2.     One-to-one check-ins (Asafu-Adjaye 2025)

3.     Asynchronous communication aids (Asafu-Adjaye 2025)

4.   Consistency with fostering a positive work environment, retention matters, and protecting team welfare (Mahesh 2024).

3.d | WBC Collaboration and Team Cohesion across departments

The Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) relies on an array of departments to collaborate and communicate effectively; these include Retail Banking, Business Banking, Technology, Risk Management, Compliance, Operations, and Customer Service. Team dynamics theory posits that cohesion and collaboration are significant determinants of communication quality, trust, information sharing, and organizational performance (Mathieu et al., 2008).

WBC utilizes various measures to foster collaboration, such as enterprise communication systems, agile ways of working, multi-functional teams, and integrated risk management systems. By using these mechanisms, departments can communicate information smoothly and collaborate. "Frequent interaction also serves to build up trust and relationships among individuals." (Beal et al. 2003)

Working toward common organizational objectives also facilitates cooperation. WBC's objectives: (a) customer satisfaction; (b) digital transformation; (c) operational excellence, and (d) compliance, require the coordination of different departments. Team cohesiveness is likely to grow when people perceive common goals and feel a shared sense of accomplishment.

These are the advantages of this approach; however, cohesion across functional boundaries is proving more difficult. The large size and scope of the WBC could create communication problems between specific teams: technology teams may prioritize innovation, while risk & compliance teams focus on control & regulation. This vein theory states that a shared mental model is required to ensure a team works efficiently together (Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006).

Hybrid and remote work arrangements also affect cohesion. Virtual settings, with fewer opportunities for communication and relationship building among colleagues, can lower trust and cohesion (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015).

Despite the challenges, WBC is effective at building cohesion through leadership action, cross-departmental teams, team-building exercises, and common performance goals. These actions effectively overcome departmental barriers and develop better relationships between departments. Cohesive teams communicate well and achieve results (Salas, Sims, and Burke, 2005).

On the whole, WBC uses effective systems to support collaboration and team cohesion. However, organizational complexity and the move towards hybrid working require a focus on communication, trust, and common goals to support long-term performance.

This challenge also bears on WBC's alignment with the United Nations Global Compact. Principle 10, which calls on businesses to combat corruption through transparency and accountability, depends on departments collaborating openly rather than withholding information within isolated departments (United Nations Global Compact 2024). Poor cross-departmental cohesion can allow risks and misconduct to go unaddressed, therefore weakening alignment. To strengthen cohesion and stay consistent with this principle, WBC could expand cross-functional project teams, hold regular inter-departmental forums, and reward collaborative rather than purely siloed performance.

It would allow employees and teams at WBC to have an environment where positive conversations are encouraged, and where they do not feel undervalued at work or that their welfare is not being attended to beyond work-related responsibilities. The appointment of an in-house psychologist would provide employees with a resource to seek help when facing difficult situations at work or in their personal lives. Having access to this resource helps remove the stigma around psychological safety-related topics, and employees would feel more inclined to reach out when necessary because the company has taken the first step to make it available.

WBC has adopted a hybrid work policy and has multiple locations throughout Australia. Integrating team retreats into their corporate calendar once a year would help employees network, build relationships, and strengthen team trust. It is an opportunity for employees at all levels to feel welcome and appreciated by the company.

Principle 3

Employee confidentiality is paramount for navigating situations dealing with sensitivity and discretion. If employees know that confidentiality at WBC is valued, they will feel safe to voice concerns or speak up without fear of judgment.

5. Conclusion

This report examined the organizational behavior challenges affecting team performance at Westpac, focusing on how communication, trust, remote work, and overall cohesion shape the team's operations. The analysis made clear that these issues are connected rather than separate. Weak communication made it harder for members to build trust in one another, and the move to remote work added distance, further reducing cohesion and a shared sense of purpose. Each problem fed into the next, which is why the team struggled to function as a unit.

Taken together, the four challenges point to a single underlying need: a workplace where people feel safe to speak openly and confident that their contributions matter. The recommendations respond directly to that need. Workshops on psychological safety, regular team building, confidential channels for raising concerns, and clearer ways of collaborating are all aimed at rebuilding trust and improving how information moves across the team.

If these recommendations are put into practice and reviewed over time, Westpac can expect stronger working relationships, more consistent communication, and a team that copes better with remote and hybrid conditions. Acting on these behavioural factors is not only about fixing current problems, but also about building the conditions for the team to perform well in the long term. A team that communicates openly and trusts one another is far better placed to reach its goals.

## 3.a — Communication problems between teams (Бобур)

Communication issues between teams have been identified as a critical organisational issue for Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC), which is one of the top financial institutions on the ASX200 index of listed Australian firms. Efficient communication is crucial in banking as departments like Technology, Risk, Compliance, Customer Service, Operations, and Retail Banking often operate and depend heavily on each other. Team dynamics research has indicated that the level of communication within a team will impact a team's level of trust, cohesion, coordination and decision-making abilities (Mathieu et al 2008). If communication systems are not properly implemented, the result is often fragmented or misinterpreted information which hinders performance of an organization and increases operational risk.

One of the key communication issues for WBC is how to keep information consistent across different departments that have contrasting perspectives and objectives. The objective of Technology team members tends to be more about innovative new products and digital transformations, whereas risk and compliance teams are driven more by governance, regulation, and the avoidance of risks. The differing objectives of various departments are a contributing factor to the lack of cooperation and communication barriers. As suggested in the team mental model theory, higher team performance can be achieved when members share similar understandings about the team's goals, their roles, and tasks (Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006). If departments have differing expectations and assumptions, this will more than likely lead to misunderstanding and lack of coordination.

It also relates to team trust and cohesion. Team trust is employees' positive beliefs about whether or not colleagues can be relied upon and are knowledgeable. Trust between teammates has been found to be vital in effective teamwork, and the basis for an information-sharing environment and the willingness to work together (Edmondson 1999). Breakdowns in communication may also reduce the level of trust between departments if employees believe that information is incomplete, contradictory or simply slow in its transmission. Cohesion may also be impacted on by insufficient interaction with teammates outside of immediate working groups. Team Dynamics discusses how member interaction and shared success impact on team cohesion; in a large organization such as WBC, departmental barriers can inhibit this and also reduce the collaborative spirit between groups.

Furthermore, remote and hybrid working conditions can exaggerate the issues with communication. Studies into remote teams have shown how virtual environments may limit informal communication, interpersonal bonds, and opportunities for informal knowledge sharing (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015). Although WBC has invested in technology for digital communication, virtual communication cannot replace face-to-face interaction. Evaluation apprehension, and the need to conform, are both discussed in Team Dynamics as influences which inhibit effective communication. This is the apprehension which individuals have of being judged by managers or peers; this means employees may be reluctant to express problems, contradict decisions or present alternative solutions, leading to innovation stifled and poor decision-making enhanced.

Poor communication in WBC has consequences for organizational performance. Slow transmission of communication will affect the speed at which decisions are made, quality of services provided and cause inefficiencies between different departments. In the highly competitive banking industry this may also have a negative impact on customer perception of services provided and the company's image. Numerous studies prove that effective communication is linked positively to team efficiency, performance and employee satisfaction (Salas, Sims and Burke, 2005). Therefore, poor communication at WBC may negatively impact strategic objectives.

This challenge also has significant consequences for sustainability of the organization. In the long term WBC is dependent on positive relationships with its stakeholders, compliance with regulations and ethical decisions. Poor communication can contribute to employee stress, lower levels of job satisfaction, and affect turnover rates negatively. It will also increase the risk factors for the organization, regarding operational and compliance risks. This problem is linked to principle 10 of the United Nations Global Compact: it focuses on promoting integrity, accountability and anti-corruption actions. Effective communication will help ensure that employees comply with the rules, feel safe when reporting problems and take decisions that are morally correct (United Nations Global Compact, 2024). Therefore, poor communication should not be perceived only as a performance but also as a sustainability issue.

**Recommendations.** WBC should improve inter-departmental collaboration through setting regular meetings, inter-departmental project teams and performance metrics across the departments (Mathieu et al. 2008; Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006). The company should invest in developing their leaders through leadership training in psychological safety and open communication (Edmondson 1999). WBC needs to improve their communication systems for teams that work hybrid or remotely — structured protocols, virtual collaboration technologies, frequent virtual team engagement (Allen, Golden and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015). Finally, WBC needs to expand team-building activities that encourage interaction and boost team cohesion (Beal et al. 2003; Salas, Sims, and Burke 2005).

## 3.b — Team trust (Faiaz / ты)

While communication problems and team trust are closely linked, trust is worth treating as a dynamic in its own right, one that shapes how teams at Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) cooperate, share information and ultimately perform. Having already established the connection between communication and trust, this section turns to what team trust is actually made of, how it takes hold in dispersed teams, and what that means for WBC.

Trust is rarely a single thing. It tends to rest on three foundations: integrity, benevolence and ability (Robbins and Judge 2023). People are ready to rely on a colleague or manager they see as honest and principled, as genuinely interested in their wellbeing, and as good at the job. The catch is that a shortfall in any one of these is enough to erode trust. WBC employees might doubt whether another department can be counted on for accurate information, or sense that a manager cares more about hitting targets than about the people who have to hit them. And because trust accumulates slowly but collapses fast, a single communication failure or a moment of perceived unfairness can undo a great deal that is then hard to win back.

Hybrid and remote working make all of this more precarious. Distributed employees simply have fewer of the casual, in-person moments through which trust normally grows, which makes it both more important and harder to sustain than in a team sharing one office (Cascio and Shurygailo 2003). To get work done before close relationships have had time to form, dispersed teams often fall back on "swift trust", a provisional trust extended on the basis of shared roles, professional norms and common goals rather than personal familiarity (Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). For WBC, the practical lesson is that clear roles, dependable processes and consistent leadership do much of the work that face-to-face contact would otherwise do.

Trust also sits underneath psychological safety: the confidence that you can raise a concern, own a mistake or push back on a decision without fear of repercussions. When trust is thin, staff in a tightly regulated bank may stay quiet about errors or operational risks, which narrows problem-solving and quietly widens compliance exposure. Leadership is decisive here. Leaders who behave consistently, communicate openly and treat people fairly create the conditions in which honest conversation and real teamwork become possible (Yukl and Gardner 2020). Strengthening trust therefore feeds directly into WBC's operational performance, risk management and long-term resilience, since a high-trust culture makes for quicker decisions, stronger collaboration and more engaged employees.

These trust dynamics feed straight into how WBC performs from one day to the next. When people trust each other, information moves faster and decisions get made without endless second-guessing, no small thing in a bank where speed and accuracy both have to hold at once. Where trust is low, the reverse takes over: staff double-check, hold things back, or push information through slower formal channels, and coordination between departments like compliance, risk and customer service starts to drag (Robbins and Judge 2023). Since communication and the trust beneath it bear directly on motivation, collaboration and performance (Yukl and Gardner 2020), a trust deficit isn't some soft cultural footnote. It surfaces as slower service, a weaker customer experience and higher operating costs.

The longer view matters just as much. Sustainable performance rests on holding on to good people and keeping them engaged, and trust runs through both. In remote and high-pressure settings especially, thin trust and the isolation that tends to come with virtual work go hand in hand with more stress, less satisfaction and a stronger urge to leave (Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). For WBC, trust that stays low over time would mean higher turnover, institutional knowledge walking out the door, and a workforce less inclined to raise the very risks the bank most needs to hear about. A high-trust culture does the opposite, underpinning the stable, transparent and accountable environment that sustainable organisations depend on.

This ties directly to the United Nations Global Compact, and to Principle 10 in particular, which asks businesses to work against corruption in all its forms (United Nations Global Compact 2024). The connection runs through psychological safety. Anti-corruption only works if employees are willing to speak up about misconduct, mistakes and operational risk, and people speak up only when they trust that doing so won't cost them. Where trust is weak, staff stay quiet, problems go unreported, and the space for unethical behaviour quietly opens up. A bank that never builds trust risks slipping out of step with Principle 10; one that works at it makes transparency and ethical conduct far more likely.

**Strategies.** (1) Leadership development aimed at consistency, fairness and open communication (Yukl and Gardner 2020). (2) Clear, protected speak-up channels reinforcing psychological safety and anti-corruption at once. (3) Firmer role clarity and dependable processes to support swift trust across hybrid/dispersed teams (Cascio and Shurygailo 2003; Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). (4) Regular cross-team and in-person contact to rebuild informal interaction through which trust grows.

---

## 3.c — Remote / hybrid work challenges at WBC (Onethu / Wethu)

According to McShane and Von Glinow (2024), remote teams are teams whose members work across time, space and organizational confines and are connected through information and communication technologies. An article by Peacock-Smith, Du, and Graham (2025) explores the case of *Karlene Chandler v Westpac Banking Corporation 2025, 3115*, where WBC adopted a 2-days-per-week in-office rule regardless of travel distance. Karlene Chandler could not make the commute (2-hour travel time + family commitments), highlighting the issue of distance in WBC's remote-work policy and the difficulty of maintaining both rapport and work-life balance. Muddit (2022) explores workplace bullying through virtual environments — not explicit, only inferred through subtle hints — which can lead to low morale, internal conflict, decreased productivity and weakened organizational goals (Mehmood and Mushtaq 2020). Remote teams at WBC without a concrete foundation face a lack of team cohesion (Asafu-Adjaye 2025). Work-family conflict (WFC) was an issue under WBC's hybrid policy, impacting occupational stress; the time-based conflict harmed WBC's reputation and reliability because the policy was not inclusive/adaptable to employee lifestyles (Junça Silva and Lopes 2025). WBC's issues with navigating remote teams can be seen as misaligned with **Principle 4 of the UN Global Compact** ("the elimination of all forms of forced and compulsory labour"). WBC must be open to feedback and flexibility in work arrangements to maintain team cohesion and employee satisfaction.

**Potential recommendations:** (1) Team-building exercises (McShane and Von Glinow 2024); (2) One-to-one check-ins (Asafu-Adjaye 2025); (3) Asynchronous communication aids (Asafu-Adjaye 2025); (4) Consistency in fostering a positive work environment, retention and protecting team welfare (Mahesh 2024).

---

## 3.d — WBC collaboration and team cohesion across departments (Бобур)

The Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) is a major player within the ASX200 financial organizations in Australia. WBC's business is a co-operative between divisions such as Retail Banking, Business Banking, Technology, Risk Management, Compliance, Operations, and Customer Services. As banking is a highly co-operative structure it is necessary that staff work together by communicating information, co-ordinating action and supporting organizational objectives. Team dynamics theory indicates that teamwork cohesion and collaboration are important predictors of organizational effectiveness — indicators of good communication, trust, knowledge sharing and job performance (Mathieu et al 2008).

Team cohesion is the extent to which individual employees are drawn to their team and are eager to stay in that group. Per the Team Dynamics material, cohesion is driven by: frequency of member interaction, group success, a clear common goal, group size, and facing obstacles. Higher cohesion → higher individual commitment, communication and performance — though too much cohesion can raise conformity pressure and reduce internal criticism.

There are several systems in WBC that foster cross-departmental collaboration: organization-wide communication systems, agile/flexible working environments, cross-functional teams, and integrated risk management. High interaction frequency is one of the strongest predictors of cohesion as it strengthens interpersonal relationships and trust (Beal et al. 2003). WBC's commitment to common organisational goals (customer satisfaction, digital transformation, operational excellence, regulatory compliance) is also conducive to cohesion — cohesion improves when members share and achieve common goals.

Keeping teams coherent across departmental boundaries is difficult. WBC's large size and complexity can pose communication barriers across specialised teams (e.g. technology valuing innovation vs. compliance/risk valuing governance), leading to conflict, confusion and delayed decisions. Effective teamwork requires a shared organizational mental model — shared understanding of objectives, roles and processes (Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006). Hybrid/remote working poses further challenges to cohesion, as remote teams are less likely to establish trusting relationships and tend to reduce interpersonal communication (Allen, Golden and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015).

WBC implements several strategies to maintain cohesion: leadership training (trust, responsibility, collaboration), cross-functional projects (breaking silos), and team-building activities. High cohesion correlates with members' capacity to communicate openly and collaborate successfully (Salas, Sims and Burke 2005). Overall WBC's systems are effective at enabling cohesion and cross-departmental cooperation, but organizational complexity, departmental heterogeneity and the hybrid format bring potential problems. Continuing to promote trust, communication and shared goals will improve cohesion and long-term performance.

## 📄 04-team-report/Team_Trust_3b_FINAL.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Team Report]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

# Team Trust at Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC)

Communication problems and team trust are closely connected, but trust deserves attention on its own. It shapes how teams at Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) cooperate, share information and perform. This section looks at what team trust consists of, how it develops in dispersed teams, and what that means for WBC.

Trust usually rests on three things: a person's integrity, their benevolence, and their ability (Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman 1995; Robbins and Judge 2023). Employees are more willing to rely on a colleague or manager they see as honest, as genuinely concerned for their wellbeing, and as competent at the work. A weakness in any one of these can undermine it. WBC staff might doubt whether another department will give them accurate information, or feel that a manager cares more about targets than about the people meeting them. Trust is also slow to build and easy to lose, so one communication failure or a single episode of perceived unfairness can damage a relationship that then takes a long time to repair (Greenberg and Baron 2008).

Hybrid and remote work make this harder. Distributed employees have fewer of the informal, in-person moments that normally let trust grow, so it is more difficult to sustain than in a co-located team. Trust also matters more for team performance in virtual settings than in face-to-face ones (Breuer, Hüffmeier, and Hertel 2016; Cascio and Shurygailo 2003). To get work done before close relationships have formed, dispersed teams often rely on "swift trust," a provisional trust based on shared roles, professional norms and common goals rather than personal familiarity (Meyerson, Weick, and Kramer 1996; Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). For WBC, the practical implication is that clear roles, dependable processes and consistent leadership can do much of the work that face-to-face contact would otherwise do.

Trust also underpins psychological safety, the belief that an employee can raise a concern, admit a mistake or challenge a decision without fear of punishment (Edmondson 1999). When trust is low, staff in a heavily regulated bank may stay quiet about errors or operational risks, which narrows problem-solving and widens compliance exposure. Leadership is decisive here. Leaders who act consistently, communicate openly and treat people fairly create the conditions for honest discussion and genuine teamwork (Yukl and Gardner 2020). Building trust therefore supports WBC's operational performance, risk management and resilience, since a high-trust culture tends to produce faster decisions, better collaboration and employees who stay engaged.

These dynamics affect WBC day to day. When employees trust one another, information moves faster and decisions are made without constant second-guessing, which matters in a bank that has to be quick and accurate at the same time. When trust is low, people double-check, withhold information or route it through slower formal channels, and coordination between functions such as compliance, risk and customer service starts to slow (Robbins and Judge 2023). Because communication and the trust beneath it influence motivation, collaboration and performance (Yukl and Gardner 2020), a trust deficit has concrete costs: slower service, a weaker customer experience and higher operating expenses.

The longer-term picture is similar. Sustainable performance depends on keeping capable people and keeping them engaged, and trust runs through both. In remote, high-pressure conditions, weak trust and the isolation common to virtual work are associated with more stress, lower satisfaction and a stronger intention to leave (Zakaria, Amelinckx, and Wilemon 2004). For WBC, trust that stayed low over time would mean higher turnover, loss of institutional knowledge, and a workforce less willing to raise the risks the bank most needs to hear about. A high-trust culture supports the stable, transparent and accountable environment that sustainable organisations depend on.

This connects directly to the United Nations Global Compact, and to Principle 10, which calls on businesses to work against corruption in all its forms (United Nations Global Compact 2024). The link runs through psychological safety. Anti-corruption depends on employees being willing to report misconduct, errors and operational risk, and they do that only when they trust that speaking up will not cost them. Westpac's own history shows what is at stake: in 2020 the bank agreed to a record A$1.3 billion penalty for more than 23 million breaches of anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing law (AUSTRAC 2020), failures of monitoring and escalation that have since shaped its focus on conduct and risk culture (Westpac Banking Corporation 2024). Where trust is weak, staff stay silent, problems go unreported, and unethical behaviour has more room to take hold. Strengthening trust makes transparency and ethical conduct far more likely, and keeps WBC closer to Principle 10.

Several measures could help WBC strengthen trust and stay aligned with this principle. One is leadership development focused on consistency, fairness and open communication, so that managers model the behaviour trust is built on (Yukl and Gardner 2020). A second is clear, protected speak-up channels that give employees a safe way to raise concerns, reinforcing psychological safety and anti-corruption together. A third is firmer role clarity and reliable processes, which help swift trust hold across hybrid and dispersed teams (Cascio and Shurygailo 2003; Meyerson, Weick, and Kramer 1996). Regular cross-team and in-person contact would also help rebuild the informal interaction through which trust between people usually grows.

# WBC_Collaboration_Cohesion_Condensed_FINAL

> Конвертировано из `WBC_Collaboration_Cohesion_Condensed_FINAL.docx`

# WBC Collaboration and Team Cohesion Across Departments

The Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) depends on an array of departments to cooperate and communicate to function optimally; these include Retail Banking, Business Banking, Technology, Risk Management, Compliance, Operations and Customer Service. Team dynamics theory posits that cohesion and collaboration are significant determinants of the quality of communication, trust, information sharing and organizational performance (Mathieu et al. 2008).

WBC utilizes various measures to foster working-togetherness such as: enterprise communication systems, agile way of working, multi-functional teams, and integrated risk management systems, etc. By utilizing these kinds of ways and mechanisms, departments can communicate information with each other smoothly and can collaborate together. "Frequent interaction also serves to build up trust and relationship among individuals." (Beal et al. 2003)

Working toward common organizational objectives also facilitates cooperation. WBC's objectives: (a) customer satisfaction; (b) digital transformation; (c) operational excellence and (d) compliance, require the coordination of different departments. Team cohesiveness is likely to grow when people perceive common goals and feel a shared sense of accomplishment.

These are all advantages of this approach however cohesion across functional boundaries is proving to be more difficult. The large size and scope of the WBC could perhaps create communication problems between specific teams, technology teams could have priorities related to innovation and risk & compliance teams have a focus on control & regulation. In this vein theory states that a shared mental model is required to ensure a team works efficiently together (Kozlowski and Ilgen 2006).

Hybrid and remote work arrangements have an impact on cohesion too. Virtual settings, where there is less communication and relationship building opportunities between colleagues, can lower trust and cohesion (Allen, Golden, and Shockley 2015; Gilson et al. 2015).

Despite the challenges, WBC is effective at building cohesion via leadership action, cross-departmental teams, team building exercises and common goals related to performance. These actions effectively overcome departmental barriers and develop better relationships between departments. Cohesive teams communicate well and get results (Salas, Sims and Burke 2005).

On the whole WBC uses effective systems to support collaboration and team cohesion, but organisational complexity and the move towards hybrid working needs focus on the communication, trust and common goals element to support long term performance.

> Разбор рабочего WhatsApp-чата «BUS293 assignment». **Обновлено по экспорту от 15 июня 2026 (вечер), 750 строк.** Полная история работы команды над групповым отчётом. Источники: переписка (полный текст), голосовые (расшифрованы локально), документы, фото. Последние версии секций — в `материалы/документы/`.

**Задание:** BUS293 Team Report (групповой, **30%**, дедлайн **Session 8**)
**Компания:** Westpac Banking Corporation (WBC) — ASX200
**Тема:** Team Dynamics (глава 8 учебника)
**Группа:** **11**

## ✅ Требования к отчёту (важно — чтобы не потерять баллы)

- **Объём:** 3000 слов всего (body > 2000); затем **сжать весь отчёт до ~2500 слов**.
- **Ссылки:** **30+** на HD, **8+ на каждого**. Стиль **Chicago** (in-text + reference list). Кавычки для цитат.
- **Источники:** только **scholarly / peer-reviewed** вторичные (журналы, академические книги) — **не** обычные веб-статьи.
- **Каждую секцию** строить по 6-частному каркасу (гайд Onethu, `материалы/документы/...Structure breakdown.pdf`):
  1. Определить/объяснить challenge → 2. Привязать теории/концепции → 3. Влияние на текущую performance WBC → 4. Влияние на sustainability → 5. Связь с ≥1 из 10 принципов **UN Global Compact** → 6. 3–4 потенциальных решения.
- **AI запрещён** (= academic misconduct, см. ниже).
- **Каждую среду до 20:00 (Dubai)** — выкладывать на Team Discussion Forum доказательство прогресса, иначе штраф к оценке.

# Nations United: Urgent Solutions for Urgent Times

This is a very important story. The important story. In the 75 years since the United Nations was founded, the human race has never had to face a set of challenges like we do right now. But together, we can overcome them. COVID-19 has been likened to an X-ray, exposing fractures in the skeleton of the societies we have built... a world with great inequality, which must be righted... and a world which must win the battle against climate catastrophe. The whole planet is at stake, so this is a moment to recognize that the way we have been moving leads nowhere and that we need to change course. Lions have reclaimed the roads in Kruger National Park. In Venice, the canals run clear once more. And across Italy, dolphins have returned. If you look at the response of people to COVID-19, people dramatically changed their lives. Delhi on Tuesday recorded the hottest day... -Temperatures... -Spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit... Climate change is here now and it is killing people right now - the people who are looking at it right in the face. The next eight to ten years is going to determine the quality of life for the next 100 to 200 years. We all watched with amazement when exactly one year ago, young people from all over the world took to the streets to express their feeling that we're not doing enough about climate change... Today, we take a stand for Mother Nature. That we're not treating it like the emergency it is. It's a year later now. Have we done enough? No, we have not. And climate change is only part of this story. Our rainforests are disappearing at an extraordinary rate. One football field of rainforest is destroyed every six seconds. One million plant and animal species are on the brink of extinction. By 2050, there will be more plastic in the oceans than fish. And so, climate change and our treatment of the natural world are colliding and exacerbating each other to create a perfect storm. This cannot go on. You know it, I know it, and we know what we need to do. We need to reduce global emissions by 50% by 2030. To do this, we need a rapid but just transition to renewable energy. That means an end to the building of new coal power stations, and an end to the subsidizing of fossil fuels. Governments should also shift the tax burden from payrolls to carbon. Taxing carbon rather than people will increase output and employment while reducing emissions. And we need to stop deforestation in its tracks - planting trees instead of chopping them down. We need to think about what we eat and how we produce food, embracing healthy, nutritious diets, sustainable farming methods and reducing food waste. The climate crisis is an opportunity. Renewable energy is cheaper than fossil fuels. Thousands of businesses are working to go carbon neutral and the opportunity to generate clean, safe and decent jobs is enormous. The passion for protest can turn into a passion for changing all of our behavior to create a better, safer, just, sustainable world. The big question we have to ask ourselves now is this... This is largely determined by their circumstances at birth and these high levels of inequality work against better opportunities for all, opportunities that could change the world. I want to tell you a story... about 1999. I used to teach people how to write computer programs... and I had a very, you know, flash office and everything. And just outside of these offices, there was this large, sprawling urban slum... full of children. So, one day I tried an experiment. I made an opening in the boundary wall that separated my offices from the slum, and then I fixed a computer so that from the other side of the wall, you could see the computer and a touch pad. On the first day, we saw this eight-year-old boy... teaching a six-year-old girl how to surf. How on earth did he figure that out? How did he know what the computer was doing? Three months after I had first put that computer in the wall, the children said they wanted a faster processor and a better mouse. I asked them, “How on earth do you know these words? I repeated the hole-in-the-wall experiment for five years across the length and breadth of India. In a village 300 miles away from Delhi, one girl is explaining to the other girl what a neuron is. Connecting every school, every person to the Internet... this can be done. The recovery from COVID must lead to an economy that works for everyone. Let's start with tax. We have widespread tax concessions, tax avoidance and tax evasion, which means that there's so much less money for all the crucial things. Many developing countries are weighed down by historical debts, spending more money on debt repayments than they are spending on healthcare. And then, there's the importance of global investment in peace. The peace dividend for the world is immeasurable, and we must break the vicious cycle of corruption and increase the power of the people to keep check on the people in power. A free independent media and responsible social media platforms that encourage healthy debate. Equality unleashes the potential of everyone to improve their own lives and contribute to the lives of everyone else. "Whatever it is... coronavirus has made the mighty kneel and brought the world to a halt like nothing else could. Our minds are still racing back and forth longing for a return to 'normality,' trying to stitch our future to our past and refusing to acknowledge the rupture. But the rupture exists. And in the midst of this terrible despair, it offers us a chance to rethink the doomsday machine we have built for ourselves. Nothing could be worse than a return to normality. Historically, pandemics have forced humans to break with the past and imagine their world anew. This one is no different. It's a portal, a gateway between one world and the next. We could choose to walk through it, dragging the carcasses of our prejudice and hatred, our avarice, our databanks and dead ideas... or we can walk through it lightly, with little luggage, ready to imagine another world. ## 📄 05-csr-sustainability/SDGs_Booklet_Web_En.pdf.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) - Sustainability]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

_📥 Скачано из Moodle автоматически (2026-07-13); конвертация: markitdown. Возможны ошибки распознавания — оригинал: SDGs_Booklet_Web_En.pdf._

# SDG Goals Booklet

IN THE YEAR 2015, LEADERS FROM 193 COUNTRIES OF THE WORLD

CAME TOGETHER TO FACE THE FUTURE.

And what they saw was daunting. Famines. Drought. Wars. Plagues. Poverty.

Not just in some faraway place, but in their own cities and towns and villages.

They knew things didn’t have to be this way. They knew we had enough

food to feed the world, but that it wasn’t getting shared. They knew there

were medicines for HIV and other diseases, but they cost a lot. They knew

that earthquakes and floods were inevitable, but that the high death

tolls were not.

They also knew that billions of people worldwide shared their hope for a

better future.

So leaders from these countries created a plan called the Sustainable

Development Goals (SDGs). This set of 17 goals imagines a future just 15 years

off that would be rid of poverty and hunger, and safe from the worst effects of

climate change. It’s an ambitious plan.

But there’s ample evidence that we can succeed. In the past 15 years, the

international community cut extreme poverty in half.

Now we can finish the job.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is one of the leading

organizations working to fulfil the SDGs by the year 2030. Present in nearly

170 countries and territories, we help nations make the Goals a reality.

We also champion the Goals so that people everywhere know how to

do their part.

UNDP is proud to continue as a leader in this global movement.

Learn about the Sustainable Development Goals.  What’s your Goal?


END EXTREME POVERTY IN ALL FORMS
BY 2030.

Yes, it’s an ambitious goal—but we believe it can be done. In 2000, the

world committed to halving the number of people living in extreme

poverty by the year 2015 and we met this goal. However, more than

800 million people around the world still live on less than $1.25 a day—

that’s about the equivalent of the entire population of Europe living in

extreme poverty. Now it’s time to build on what we learned and end

poverty altogether.


END HUNGER, ACHIEVE FOOD SECURITY
AND IMPROVED NUTRITION AND PROMOTE
SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE

In the past 20 years, hunger has dropped by almost half. Many

countries that used to suffer from famine and hunger can now

meet the nutritional needs of their most vulnerable people. It’s an

incredible accomplishment. Now we can go further and end hunger

and malnutrition once and for all. That means doing things such as

promoting sustainable agriculture and supporting small farmers. It’s a tall

order. But for the sake of the nearly 1 out of every 9 people on earth who

go to bed hungry every night, we’ve got to try. Imagine a world where

everyone has access to sufficient and nutritious food all year round.

Together, we can make that a reality by 2030.


ENSURE HEALTHY LIVES AND PROMOTE
WELL-BEING FOR ALL AT ALL AGES

We all know how important it is to be in good health. Our health affects

everything from how much we enjoy life to what work we can perform.

That’s why there’s a Goal to make sure everyone has health coverage

and access to safe and effective medicines and vaccines. In the 25

years before the SDGs, we made big strides—preventable child deaths

dropped by more than half, and maternal mortality went down by

almost as much. And yet some other numbers remain tragically high, like

the fact that 6 million children die every year before their fifth birthday,

or that AIDS is the leading cause of death for adolescents in sub-Saharan

Africa. We have the means to turn that around and make good health

more than just a wish.


ENSURE INCLUSIVE AND EQUITABLE QUALITY
EDUCATION AND PROMOTE LIFELONG
LEARNING OPPORTUNITIES FOR ALL

First, the bad news on education. Poverty, armed conflict and other

emergencies keep many, many kids around the world out of school. In

fact, kids from the poorest households are four times more likely to be

out of school than those of the richest households. Now for some good

news. Since 2000, there has been enormous progress on the goal to

provide primary education to all children worldwide: the total enrolment

rate in developing regions has reached 91%. By measures in any school,

that’s a good grade. Now, let’s get an even better grade for all kids,

and achieve the goal of universal primary and secondary education,

affordable vocational training, access to higher education and more.


ACHIEVE GENDER EQUALITY AND
EMPOWER ALL WOMEN AND GIRLS

We can celebrate the great progress the world has made in becoming

more prosperous and fair. But there’s a shadow to the celebration. In

just about every way, women and girls lag behind. There are still gross

inequalities in work and wages, lots of unpaid “women’s work” such as

child care and domestic work, and discrimination in public decision-

making. But there are grounds for hope. More girls are in school now

compared to in 2000. Most regions have reached gender parity in

primary education. The percentage of women getting paid for their work

is on the rise. The Sustainable Development Goals aim to build on these

achievements to ensure that there is an end to discrimination against

women and girls everywhere.


ENSURE AVAILABILITY AND SUSTAINABLE
MANAGEMENT OF WATER AND SANITATION
FOR ALL

Everyone on earth should have access to safe and affordable drinking

water. That’s the goal for 2030. While many people take clean drinking

water and sanitation for granted, many others don’t. Water scarcity

affects more than 40 percent of people around the world, and that

number is projected to go even higher as a result of climate change.

If we continue the path we’re on, by 2050 at least one in four people

are likely to be affected by recurring water shortages. But we can take

a new path—more international cooperation, protecting wetlands

and rivers, sharing water-treatment technologies—that leads to

accomplishing this Goal.


ENSURE ACCESS TO AFFORDABLE, RELIABLE,
SUSTAINABLE AND MODERN ENERGY FOR
ALL

Between 1990 and 2010, the number of people with access to electricity

increased by 1.7 billion. That’s progress to be proud of. And yet as the

world’s population continues to rise, still more people will need cheap

energy to light their homes and streets, use phones and computers,

and do their everyday business. How we get that energy is at issue; fossil

fuels and greenhouse gas emissions are making drastic changes in the

climate, leading to big problems on every continent. Instead, we can

become more energy-efficient and invest in clean energy sources such

as solar and wind. That way we’ll meet electricity needs and protect the

environment. How’s that for a balancing act?


PROMOTE SUSTAINED, INCLUSIVE AND
SUSTAINABLE ECONOMIC GROWTH, FULL
AND PRODUCTIVE EMPLOYMENT AND
DECENT WORK FOR ALL

An important part of economic growth is that people have jobs that

pay enough to support themselves and their families. The good news

is that the middle class is growing worldwide—almost tripling in size

in developing countries in the last 25 years, to more than a third of the

population. But today, job growth is not keeping pace with the growing

labour force. Things don’t have to be that way. We can promote policies

that encourage entrepreneurship and job creation. We can eradicate

forced labour, slavery and human trafficking. And in the end we can

achieve the goal of decent work for all women and men by 2030.


BUILD RESILIENT INFRASTRUCTURE,
PROMOTE INCLUSIVE AND SUSTAINABLE
INDUSTRIALIZATION AND FOSTER
INNOVATION

Technological progress helps us address big global challenges such as

creating jobs and becoming more energy efficient. For example, the

world is becoming ever more interconnected and prosperous thanks to

the internet. The more connected we are, the more we can all benefit

from the wisdom and contributions of people everywhere on earth.  And

yet four billion people have no way of getting online, the vast majority

of them in developing countries. The more we invest in innovation

and infrastructure, the better off we’ll all be. Bridging the digital divide,

promoting sustainable industries, and investing in scientific research and

innovation are all important ways to facilitate sustainable development.


REDUCE INEQUALITY WITHIN AND AMONG
COUNTRIES

It’s an old story: the rich get richer, and the poor get poorer. The divide

has never been starker. We can and must adopt policies that create

opportunity for everyone, regardless of who they are or where they

come from. Income inequality is a global problem that requires global

solutions. That means improving the regulation of financial markets

and institutions, sending development aid where it is most needed

and helping people migrate safely so they can pursue opportunities.

Together, we can now change the direction of the old story of inequality.


MAKE CITIES AND HUMAN SETTLEMENTS
INCLUSIVE, SAFE, RESILIENT AND
SUSTAINABLE

If you’re like most people, you live in a city. More than half the world’s

population now lives in cities, and that figure will go to about two-thirds

of humanity by the year 2050. Cities are getting bigger. In 1990 there

were ten “mega-cities” with 10 million inhabitants or more. In 2014, there

were 28 mega-cities, home to 453 million people. Incredible, huh? A lot

of people love cities; they’re centers of culture and business and life. The

thing is, they’re also often centers of extreme poverty. To make cities

sustainable for all, we can create good, affordable public housing. We

can upgrade slum settlements. We can invest in public transport, create

green spaces, and get a broader range of people involved in urban

planning decisions. That way, we can keep the things we love about

cities, and change the things we don’t.


ENSURE SUSTAINABLE CONSUMPTION AND
PRODUCTION PATTERNS

Some people use a lot of stuff, and some people use very little—in fact,

a big share of the world population is consuming too little to meet even

their basic needs. Instead, we can have a world where everybody gets

what they need to survive and thrive. And we can consume in a way

that preserves our natural resources so that our children can enjoy them,

and their children and their children after that. The hard part is how to

achieve that goal. We can manage our natural resources more efficiently

and dispose of toxic waste better. Cut per capita food waste in half

globally. Get businesses and consumers to reduce and recycle waste.

And help countries that have typically not consumed a lot to move

towards more responsible consumption patterns.


TAKE URGENT ACTION TO COMBAT CLIMATE
CHANGE AND ITS IMPACTS

Every country in the world is seeing the drastic effects of climate

change, some more than others. On average, the annual losses just

from earthquakes, tsunamis, tropical cyclones and flooding count in the

hundreds of billions of dollars. We can reduce the loss of life and property

by helping more vulnerable regions—such as land-locked countries

and island states—become more resilient. It is still possible, with the

political will and technological measures, to limit the increase in global

mean temperature to two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels—

and thus avoid the worst effects of climate change. The Sustainable

Development Goals lay out a way for countries to work together to meet

this urgent challenge.


CONSERVE AND SUSTAINABLY USE THE
OCEANS, SEAS AND MARINE RESOURCES
FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT

The oceans make human life possible. Their temperature, their chemistry,

their currents, their life forms. For one thing, more than 3 billion people

depend on marine and coastal diversity for their livelihoods. But today

we are seeing nearly a third of the world’s fish stocks overexploited.

That’s not a sustainable way of life. Even people who live nowhere near

the ocean can’t live without it. Oceans absorb about 30 percent of the

carbon dioxide that humans produce; but we’re producing more carbon

dioxide than ever before and that makes the oceans more acidic—26%

more, since the start of the industrial revolution. Our trash doesn’t help

either—13,000 pieces of plastic litter on every square kilometer of ocean.

Sounds bad, right? Don’t despair! The Sustainable Development Goals

indicate targets for managing and protecting life below water.


PROTECT, RESTORE AND PROMOTE
SUSTAINABLE USE OF TERRESTRIAL
ECOSYSTEMS, SUSTAINABLY MANAGE
FORESTS, COMBAT DESERTIFICATION, AND
HALT AND REVERSE LAND DEGRADATION
AND HALT BIODIVERSITY LOSS

Humans and other animals rely on other forms of life on land for food,

clean air, clean water, and as a means of combatting climate change.

Plant life makes up 80% of the human diet. Forests, which cover 30%

of the Earth’s surface, help keep the air and water clean and the Earth’s

climate in balance. That’s not to mention they’re home to millions of

animal species. But the land and life on it are in trouble. Arable land

is disappearing 30 to 35 times faster than it has historically. Deserts

are spreading. Animal breeds are going extinct. We can turn these

trends around. Fortunately, the Sustainable Development Goals aim to

conserve and restore the use of terrestrial ecosystems such as forests,

wetlands, drylands and mountains by 2030.


PROMOTE PEACEFUL AND INCLUSIVE
SOCIETIES FOR SUSTAINABLE
DEVELOPMENT, PROVIDE ACCESS TO
JUSTICE FOR ALL AND BUILD EFFECTIVE,
ACCOUNTABLE AND INCLUSIVE
INSTITUTIONS AT ALL LEVELS

How can a country develop—how can people eat and teach and learn

and work and raise families—without peace? And how can a country

have peace without justice, without human rights, without government

based on the rule of law? Some parts of the world enjoy relative peace

and justice, and may come to take it for granted. Other parts seem to

be plagued by armed conflict, crime, torture and exploitation, all of

which hinders their development. The goal of peace and justice is one

for all countries to strive towards. The Sustainable Development Goals

aim to reduce all forms of violence and propose that governments

and communities find lasting solutions to conflict and insecurity. That

means strengthening the rule of law, reducing the flow of illicit arms,

and bringing developing countries more into the center of institutions

of global governance.


STRENGTHEN THE MEANS OF
IMPLEMENTATION AND REVITALIZE THE
GLOBAL PARTNERSHIP FOR SUSTAINABLE
DEVELOPMENT

The Sustainable Development Goals are pretty big to-do list, don’t you

think? In fact, it’s so big, you may just want to throw your hands up in the

air. “Forget it! Can’t be done! Why even try!” But we’ve got a lot going for

us. The world is more interconnected today than ever before, thanks to

the internet, travel and global institutions. There’s a growing consensus

about the need to work together to stop climate change. And the

Sustainable Development Goals are no small matter either. 193 countries

agreed on these goals. Pretty incredible, isn’t it? 193 countries agreeing

on anything? The final goal lays out a way for nations to work together to

achieve all the other Goals.


?

WHAT CAN
I DO TO HELP

There are many ways to show your support and help us reach

the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. Here are a few :

Make a donation
Money doesn’t just make the world go around; it’s also the most direct

way to reduce and eradicate all forms of poverty.

Start a fundraiser
Fundraising is a great way to raise money, create awareness, and inspire

others. Plus, it’s fun!

Go shopping
Visit shop.undp.org for SDG merchandise, and show off the goals you’re

most passionate about.

Spread the word
Search for @UNDP on Twitter, Facebook and Instagram, and share the

content you love.

To donate or learn more about fundraising, visit undp.org/takeaction


NOTES

## 📄 05-csr-sustainability/fs_sustainabledevelopmentgoals_may2018.pdf.md

Связь: [[BUS293 — Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) - Sustainability]] · _материал темы (курс BUS293)_

_📥 Скачано из Moodle автоматически (2026-07-13); конвертация: markitdown. Возможны ошибки распознавания — оригинал: fs_sustainabledevelopmentgoals_may2018.pdf._

# SDG handout

http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment

visit.un.org

       Facebook: UN Visitor Centre


What are Sustainable Development Goals?

The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), also known as the Global Goals, are a shared agenda to end poverty, fight inequality & injustice, and
protect the planet.

The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), adopted in 2000 were aimed at an array of issues that included slashing poverty, hunger, disease,
gender inequality, and access to water and sanitation. Enormous progress has been made on the MDGs, showing the value of a unifying agenda
underpinned by goals and targets. Despite this success though, the indignity of poverty has not been ended for all.

The new SDGs, and the broader sustainability agenda, go much further than the MDGs, addressing the root causes of poverty and the universal
need for development that works for all people. The SDGs will now finish the job of the MDGS, and ensure that no one is left behind.

There are 17 goals specifically:

Goal 1. End poverty in all its forms everywhere
Goal 2. End hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition and promote sustainable agriculture
Goal 3. Ensure healthy lives and promote wellbeing for all at all ages
Goal 4. Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all
Goal 5. Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls
Goal 6. Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
Goal 7. Ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all
Goal 8. Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all
Goal 9. Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation
Goal 10. Reduce inequality within and among countries
Goal 11. Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable
Goal 12. Ensure sustainable consumption and production patterns
Goal 13. Take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts
Goal 14. Conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development
Goal 15. Protect, restore and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, and halt

and reverse land degradation and halt biodiversity loss

Goal 16. Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable

and inclusive institutions at all levels

Goal 17. Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

# 2026-05-11-bus293-tmd2026-bus293-obm-week-2__Prep-notes-week 2

> Конвертировано из `2026-05-11-bus293-tmd2026-bus293-obm-week-2__Prep-notes-week 2.docx`

# Organisational Theory and Behaviour-Week 2

## Introduction to Teams and Groups

Explain that teams are more structured than general groups because members share accountability and work toward organisational goals. Example: A hospital emergency response team works together with defined roles, unlike a casual friendship group at work.

## Advantages of Teams

Discuss how teams combine skills and perspectives to improve decisions and innovation. Example: A marketing team combining designers, analysts, and writers can create stronger campaigns than one individual.

## Disadvantages of Teams

Explain coordination losses and social loafing. Example: In a university group assignment, some members may rely on others to complete the work.

## Types of Teams

Describe self-directed, multicultural, and virtual teams. Example: Remote software developers collaborating online form a virtual team.

## Team Effectiveness Model

Explain that effective teams benefit both organisations and members. Example: Companies with supportive leadership often have higher employee satisfaction and productivity.

## Team Design Factors

Describe how tasks and interdependence influence teamwork. Example: In manufacturing, one worker’s output may become another worker’s input.

## Team Composition

Explain the Five C’s and diversity. Example: Diverse healthcare teams improve patient care by combining different expertise.

## Team States

Discuss norms, cohesion, trust, and efficacy. Example: Sports teams often perform better when players trust one another.

## Tuckman’s Stages

Walk through forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Example: New project teams usually experience conflict before becoming productive.

## Team Building

Discuss brainstorming and trust-building activities. Example: Team retreats can improve communication and relationships.

## Decision Making Challenges

Explain groupthink and evaluation apprehension. Example: Employees may avoid challenging a manager’s idea during meetings.

## Improving Decision Making

Describe brainwriting and nominal group technique. Example: Anonymous idea sharing often encourages quieter employees to contribute.

## Conclusion

Summarise that successful teams require planning, trust, communication, and positive norms. Encourage students to apply these concepts in assignments and workplaces.
